tALL RIGHTS RISERVED.I

know the interest is small, but I can't pay it. I expected a remittance a few days ago, but aave been disappointed. - The- pater has had few business reverses. No—no, I don't mean that. I mean that I—l—oh ! I can- not tell you. I can only ask you to be patient." "Look here, young man, when you were in my office I saw at once that you were a simpleton in these matters. It's pretty clear to me that if something is not done, and done quickly, I'll have to whistle for my capital, to say nothing about the interest Now, you'll have to find the money somehow. HOw, I don't know and don't care. That's your business. But, mark me, if it is not paid by to-morrow evening I'll make it -hot for you." "For Heaven's sake be merciful, Mr. Duveen," cried Chorlton, apparently in great distress. "It would be ruin if the trouble leaked out." "Trouble or no trouble, it will be out within forty-eight hours if I'm not paid. What do you propose to do?" "I don't know. I'm at my wits' end. I'll rite to you to-night. But, for Heaven's sake, don't take any steps until I have had another chance of pleading with you. Don't." "I've given you my ultimatum. Ark% re- member, young man, you're not dealing with a fool. What I've said I'll do, I'll do. 13y to- morrow night! Remember!" And he departed. And Chorlton laughed.

times previously, was sent to prison for three months, with hard _labour.. . . - WORKMEN'S SUP E S V ANISHED —A sequel to what Superintendent Williamson termed a mean, con-- temptible, cowardly theft, was heard; when John Grounds, a labourer, of no fixed abode, was charged with stealing two workmen's suppers from Bewsey Forge on the 14th August.—Supt. Williamson said that prisoner had no right on the Forge premises, and he would not be toler- ated for a moment if anyone saw him enter. The previous night John Woodall, 49, Pierpoint- street, left his supper near a furnace in the Forge, and a few moments later he discovered it had gone. He informed the foreman, and, after a search, they came across prisoner con- suming the repast in the works. Another work- man, Henry Hunter, Longford-street, placed his supper in a basket by the boiler. Prisoner took this and was eating it when caught. The piece of paper and handkerchief in which the suppers were wrapped, were found near to the prisoner. P.C. Grubb was sent for, and in answer to the first charge prisoner said: "It is a tidy price " (eightpence). In answer to the, second, he said, "It is very dear stuff." The foreman was con- tinually receiving complaints of men having their meals stolen. It was a mean, contemptible cowardly theft—ln answer to the Mayor, pri- soner said he had worked at the Forge.—Super- intendent Williamson: They will take good care he does not work there again.—Prisoner : I was very hungry at the time.—Superintendent Wil- •liamson said the prisoner had previously got three months for stealing scrap brass from the Forge and he had been discharged. On the 29th May he had had three months for stealing leather from a tannery where he was employed. —Grounds was sent to prison for two months, with hard labour. HUSBAND v. WlFE.—Matthew Thomas Knowles, 103, Bramhall-street, was summoned for assault- ing his wife, Sarah, of 5, Lloyd-street.—Mrs. Knowles said that her husband had come home on the Bth August swearing and cursing, because she had not got up, and got his breakfast ready. She had been up all. night with the babies and had over-slept- herself. Her 'husband got hold of her throat and tried to choke her. He hit her in the face twice. He had smashed all the pic- tures in the house.—Knowles was bound over for six months and ordered to pay the costs. WHEN WOMEN FALL Our.—Polly Walder and Agnes Walder, Buttermarket-street, were sum- moned for having assaulted Mary Ann. Fair- hurst, 5, Little Weint.-:Mr. Swallow, who ap- peared for the complainant, said that Mrs. Fair- hurst was talking to a neighbour, when Mrs. Welder came, out of her, shop and commenced using abusive language. 'Mrs. Fairhurst took no notice. Agnes Walder came to her mother and pulled Mrs.. Fairhurst's hair, and, struck her a violent blow. The mother also got hold of complainant by the arm and struck her sev- eral times.—Agnes Welder, who had pleaded guilty, was bound over for six months and ordered to pay 10s. costs. The case against Mrs. Walder was dismissed.

div.head: HE MONEYLENDER'S RECEIPT.
div.p: HE MONEYLENDER'S RECEIPT.
BY HEitRIOT ELLIOT
Author of "A 'Voice from the Dead," "The 11,5 p.m. Special," "His It Home Signal," "Craven'a Duty," "Just in Time," &c.
"How much does he say you owe him?" asked Chorlton.

"Two hundred pounds," I replied. "And do you mean to say that he holds a promissory note from you undertaking to re,. pay him lay to-morrow?" "Yes. tut I swear to you, Chorlton, that the note is a forgery, and that Duveen is a swindler. However, it would be utterly use- less to contest the validity of the document. I could not dispute the signature. It is such an excellent and exact reproduction of my own. And then it is witnessed by Duveen's clerk."
"You say you've had previous transactions with him? "
" I answered, "I borrowed two separate amounts of one hundred younds and one hundred and fifty from him last term. I repaid in full when the governor sent me &Ey. second allowance."

" The trouble is this, Roycroft," said Choriton. "You've been going the pace like a young, fool for some time. It's common knowledge. To contest this promissory note would lead to statements in court which would prove that you had been in financial difficnhies before, and that fact alone would lend some little weight to the veracity of Duveen's claim. And then, again, what about the discredit of the proceedings? What of your pater's anger if he knew? What of the probability of being 'sent down'?" "Oh, Chorlton !" I cried, "the disgrace must not become known. They would be broken-hearted at home. The governor— Oh: what's to be done? 'What's to be done?"

I was beside myself with impotent rage and fury. I had only been at Oxford. three years, .and expected to take my degree very soon. I received a liberal allowance from home, but, fool that I was, I had exceeded it, and in &- moment of desperation had 'fallen a victim to the seductive attractions of a 'moneylender. Two transactions had enabled me to weather the storm, and by rigid economy I was at last out of debt and, as I thought, out of danger. But the old adage had played me false. Duveen, the villain, held a promissory note for two hundred pounds, and would not allow me any extended credit. The unblushing scamp intended to act the part of Shylock with a veiwance. But the galling part of the whole business was that 'I had not signed the note. It was the neatest forgery imaginable. But who would believe me? My previous transactions would condemn me. Like a simpleton I had confided to Duveen that if the fact that I was borrowing money came to the ears of my people I would be ruined. He was taking advantage of this knowledge now. I appealed to my friend Chorlton. My parents had asked him to take a watchful in- terest in me. Evidently they had not much confidence in me. And no wonder. If I had told Chorlton all my troubles sooner I might have escaped the subsequent consequences. "Look here, .ycroft," Chorlton said, after a long and reflective pause, "I've been very careful of late, and, fortunately for you. I can settle this debt." " Oh, thanks, Chorlton, thanks!" I cried, overcome with Joy; "I will repay you before the close of the term. You are good:" "Don't bother your head about the repay- ment, old chap. I'll repay myself. This Duveen is evidently a scoundrel, and I'll snake it my business to clear him out of Ox- -ford before he's much older.

"When settling with Ifin," he continued, "demand a receipt as well as the return of the promissory note. Bring both documents to me. Keep your own counsel. Say nothing to anyone." "Rieht, Chorlton, dear old chap. know how to thank you." "Your best thanks Will be not to make a 'fool of yourself again," he replied, gently but Erm_ly.
I don'

The rebuke was merited, and I was ashamed. I repaid the two hundred pounds on the fol- lowing daY, much to Duveen's astonithment. I was no match for him at all. I fulminated and raved, and, as usual, made an ass of my- self. The wretch listened to me—an amused and innocent expression on his face. When I had ceased my tirade he calmly suggested that it would be wise if I bridled my tongue a little, as there was such a thing as defamation of character. With a mocking smile he bade me good - morning, adding ironically that ha would be delighted to execute any further little transactions I might contemplate. I handed the promissory note and receipt over to Chorlton. sHe looked at them very -carefully, said nothing, and pocketed them. Curious fellow, Chorlton. Clever, too! One of those silent, imperturbable men. I never saw him betray any sign of excitement. Even one wicket to fall and one run to win, the undergrads yelling like mad, could not disturb him.
I never knew him to ;ail in anything he un- dertook. But how he was to succeed in his undertaking against Duveen was b.2yond my poor comprehension.

What follows was related to me afterwards by Chorlton. He called upon Duveen. "Good-morning, Mr. Duveen." "Good-morning, sir. To whom have I the pleasure of speaking?" said the oily rascal. " Chorlton of Balliol. I presume that any business we may transact will be treated in the strictest confidence?"

"Quite so, Mr.—Cliorlton. It is not to my benefit to divulge my clients' business, un- less," he added, with a smirking smile, "un- less, of course, circumstances compel me." "Of course," said Chorlton. "Well, I'm in a little temporary difficulty. You will be 'familiar with many similar cases, I suppose? Living beyond allowance, &c., &c. I want the loan of two hundred and fifty pounds. What are your terms?" "Two hundred and fifty pounds. Oh, we'll manage that easily. Of course, I must ask for some kind of guarantee, Mr. Chorlton. A. mere matter of form, you know, with gentle- men from the Colleges." "Quite right. My father is in a large way of business in Bolton. You'll have no difficulty in confirming that statement" "For how long would you require the loan?" _asked Duveen.

-- I don't know exactly. longer than a month." Umph! A month. That's not long. liardly"pays me. Well, my terms are: Twenty per cent. for a month or under; fifteen per cent. for over one month and under six; special terms for longer periods." "Oh, I think be able to repay you -within the month."
Certainly not

"Right, sir. I'll just ,fill up the necessary form for you to sign." The usual hateful document was produced, and Duveen invited ChOrlton into his chair, as it was more convenient for the purpose of signing. The clerk, Croston, was called in to witness the signature. Chorlton took up the pen, and was just about to sign when, in order to create a diversion, •he jumped out of the chair as though he had been shot. "Oh ! this infernal cramp ! " he cried, try- ing to walk round the room to ease the pain in his leg. "Are you troubled with it very much, sir?" fawningly asked Duveen. "Yes; unfortunately I am. It's gone now, thank Heaven. Now then, we'll try again." He signed, and in replacing the pen on the inkstand. clumsily knocked the stand over on to the floor at the far side of the desk. _ .

"Oh! sorry; but that twinge of cramp has made me unsteady." The obsequious moneylender and his clerk obligingly darted out of sig;.7t for a few seconds to pick up the fallen stand and its contents. Quick as thougp, Chorlton's fingers flew to the stationery hex which was on the desk. He extracted three little slips of paper and transferred them to his pocket. The signature was duly witnessed, the poney. handed over, and there and then the Interview ended. A month passect, and Uhorlton and not re- deemed his promissory note. Nor had he paid any interest. He had been so emphatio in his statement that he would not require the loan for more than a month that Duveen be- came suspicious, and called at Chorlton's rooms. Chorlton simulated regret, said things had not turned out as anticipated, and would Mr. Duveen give him longer credit? "Yes, I would, but you tell me you can't pay the interest, and do not know when you 'will be able to do so." " I'm sorry. Mr. DUVeATI hut I cannot. I

div.head: SUSPICIOLS CiRCUMSTANCES. A Charge of Arson Withdrawn.
div.p: SUSPICIOLS CiRCUMSTANCES. A Charge of Arson Withdrawn.

At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, Luke Hanwright, 60, Winwick-road, was charged with having wilfully set fire to two bales of hair in the -tannery of Messrs. Arthur Waring and Co., Ltd., Winwick-road. Mr. S. Wright presided over a full bench of magistrates, tne Mayor having left the Court. Superintendent Williamson said that the pri- soner was before the Court on Monday on a charge of being found on enclosed premises, but the case had been adjourned,, in order that in- quiries could be made, and the police preferred a charge of arson that morning. Prisoner had been employed by the firm tor about two years, but on Friday, the Bth inst., he was dismissed by Mr. Hightail, the managing director, as his work was not satisfactory. He received his wages on Saturday, and later in the evening he was with a fellowrworkman in a public-house, when he said he would " knife " Mr. Higham, or do him some injury. Shortly before midnight Mr. Samuel Roberts, the works engineer, 95, Dallam-lane, heard a sound, as if someone was getting over the gate. He went home and got the keys. Wien he got to the Buckley-street gates he saw the prisoner climbing over. Asked what.he was doing, pri- soner made no reply, and made out that he was drunk. He looked a bit dazed, and, as Mr. Roberts knew him, he let him go. Mr. Roberts went into the works, and found that two bales of dry hair had been set on fire, and on the top of one of the bales there was a burning sack. The fire-proof doors, which shut off one of the rooms, had been opened. At the bottom of the bales he found seven spent matches. He pro- cured the fire buckets and extinguished the fire. Inspector Stuart was informed and saw the prisoner in bed at 2.45 on the Sunday morning. Charged with being found on the enclosed pre- mises, prisoner said "I understand." He was searched, and three boxes of matches were found in his possession. When charged with arson, he said, "I don't know how I came to be on the premises, if I was there at all. I never set fire to the place." The Bench retired to consider if the case was one for the A6SiZeS, and, on their return, the Chairman said the charge of arson. would be withdrawn, and they would deal with the one in regard to being found on the enclosed premises. Several witnesses were called, and Mr. Roberts said he always closed the fire-proof doors. He corroborated the Superintendent's statement in regard to his seeing prisoner on the gate. Prisoner said he did not think he was there. If he had been, he was drunk. If he had-been sober hews otuoldgonotto ltihaveeptllainoe. A thought of doing f ford oind g sugch a ,o thing a dirty, unmanly action, as setting the place on fire, he would not do it. He knew no more about going to the premises than a new-born baby. He was sent to prison for two months, with I hard labour.

div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

MONDAY. Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton., Suievuurst, Pierpoint and James Evans, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. w. Eurness, W • Itoberts, S. Wright, and G. Pilling. " " Risos FOR SIXPENCE.—Patrick Moran, a well-known local character, was charged with being, as a convicted thief, found loitering in Chief Constable said Moran's very novel. He stopped people Bewsey-street on Saturday for an unlawful mp uertpnoosdes.—wTehree Where it was dark and led them across the road- to a lamp, where he produced an. imitation gold ring, and said it was real gold. P.C. Bury saw him sell the ring to a forge labourer for 2s. He thought the rings were worth twopence each,— Prisoner (indignantly Oh, no; they're pence each. (Laughter.)—ln order that another - )-: charge might possibly be preferred against him, Moran was remanded until Friday. A SUSPICIOUS FlRE.—Luke Hanwright, 60, was charged with being found premises of Messrs. Waring's ,Woninth- tanyard for an unlawful purpose on Saturday. 6icketerloeseeta —The Chief Constable said that at midnight on Saturday Mr. Roberts, the engineer at the tan- yard, heard. someone climbing over tha gate. He got his keys and made a -search. He saw the prisoner climb- over one of the gates to leave the Vinyard. He asked prisoner. what he had .been doing, and Hanwright acted drunk. Mr. Roberts allowed him to. go, because he knew prisoner, who had recently been discharged from the works. Mr. Roberts was suspicious, and on making a further search lie found that someone had set fire to two large heaps of hair in the storeroom. Undoubtedly the whole Place would have been on fire if Mr. Roberts had not noticed it in time to extinguish the flames. He asked for an adjournment until Friday. when they would most likely 'prefer a charge of arson against prisoner.—Prisoner said he was drunk, and did not knoll( what he was doing.—The Chief Constable: Evidence will he called to prove that he has threatened to stab the man- ager.—Prisoner was remanded until Friday.

div.p: WEDNESDAY.

• Before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and W. T. Williams. A SINGULAR CASE.—John Nicholls, 1, Pilking- ton-street, bt. Helens, was summoned for hav- ing been guilty of cruelty to a horse by work- ing it in an unfit state on. August 2nd, and Wil- liam- Glover, Park-road, St. Helens, was swat_ moned for allowing the animal to be worked in such condition. Mr. A. Browne defended.—The evidence of Inspector Dee showed that the animal was very uneasy, and on examination he found a sore about the size of a twoshilling..4 Piece near the saddle. There was a pad there, but it offered no protection. On the near side of the shoulder there were several heat. lumps, two of which had been rubbed raw. When he saw Mr. Glover at St. Helens he said he did not know anything about it until two days after- wards.—ln answer to Mr. Browne, witness said that the date of the offence was an exception- ally hot day.—lnspector Brian corroborated Doe's statement.r—Mr. Browne said that Mr. Glover kept his horses in excellent condition. The Pad had been put• on to protect the sore, the ed caseM r . Dixon, was o y a v et e trivial one.—The r surgeon, had said magis- trates view. the animal, and on their return to court, Mr. Browne said that Mr. Glover had done his best to always keep his horses fit. They were prepared to pay the costs of the case, if no conviction would be recorded.—The magis- trates dismissed the case on payment of costs.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

Before Messrs. 3.• Rymer Young (in the chair),, A. Jr. Jolley, W. Roberts, W. Williams, Dr. aden and Mr. W. Richardson. AnJotaxEn.—Blizabeth Lavin, 24, Portland- street, was charged, on remand, with stealing an alarm clock, of the value of is. 11d., the pro- perty of Patrick Murray, of 19, Portland-street. —lnspector Williamson said that the. complain- ant Went to sleep on the sofa at 10.30 On Tuesday evening, and when he awoke on the following morning betwee,n one and two o'clock; he founu that the front door, which he had failed to lock, was open. He jumped up and went into the ' street, and saw the prisoner, who is a neighbour, running away. He Icild her that if anything was Missed he should charge her with having stolen it. The next morning he failed to find the clock, but on making' inquiries discovered that on Wednesday morning the prisoner took the clock to a man /in Rose and Crown-street, to whom she offered to sell it for sixpence, " as she was hard up and had had no breakfast." The man gave her sixpence, but said she could have the clock back when she refunded the money. There was another charge which could be pre- ferred against prisoner, hut it was necessary for a further adjournment.—The case was adjourned

Chorlton was "stroke" for the Balltol boat. There was a, meeting, with closed doors, in his rooms that night. I was not there., Only the famous eight. Duveen received a note on the following morning from Chorlton, telling him that good fortune had befallen • him and he would be able to settle the debt. He had, however, a favour to ask. He did not care to be seen going into Duveen's office again, nor as it advisable that Duveen should visit his rooms again, as suspicion might be aroused. Would Mr. Duveen be kind enough to meet Mr. Chorlton at one o'clock at the Balliol barge?

If he would he would greatly oblige. Chorlton asked me to meet him at the barge at the time arranged, and to say nothing about the matter to anyone. I did not question him. I obeyed. , When I arrived there Chorlton was on the qui vive. To my astonishment I saw Joyn- son, Grenville, Ingham—in fact, the whole Balliol crew _there. -At.- any other time I would not have been surprised; but at one o'clock, and at that time of te year, when tbe early December wind was bleak and the snow was on the ground and the river was un- attractive, I was astonished, very much. "Look out, you fellows. Here he is. And Croston, the clerk, with him, by Jove! Get into the dressing•room quiekly, and not a murmur. When I whistle, tumble out. You stay with me, Roycroft." Duveen very curtly responded to Chorlton's "Good-morning." "I'm sorry to have brought you here, Mr.- Duveen, but I think you'll appreciate my motive." .

"I'm not so much concerned about your motive, young man, as I am about your money," he offensively replied. "I beg of you to be civil, Mr. Dnyeen, if you please. Come inside, and we'll settle this business in a moment. I presume you are pre- pared to give me a receipt?", "Of course I am, you young fool." Chorlton set his teeth. His face wore an ugly look. We went into the outer room which led to the dressing-room. The dressing-room door was closed, and not a sound could be heard. There was no one else about except Griggs, the boatman. "Shut that door, Roycroft, please. Won't you sit down, Mr. Duveen? " We all sat down at the table. "'Now, then," said Chorlton, "I owe you two hundred and fifty pounds. With interest up to date at twenty per cent. the total amount due is two hundred and fifty-four pounds three shillings and fourpence. Is that right?" "Yes. But I don't want a speech." "Nor will you have one," replied Chorl- ton. "At least, it will be very short. I have a receipt from you dated yesterday in full dis- charge of my supposed debt." "Supposed debt! You have a receipt! What nonsense is this?" roared Duveen, springing out of his chair. "Do you think I m an idiot?" "Oh, no," sweetly replied Chorlton, "not an idiot. A business man," he added, mock- ingly. "A man whose eyes will, I suppose, convince him. Look at that." And he held a receipt before Duveen's eyes. The blackguard turned pale as he saw

the document. - With an oath he snatched at the paper; but Chorlton was too quick for him. He took ad- vantage of Duveen's forward movement. He withdrew his left hand, in which he held the receipt, and with his right fist gave Duveen a, blow between the eyes which sent him stag- gering to the other end of the room. Then he gave a low whistle, and in tumbled his friends. "Just hold these two beauties, you chaps. and place them here while I give them a lesson or two in caligraphy." The moneylender and his clerk were soon in the grip of those powerful athletes. Chorl- ton smilingly sat at the table, produced a sheet of paper, and wrote his own name in full, in a clear, bold hand. Then he wrote: "John Walton Duveen." With a sneer he placed the paper just be- low Duveen's signature on the receipt I had obtained a few weeks before. The similarity of the signatures was marvellous. Then he produced the receipt for the two hundred and fifty pounds. Three signatures—all won- derfully alike. I thought Duveen would have fainted. He turned livid. His clerk was trembling with fear. "You see, Mr. Duveen, you are not the only man in Oxford who can reproduce, other people's signatures. I've had to practise very hard to attain this perfection." "Where did you get that printed receipt form from, you—" His contemplated abuse was promptly checked by a little rough handling on the part of his captors. He howled with pain as they gave an extra twist to his arms. "I had to knock an inkstand over before I could obtain it. You remember, don't you? 1 You remember the simpleton." "Now, gentlemen all," Chorlton continued, "what's the verdict? This cad cheated young Roycroft out of two hundred pounds. I told you all about it last night. This same villain played the same game with Crawford, of Harrow, and Bland, of Eton. At Harrow he called himself Smithson; at Eton, Weight- man." A good guess, but effective. Duveen plainly showed he was guilty. I remembered having heard of .those two cases of unproved fraud. "What's the verdict?" "We'll show you in a minute," grimly re- plied Grenville. "Well, I'll leave it to you. Roycroft, I have already paid you your two hundred pounds. The odd fifty pounds will 13e sent to St. Guy's Hospital." The luckless Duveen and Croston roaring for mercy, were ruthlessly dragged to the landing raft of the barge. One—two—three! Far into the Isis they dropped. They both swam like ducks. In any case the eight were at hand to prevent a calamity. Two dripping forms staggered on to the opposite bank, and, amid the laughter of the merry undergrads, slouched away. They have not been to Oxford since, and are not likely again to be heard of there. * I congratulated Chorlton on his dangerous accouylishment, and again thanked him. He is a clever chap, Chorlton. His only re- ply was: "Don't you be a young fool again, Roycroft." _ _

div.head: [THE ENE.]
div.p: [THE ENE.]
WIDNES GAS SUPPLY.

An inquiry into the application of Widnes Council to borrow £36,000 for Gasworks exten- Sion was held by Mr. A. W. Brightmore at the Town Hall on Wednesday. , Mr. Carr, gas engineer, said the value of the Gasworks was ,t 1,000,000. The production of gas in thirty years had growff from 62 million cubic feet per annum to 453 million feet. This year it was estimated to reach 520 million feet. The pre- sent plant could not cope with the demand.

div.head: VALUABLE HORSE SOLD CHEAP
div.p: VALUABLE HORSE SOLD CHEAP

A horse, valued at £26, disappeared from South-lane Farm, Bold, and the St. Helens police discovered that it had been sold to a hawker for £3 10s,- Inquiries led to the arrest of Thomas E. Fowles, Cuerdley, and he was re- manded at St. Helens Police Court on Thursday for further inquiries on a charge of stealing the horse.

div.head: NO BREAD AND WATER. Amazing Letter to the Warrington
div.p: NO BREAD AND WATER. Amazing Letter to the Warrington
Board of Guardians.
NEW OFFICES TO BE ERECTED.

Gentlemen,—At a meeting of the- South Manchester Christian Mud of Guardians gave notice of the following motion: "That in the opinion of all Christian Guardians the time had come for them to prohibit the serving of bread and water as a meal to Christians in the Casual Ward." This remarkable epistle, was read at a meet- ing of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, arid provoked much amusement amongst the members. The writer of the letter did not give his name, but the missive, which was written in a neat hand, bore the heading, "Christians of Warrington—July 16th, 1913:" Why the writer should have sent • his epistle to the Guardians none of the members could guess; they laughed over it, and, as it was an anonymous document, it was not considered further.. The meeting of the Guardians was held in the Board Room at. the Workhouse, Mr. E. T. Bent (the chairman) presiding, and there were present Mr. A. J. Jolley (vice-chairman), Miss Broad- bent, Mrs. Hall, Mrs. Simpson, the. Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Messrs. A. Billinge, W. C. Brooks, T. Dale, W. Flanagan, W. Furness, J. A. Hughes, G. Mather, F. McKinley, T. Ritchie, and N. W. Setow,....Mr. Arthur Bat tornles_(olPrk) Mr Partridge (assi§tant-elerk), - Mr. W. J. Brown (Workhouse master), .and Mr. E. Lawrence (superintendent .of the Cottage Homes).

div.head: APPOINTMENTS AND SALARIES
div.p: APPOINTMENTS AND SALARIES

The Houk Committee reported that, acting in accordance with a resolution of the Board, they had considered the question of the salary of the Medical Officer to the Workhouse (Dr, Alexander Hodgkinson), and recommended unanimously that, in recognition of the able and devoted ser- vice of Dr. Hodgkinson, his salary be increased from £lOO to £l5O per annum. , _ On the recommendation of the sub-committee, the Clerk \\his instructed to issue an advertise- ment for the filling of the vacancy of liesident Medical Officer, at a commencing salary of £125 per annum, together with the usual residential allowances.

It was reported that Miss Eva Henry, of Pres- ton, and Miss L. E. Shaw, Wolverhampton, had been appointed probationary nurses at the Workhouse Infirmary; that Miss E. Davies, Hereford, and Miss A. Roberts. Huddersfield, were appointed female lunatic attendants at the salary of .X 25 per annum, with the usual resi- dential allowances.
The minutes were moved for adoption by Mr. G. NIATHER (chairman of the House Committee), seconded by Mr. W. C. Bnooxs, and carried un- animously.

div.head: NEW OFFICES REQUIRED
div.p: NEW OFFICES REQUIRED

A scheme for providing new offices aild cen- tralising the. staffs under the control of , the Guardians came up for brief discussion. Mr. W. FURNESS raised the topic by moving the following resolution That in view of the letter received from the Registrar-General, calling attention to the un- suitable office accommodation provided by the Guardians for ,registration purposes, in, the opinion of this Board the time has now arrived for the erection of suitable central offices, to accommodate tho Poor Law and District Council staffs • further, that a sub-committee be now ap- pointed, with the object of selecting 'a site, or sites, and formulating plans, the final report of such sub-committee to be in, due course sub- mitted to the Bpard." Mr. Fu mess said the, present, accommodation' as was well known, by every member, was very inadequate,-more especially for registration pur- poses. The centralising.of the,staffs teldnging to the Guardians would lead to greater efficiency and much better administration. It was now anomalous that ratepayers who appealed against assessments should have to go to the Workhouse to have their appeals heard. It would be greatly to the 'convenience of the ratepayers if they could attend at same central office in 'the borough, instead of having to go to the Board Room at,, the Workhouse. (Helm hear.)

DOOM OF THE 'HELLO GIRL'
Automatic Exchanges to be Used in the Future.
SOME NOVEL DEVICES.
[" Examiner" Special.]
The day of the telephone appears to be
nearing the end. The hum of the automatic switch-board will take
the place of the angelic voice (except when crossed) of the "hello damsel," and a good deal of the romance attached to the telephone will vanish.
So will several mild flirtations that frequently flitter over the wires between the offices and the 'phone room.

It is expected that the automatic system will be applied to telephone exchanges as soon as possible, and Warrington will get it in due course. This method has long got past the experimental stage. We might have had it here long ago, but for the conservative caution so characteristic of our telephone authorities. When we do get it, however, it will be of the

most improved type. In the United States the system has been in operation for nearly three years. Graye de- fects were discovered in the early days, but these have been removed, and the automatic switch-board works now in a satisfactory man- ner. The British Post Office will thus reap the advantage from the American experiments and
discoveries. There are now upwards of three, hundred thousand telephone exchanges in‘opera- tion in the States and Canada.

The Speaking Wire. There seems no numerical limit to the work of such exchanges. In the San Francisco area there are over 100,000 lines laid on to one ex- change, and close upon 300;000 on another. The record, however, at present rests with the auto- matic exchange at Chicago, which allowed fOr 1,000,000 lines. These are now in use, and still subscribers are clamouring for more. Another million lines may possibly have to be established

_ at an early date. 'Chicago, it must be remem- bered, is the beau of the telephone world. Everybody uses the "speaking wire," every house has a telephone installed, and instruments can be found in the abodes of farmers for miles around.

An expert, who has studied the Chicago sys- tem, as well as that in other American towns, assures me that the adoption of the automatic system in Warrington would prove a decided boon. All the present facilities would be available, but the service would be quicker and more accurate. It would be impossible to get on to wrong numbers, as so frequently happens at present. Junction work is scarcely neces- sary, the subscriber is rung up automatically, and all calls are 'recorded in print by the appa- ratus, and disputes over the bill are avoided. In the exchange the machinery is rather com- plicated, yet rarely gets out of order. Th subscriber's end of the wire, however, sees a much simpler apparatus. In one system, which has been experimented with by the Post Office telephone authorities at Epsom, with a possible view of adoption in large centres, the existing instrument remains in the subscriber's office, but to its base is attached a small dial. Upon the dial are painted figures ranging from oto 9. Beneath are small holes with discs, which can be pushed in with the finger, just like pressing the button of an electric bell.

A Local Illustration. Suppose a subscriber desires to ring .tip the. "Examiner," 'Number 355 Y. His first coma- lion would be to turn the figure three round to one of the finger holes and press. For the second five would be rung, repeated, and then Y signalled. Released, the dial returns to its original position, the complicated, machinery in the exchange has made up the number, and talk can be commenced 'at once. There is thus practically no waltliig;--arraThittr-c:vpericnO irr manipulating- the dial-. a number can 'be Made. -up in a few seconds---a speed which a human operatOr,cannOt ,equal. If, 355 Y is engaged-, a buzzer sings out the fact, and the subscriber has to try again later on. In the working of local exchanges ,the matter is very simple, and I learn that the Epsom ex- periments have proved emphatically to the telephone department of the Post Office that the automatic system would prove of the greatest advantage in important centres as Warrington To deal with trunk calls on such a method is

the problem of the hour, and it has, so far aF can be ascertained at present, not nearly been solved. What is known as the semi-automatic system may lead to a solution, but in this, while part of the connection may be made by ar. automatic call, the telephone girl would have to be retained in order to make the trunk connec- tions. Still the science of telephony has not
reached its final stage, and, in a few years, it may be possible for a Warrington subscriber to automatically ring up an office in London, or even in Paris.

Popularising the 'Phone. Of course, the introduction of the new type. means that the human agency will be done away with, but, so far as can be learned, the Post Office will find other work for the evicted young ladies who at present arq engaged " helloing " over the 'phones. At the same. time these would be released from a calling which is arduous and nerve-racking, not to mention the question of temper-testing. Very few not connected with the telephone system have an idea of the work the operatives have inflicted upon them: On an average each operator deals with 1.000 calls per day, or, roughly, 300,000 per annum. This alone woutl be sufficient to try the nerves, but also indis tinct voices and bad temper have to be (on- tended with. Even the patience of Jo.) .!nght• have given way if he had to suffer the train imposed upon the 'Change girls

div.head: ANCIENT HERO.
div.p: THE ANCIENT HERO.

It is curious, writes Mr. F. Day in the West. minster Review, to notice the nature of the influ- ence which religion brings to bear on its different followers, and also to consider' how it comes to piss that the growth of civilisation and pros- perity seenis invariably to undermine and e;eaken the religion of a nation. In bygone times it was customary for a knight, on the eve of battle, to pass the hours from sun- set to sunrise in prayer before the altar; and in the middle of the twelfth century King Roger the Norman, on escaping from shipwreck off the coast of Cephalu, in North Sicily, during his con- quests there, at once set to work, and as a thank-offering to God raised that glorious cathe- dral which still enthrals with wonder and admi• ration the, feelings of all who gaze upon it. His son and successor, William 11., also erected the beautiful cathedral of Monreale, near Palermo, an e7rquisite poem in mosaics, far finer and more extensive than those at St. Mark's, in Venice, one mosaic picture representing him receiving hit) crown from Christ himself, by no Means in a rpirit of braggadocio, as the humility ,and devoutness of his portrait testify. Notwithstanding the piety of these ancient heroes, after a night-long vigil passed in prayer, they would be guilty of the most terrible cruel- ties towards their enemies, an anomaly which I seems inexplicable.

div.head: RISE OF THE TELEPHONE.
div.p: THE RISE OF THE TELEPHONE.

A Ettle while' ago the Postal Authorities took over the telephone systems belonging to into a companies and converted them a great national undertaking. A few mdlions of pounds were transferred to, the original shareholders, a few thousand new servants were added to those already employed by the Government, and with the minimum of fric- tion and dislocation the nation became pos- sessed of a new instrument of modern civili- sation.

div.head: A. TOY THIRTY YEARS AGO.
div.p: A. TOY THIRTY YEARS AGO.

We have grown so accustomed to the use of the telephone that it is rather difficult to be- lieve that only about thirty years ago it was scarcely anything .but a toy. 'Nothing is much i more surprising n the wonderful epoch in which we Eve than the way in which the sug- gestions of apparently impracticable story writers like Jules Verne have become realised, and toys for children the means of amuse- and- money, making. The Zoet,rope is nova the cinematograith, the talking toy is the modern telephone, and the vessel that tra- velled under water is the submarine. TELEPHONES IN FINLAND.

And yet we have not, so far as the tele- phone is concerned, achieved anything like the efficiency of some of our foreign competi- tors. In Finland, for instance, telephones are so cheap that even the cottages in the far north use them. From one end of the land to the other they are to be found, and they are EQ common that people use them for the pur- poses of ordinary conversation at almost all hours of the day and night. The cla,ildren consult one another about their homework and not infrequently worry their harassed teachers with questions as to the solution of difficulties, long after their overworked in- structors should have been freed from the cares of the day.

div.head: INVENTOR.
div.p: THE INVENTOR.

It is difficult to say who invented the tele. phone. In some form or other, its principles were understood at a very early time. Hooke, as early as 1667 had propagated sound along a wire, but his experiments were to remain without practical results for many years After that. Not till 1821 is there-any great ad- vance, and then Wheatstone steps to the front with a device for sending musical sounds along his telegraphic wires and the invention of the word telephone. Yet anotter fifty years elapsed before the instrument in anything like the form that we know it was patented by Robert 8011. and it was just be- cause he was the person to give it commer- cial value that he is usually regarded as the inventor of the telephone.

div.head: CURIOUS CAREER.
div.p: A CURIOUS CAREER.

Bell had a curious career. He came to Lon- don to teach elocution, met Wheatstone, con- ceived the idea of the telephone, and returned to America to study and work out his notion. For a long time his efforts to realise the dream that was in his brain were without result. Time and money were spent, and little if any practical result followed. He neglected his ordinary duties, and almost lost his sweet- heart, for her father refused to allow lier union with a man who spent most of his time with his head in his hands. Then the idea came to fruition, and the first real telephone, duly patented and protected, was sent to an exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876. There no- body took much n-otice of it except as a new development of a toy. It might have died a quiet death if it had not been for Dom Pedro of Brazil. As he was walking round the exhi- bition, someone call-d his attention to the ilue,.l lieu was sent to the trans. mitter while Dom Pedro sat at the receiver. His face gradually became more and more -astonished, 'and after a while he could eon- tain hi wonder no longer, but burst out with the expression, "Good God! it talks." Some enterprising journalist heard the remark, took it down in his notebook, put it in his paper, and in a few days, the short sentence had been flashed round the globe, and the telephone as a commercial enterprise was born. Bell, who had been unable when the Exhibition opened, to get to the show for want of the necessary funds with which to pay his fare, was on the highway to fame and fortune, and incidentally to the posses- sion of a wife. That was in 1876, and to-day, peasants in districts not far removed from the Arctic Circle, send messages to' one another over the instrument that they owe partly to Dom Pedro of Brazil. EDISON'S CLAIM.
Mr. Edison, the great American inventor,

also claims to have invented the telephone, and there is this much to be said for his claim, that he filed a description of such an instrument at least a month before Bell askeeu for his patent. Edison'S instrument, however, was a device for analysing complex sounds, and it was not until Bell's instrument had been put on the market that his American competitor discovered that the earlier in- strument of his own invention was capable of being used for the transmission of human speech. Edison has .always given credit to Bell for his work, but justly asks that a portion of the credit due to the perfection of the instrument should be given to him. For Bell's telephone could transmit sounds only over short lines. It had no separate transmit- ter and a single piece of apparatus was used both for transmitter and receiver. IMPROVING THE TELEPHONE.

It was at the suggestion of the Western Union Company that Ed.son took up the idea of improving the telephone. He set to work with .his customary energy and zeal, worked day and night, and periormed thousands of experiments. His own story of his results re- cently given in Meadowcroft's Boys Life of Edison is full of interest. He says, "In 1876 I started to experiment for the Western Uni- on and Mr. Orton- . I started in and soon produced the carbon transmitter, which is now universally used. Tests were made . . The noises were so great that not a word could be heard with the Bell receiver when used as a transmitter between New York and Newark, New Jersey. Mr. Orton and W. K. Vanderbilt and the board of directors wit- nessed and took part in the tests of my trans- mitter. They were successful. Mr. Theodore Puskas, of Buda-Pest. Hungary, was the first man to suggest a telephone exchange, and soon after exchanges were established. The telephone department was put into the hands of Vanderbilt's ablest son-in-law, who made a success of it. The Bell Company- of Boston, also started exchang4s, and the fight was on, the Western Union pirating the Bell receiver and the Boston Company pirating the Wes- tern Union transmitter. About this time I wanted to be taken eare of. I threw out hints of this desire. Then Mr. Orton sent for me. He had learned that, inventors didn't do busi- ness by the regular process, and concluded he would closet right up. He asked. me how i much I wanted. I had made up my mind it was certainly worth 25,000 dollars if it ever amounted to anything for central station work; so that wa's the sum I had in my mind to obstinately stick to and get. Sall it had been an easy job, and only required a few months, and I felt a little shaky and uncer- tain. So I asked him to make me an offer. He promptly said he Would give me a hundred thousand dollars." Needless to say, the offer was accepted, but Edison did not want all the money at once, and he received instead 6,000 dollars a year for a period of seventeen years—the life of the patent.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
FEEDING PIGS FOR BACON.

About the best time for shutting up pigs for fattening (says "Farm and Mime ") is when they are about five, months old, as they are geneerally on their legs well at this time. At arst they nee. to be very carefully looked after, as too much food should not be given them. Food should never be left in the trough .after they have .had a feed, or else they become sick- ened of their food and lose their appetites, which is a great drawback. We find it much better to give them small quantities of food for the first few days till they get used to it.. We find it much better to feed them three times a day than twice, as the pigs seem much more satisfied and do better. A very good diet for such pur- pose is a mixture of equal quantities of bean, barley, maize and wheat meals. Potatoes and other vegetables are much more valuable as pig foods than many people suppose. Russian barley is more beneficial to pigs than English. Soya bean meal should not be used, as it iS too relaxing. .The bacon feeder,: of course, should obtain the right class of pigs for .'his purpose, otherwise, he cannot expect them to go on well.

div.head: HARVESTING COMMENCED
div.p: HARVESTING COMMENCED

Harvest is now general in the South of Eng- land (says "The Times "), and during the past week substantial progress was made with the work. Though. the weather has not been as warm as might be expected in August, grain is ripening quickly under the influence of periods of bright sunshine, and the harvest is rapidly spreading northwards. It will be in full swing in Norfolk this week, but it will be late in the month before the binders are in full commission in the northern counties. Every one is certainly ready for it, as haymaking has been practically completed, and with weeds easily kept in subjection on all reasonably well farmed land, no urgent- work stands between farmers and the 'gathering of-the grain crops. • On We whole the, supply of labourers appears to be sufficient for requirements. Indeed, in some districts more men are offering their ser- vices than can be employed. Farm labour, however, is not a very mobile commodity, and this over-supply, in some cases does 'not pre- vent other farmers from working with. rather fewer labourers than they migarit desire. If the weather is favourable, however, the work should prove lighter than usual, for crops are standing well and present much fewer difficul- ties than, for instance, they did last year. When the binder can make the full .circuit of a field and has not to travel empty on one or more sides. and above all when the use of the scythe for. very untractable pieces can be dispensed with, the progress is much More satisfactory.

div.head: SELECTION OF SEED.
div.p: SELECTION OF SEED.

Seed should not be saved from diseased crops, for .unsound tubers cannot produce healthy and robust plants. Though apparently sound, seed from a blighted crop may carry the potato dis- ease, which is liable to be transmitted in turn to the produce of such seed. Seed selected from a crop dug before the tubers are fully ripe win give superior results to that selected from a mature crop. It is questionable, however, whether when the crop is not being grown solely for seed purposes. the advantage thus gained is not outweighed by the reduction in yield occasioned by premature digging. A por- tion of the crop might, however, be harvested a little earlier for the purpose of saving seed. There is little question that many, growers, particularly those with small areas under pota- toes, frequently make use of seed so small that it is incapable of producing a • remunerative i crop: Although tis scarcely possible to secure ail the seed of a umform size, an effort should be made to avoid using either abnormally large or very small seed. Potatoes dressed over a 1,1--inch riddle are a suitable size for 'planting. The largest tubers should be removed if a suffi- cient supply of medium-sized .ones, is available. Large seed may be cut a few days previous to planting, care being taken to leave two.or three eves in each portion. The cut surfaces should at once be dusted with fine air-slaked lime to prevent undue shrivelling. For general pur- poses a potato should never be cut so as to form a set from each eye, and not more than two, or at the most three, sets ought to be cut from a single tuber. . The crop resulting from very small sets cannot be satisfactory.

div.head: GARDEN.
div.p: THE GARDEN.
REMOVING SEED-PODS

To obtain as much bloom as possible from plants, it is very unportant to remove all seed- pods as soon as they appear. By doing so the majority of plants, particularly annuals, will continue to flower for a very much longer period than they would if allowed to develop their seeds.

div.head: DIVIDING PiEONIAS.
div.p: DIVIDING PiEONIAS.

As soon as the foliage of the plants is get- ting dry, it will be a suitable time to divide them where necessary. By 'doing So now the succulent roots will suffer less than if dis- turbed in the autumn or spring. It is advis- able to -select dull weather ;for the operation, if possible,. although this is not , absolutely necessary, but an occasional watering will he found very beneficial.

div.head: TRANSPLANTING MADONNA LILIES
div.p: TRANSPLANTING MADONNA LILIES

Anyone desirous of transplanting the beau- tiful Madonna lily, lilium candidum, will find the present time most suitable. Seldom are the plants seen to better advantage than in a cottage garden where they are left undisturbed for years, which goes to prove that they should only be taken up when absolutely necessary through overcrowding, Then the largest bulbs should be replanted and the smaller ones grown for .ti year or two in the nursery. If the plants are Suffering from the disease which often-attacks:them, the bulbs ought to be freely dusted with sulphur before they are replanted.

div.head: NENIESIAS FOR SPRING FLOWERING.
div.p: NENIESIAS FOR SPRING FLOWERING.

These lovely South African flowers are Much appreciated in the conservatory or greenhouse in springtime. The plants are easily grOwn in pots from • seeds sown in August. Nemesia strumosa namt compacta and N. s. Suttonii, both producing mixed colours,l are suitable varieties for pot 'culture. If the seeds are sown in boxes or pans, the resultant seedlings must be transplanted in pots while quite small, five in a 61-inch 'pot tieing sufficient: or they may be sown in the larger pots, and surplus plants drawn out, the after-treatment being similar to that given to pot mignonette.

div.head: ROMAN HYACINTHS
div.p: ROMAN HYACINTHS

To secure early blooms, Roman hyacinths should be potted up at once, or at least as soon as they are received . from the nursery- man. For cutting purposes boxes will do •as yell as pots., though, where they are required as pot plants, 41-inch and 6-inch pots are de- sirable.

div.head: TRAPPING WASPS.
div.p: TRAPPING WASPS.

As fruits ripen, wasps will be ready to p)ounce upon them, and unless- they are destroyed they will work much harm. • We saw a very .ingenious and apparently effica- cious wasp trap this season, but it is not on the market yet. Numbers, however, can be lured to their doom by placing some jun and sugar with a proportion of *water in narrow- mouthed jars, which should be placed near the fruit trees. - A look-out should also be kept for nests,, and when found they should 13-e promptly destroyed. Hanging nests can be demolished by means of a torch formed of "waste" or rag tied on the end of a cane and saturated with .. petroleum. Those in the ground should havO tar poured into them. The work must be done late in the evening.

div.head: PRISONER OF THE MAHDI.
div.p: PRISONER OF THE MAHDI.
Father Ohrwalder, _wh9 was for ten years a prisoner- among the Dervishes, and escaped, has died at Omdurman. The career of Father Ohrwalder is one of the romtnces of the Soudan. . _ _ - _

Born at Lana, near Meran, in the Tyrol, in 1856, Father Ohrwalder went to Cairo in 1879, after being trained as a missionary at Verona. In the following year he went up to Khartoum, and in 1882 he was captured by the Mandists in the Dar Nuba. For many years he was held in captivity by the Dervishes, and, after Several fruitless attempts to escape, he succeeded, after eluding his captors, in reaching the Egyptian outposts.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
AT THE WHIM OF A POMPERO.

Though I have often been to sea, and for long voyages at that, I am not a seafaring man, and that is one of the reasons why I have refrained so long in this•country from putting in print an account of the incident I am now about to relate. .nother reason is that, when I have told the story to those but little acquainted with me, I. have been gen- erally diEbelieved. To alter somewhat a well- known proverb, I !-:ave nearly always found fiction to be more convincing than truth, for the general public is very like the old woman who believed her sailor son's account of his v.sit to thee Valley of Diamonds, and his re- sidence amongst the Lilliput:ans, but could not credit his story of the flying fish. After having unsuccessfully experimented with farming in the Argentine Settlement of La Viticolas I went into the town of Balhia Blanca in search of a less precarious mode of •flaking a living. As it turned out, I was for- tunate in the moment of my arrival, for next day I was put on to one of the easiest and pleasantest jobs the laziest man in the world need desire. All I had to do was to write down the he.ght of the tide, indicated on an upright pole, every quarter of an hour, and. at the same time note the direction of the wind. This work, however, was only tempor- ary; I was taking the place of a man down with fever, and on his recovery I was sent up to Buenos Ayres by the railway company (Ferro-carril-del-Sud) to fit me for a better paying office. In the capital, however, I made the acquaintance of Don Robert Payro, owner and editor of "La Tribuna," Bahia Blanca, but at present on the editor;al staff of the great Buenos Ayres daily "La Na- cion," and he made me a proposal, the carrying out of which accorded far batter with my humour than could any kind of rail- way work. One page of "La Tribuna" was to agiser in English every day and I was to edit it.

div.head: STORM BREWING
div.p: A STORM BREWING

I had a pass which would enable me to go back to Bahia Blanca by rail, free of charge, but I happened to know that a coasting steamer (the "Esperanza " I will call it, for I have forgotten the real name) was to sail next day with railway material for the southern port and I thought the journey would be pleasanter by sea. Captain Foley, whom I had already met, was rather glad of my company than otherwise, and laughed at the idea of paying anything for my passage. Had I known what was before me I should certainly have considered the fare a dear one, even on the captain's terms. The " Esperan- za " was heavily 'loaded with rails and metal sleepers, but she had also to tow an enormous dredger, intended for deepening the new port of Bahia Blanca.

As the port was then, the big ocean-going steamer could not enter, and the cargoes brought from Europe had to be transferred to smaller vessels, such as the "Esperanza." The hundred miles journey along the broad Plata river to Montevideo passed without no- table event of any kind, but when we got to the open sea there, was a swell on the water that set the ship rolling from side to side with a swing that threatened, to over- balance her at every moment. Each side of the deck stooped down in turn to the very edge of the sea, as if to kiss the waves, or look at its own reflection, and I thought that the least 'displacement of the cargo would surely send us to the bottom. I have never felt so much afraid in my life, for there was nothing in the smooth-faced sullen undula- tions of the ocean in the least calculated to arouse one's spirits to meet a crisis, or death. And it seemed such a cold-blooded death, to topple over side-wise in a calm, to cease to draw one's breath in a nightmare. That others also were frightened I could see, for the sailors kent look.ng. at the boats, and the usually cheery captain had anxiety plainly graved on his face. But this aaner, if danger it was, passed away with the 'sun and our steady advance to the south. The short twilight was marked by a steely, treacherous-looking, western Eiky where the level Pampas gave a near horizon and the sense of distance only came from where the tops of the Sierra de la "Ventana began to 'how towards the south.

" Por Dios, we shall catch it to-night," said, Capt. Foley, swearing in Spanish, as everyone does, except , parsons in those waters, and at the same time casting an anxious look at the dredger which came lum- bering behind like a big stupid boy being dragged to school by his mother.

div.head: TORNADO
div.p: THE TORNADO

While light continued the weather re- mained calm, and we proceeded at the regu- lation ten knots, notwithstanding our doa- ble load. But night had scarcely fallen when the pompeTo that the captain had anticipated burst suddenly upon us. Had it struck us broadsides we must, I am sure, have gone over at once, but Captain Foley's long expo- rien;ce of the South American pompero, or tornado, had enabled him to calculate more or less the coume it would take, and he had turned, the head of the ship in the nick of time. As it was, I had a sensation as if we were being lifted out of. the water, .and be• fore this feeling had passed 4,way the dredger was hurled right up against us with a force that thrilled through the whole frame of the ship, and shot through the bodies of the men as with an epidemic paralysis. I happened to be in the saloon at the time, trying to read something, perhaps a prayer book, and was flung into the air, high enough to receive a shock that nearly stunned me when I fell.

The Captain had ordered me below just as the pompero began to break, but now I felt I could not -remain under deck any longer. Even if I had to lash myself to the mast on top, I thought I should' fecl safer in sight of my fellow human beings than in _ keeping such dreadful solitary vig:l below.

The• wind was roaring as thOugii through an organ pipe a 'thousand miles long with a mouth of eighty degrees. In contact with its mighty force, the Esperanza seemed no more than a bubble, and that we could survive be- yond a few minutes it did not enter into my head_ to hope. some hours before when we had only the rolling of the sea to contend with, I had been speculating fear,fully as td- the, condition of things in the life to come, and I dreaded to face the future. Now, however, I became suddenly conscious of a kind of exultation that the next few moments could bring me a knowledge greater than that possessed by any living man, that the thoughts which had puzzled me would puzzle me no longer, and I feel quite certain that for an instant or two I did not wish to live.

As I crept up the companion ladder the water was raging over the deck as over a reef and my eyes were blinded. I could see no- thing, but I learned somehow that the dred- ger was being cut loose, and I thought of it as of sometting with a soul to be saved or lost. That is th,2 last thought I remember. for a mighty wave, which must have stunned me by its force, hurled me from the deck into the boiling sea. The first mate saw me go over, a Mere straw in a cataract, and he uttered a prayer for my soul.

div.head: PREMATURE OBITUARY NOTICE,
div.p: A PREMATURE OBITUARY NOTICE,

The pompero died out as suddenly as it had come, but it was a very dishevelled and forlorn looking Esperanza that dfew up alongside the new .pier, or mole, of Bahia Blanca. Captain Foley told of my death, and my new friend, Sefior Payro, wrote a nice obituary notice in the "La Tribuna." There was one or two people far away to whom my death meant some slight loss, for I was not insured, and the bad news found them out. But what troubled Bahia Blanca atm the radway company most was the pro- bable loss of the dredger, though that was insured. Tugs, were at once sent out to search the sea, one from Bahia Blanca, two from Montevideo.

In a week she was found, almost uninjurea, ten degrees east from Cape Corrientes. As the men who boarded her were about to descend to the saloon, they were aghast at the sight of a head emerging froli the companion way. I had seen them come and had prepared the climax, putting on an air of unconcern, and jauntily puffing at my last cigarette. I had been washed off the shin bv one Avr lifted on to th dredger by another. Through the rest of the pompero I remained uncon- scious but the high bulwarks of the dredger kept me safe until the storm was over. There was not a morsel of food on the dredger, be- yond a box of oranges, which one of the men of the Esneranza, for some reason of his own, had placed there. But I was one who had al- ways believed in the possibility, not to say (Continued in next Te(eran.)

div.head: SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.
div.p: SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.
DEATH DEFRAUDED.
Mr. Lloyd George and the Triumphs
of the Insurance Act.
SIMPLE-MINDED MR. LAW.

Mr. Lloyd George delivered one of his most characteristic speeches to a huge. gathering of Nottingham miners. on . Saturday. Dealing with the Insurance Act, he said :- Amongst my diverse evil deeds,-and I am judg- ing by the torrent of abuse poured upon it—the very worst has been the Insurance Act. Oppres- sive, tyrannical, cruel.; inhuman, a fraud, a sham, gross deception--(laughter)—these are some of the choice samples of the epithets flung at it.

There is one thing about the attitude of the Tories which must have struck you. This most wicked Act of modern times, so they say, robs the people, gives them nothing in return, is a great fraud, and is inflicting intolerable injury upo:.. the millions •of people whose votes they seek, and yet they have not pledged themselves to abolish this wicked Act. Now, that is re- markable. I want to know why. There is nothing which is irrevocable about it, except the good which it has done, and you cannot undo that.

div.head: 'RETURN THE GATE. MONEY."
div.p: 'RETURN THE GATE. MONEY."

After all, if they decided to abolish it, they could return the gate-money—(lar,ghter)—all except that proportion of it which has already been expended in relieving distress and in saving life. Thank God they cannot get that back. (A Voice: "Never.") They know full well that the best,. the most high-minded, the most upright men in their, own party. would revolt against the callous selfishness of a pledge to abolish this Act. Mr. Bonar Law—(cries of "Oh, oh !" and laughter)—l am not surpiised.at that ebullition. —(laughter)—has, one quality—he has the merit of believing implicitly all the .evil things which are said about his opponents. (" Oh, oh !") That is what commends him to all the most intoler- ant and malignant partisans of his own side, and he one day pledged himself to abolish this Act. Poor, simple-minded soul! (Laughter.) He thought they meant it. (Laughter.) He had no notion that their abuse of it was a mere political device! But they 'soon disillusioned him on that sub- ject. No sooner had he uttered the fateful words than they fell upon him one and all, as if he were Mr. Balfour. They wrote out a retrac- tation for him on a piece of paper, put it in front of him, and said, "You see your 'initials at the bottom which we have written in pencil. Take that paper and write your name, withdrawing what you said, otherwise out you go !" (Laugh- ter.) And yet this is the most monstrous Act of Parliament of' modern times—at least, every Tory will tell you so, except those who know something about it. (Laughter.)

div.head: ALL ON SICK PAY.
div.p: ALL ON SICK PAY.
What is the charge against the Act? Let us examine their pretended objections. They are most conflicting. They used to say, "You pay, pay, pay, and you lick stamps, and never get anything in return."

What do they do now? They say we are pay- ing too much! They say there is excessive sickness, and that ,there is malingering, and that too much money has been paid out. I have no doubt that there are men amongst the working classes, as amongst other classes, who have over-coddled themselves. (Laughter.) But they are not all of the working class. (Hear, hear.) If you listened to them you might imagine that half the working classes of this country had retired on sick pay. (Laughter.) I wonder who is carrying on these great indus- tries in the meantime. (Hear, hear.) Have you met any dukes with pick in hand "at the face"? (Laughter.) There may be something in that charge of excessive sickn&s, and we must inquire into it to see who is responsible for it, whether it be through slackness of adminiS"tration' by any of the societies, absence.' of rigid,.supervision and inspection; •or the culpable ease with which doctors grant certificates. (Hear, hear, and a voice: "That is where it is.") What was the position of the working classes in case of sickness before tbe Act came into operation? Just 'one-third, and no more, had been able to ensure themselves a provision for the days of sickness. What happened to the rest, God knows.

It is idle to say that the failure of the re- maining two-thirds to make a similar provision was due to thriftlessness. Men who are receiv- ing 255. an hour would do well not to lecture the, working classes about their improvidence in not making voluntary provision for the future out of their 255. a week. (Cheers.)

div.head: MONEY NOT SQUANDERED.
div.p: MONEY NOT SQUANDERED.

. Those who are attacking the Act suggest that the money has been squandered upon State offi- cials. Not a penny of this great sum is devoted towards paying the salaries and expenses of a single official of the State, 'except out of a special fund raised for that purpose. Luckily we fore- saw the kind of innuendo of which our opponents are capable, and we decided to put the whole charge on the State officials outside that sum of money. The gigantic sum of which the bulk is found ,by the State. either through the tax- payers or through the employers, is spent in assisting working men and women in times of sickness and unemployment, and if that is a fraud, all I can say is, it is a fraud of which the Tories are quite incapable. (Cheers.) Whilst this Act is hurrying about on its errand of mercy, visiting the sick, healing those. who are afflicted with disease, feeding hungry children whose parents have been prostrated by sickness and cannot look after them—whilst if is doing the work of the Man of Nazareth in the stricken homes of T3ritain, it is being stoned by Tory speakers, reviled, insulted, and snat upon. Their reckoning is piling up. It will soon be demanded at their hands to the last ,nenny— (cheersl—by a neonle who have been misled by them into disdaining one of the greatest gifts the Imperial Parliament has ever delivered to the people of this land, (Renewed cheers.)

div.head: RELIEF FOR TENDER FEET. WALKING MADE A PLEASURE INSTEAD OF A TORTURE.
div.p: RELIEF FOR TENDER FEET. WALKING MADE A PLEASURE INSTEAD OF A TORTURE.

Bright sunny summer days bring pain and torture in the form of tired, tender, burning feet to thousands of men and women. The pave- ments are hot to the touch, and it is no wonder that literally millions of people find walking a torture on account of their hot, perspiring, and blistered feet. Tight boots are sometimes .to blame, but more often the trouble is due to acid perspiration .of the feet, which actually destroys the cuticle, leaving the soft under-skin tender and raw to the touch, and easily blistered. To overcome this trouble, the acid must be neutral- ised by a. soothing and cooling neutralising agent, such as synthated talc, which should be shaken into the shoes and stockings every morning. Synthated talc, which can be obtained from any ghemist, not only neutralises the acid, cools the hot feet, and toughens the tender skin, but it also makes tight 'boots feel comfortable and roomy.

Soldiers and policemen, who a—re obliged to spend a large part of their time on their feet, find synthated talc- invaluable, as it keeps the feet . cool and comfortable in the hottest weather, and abscklutely prevents the formation of blisters..

div.head: MILLION RENT ROLL.
div.p: MILLION RENT ROLL.
Capital and Landownership.
(By F. C. IL DOUGLAS, M.A.)

The fact that the ownership of haduskrial capital in this country, and in most parts; of the world, is concentrated into the hands of a ' comparatively Iftw individuals is too notorious to be denied. Mr. Lloyd George told. us; in his Budget speech, that last year death duties "were paid upoill property which aggregated to £276,000,000. There were about 425,000 adult deaths last year. Of that £276,000,000 of pro- perty, one-third belonged to 292 persons; one- half to 1,300 persons; and two-thirds to 4%000 persons; while 350,000 adults died without any property upon which it WaS worth i anybody's while to pay the fewl shillings to obtain' the authority of the \lnland Bevenue legally to deal with."

It has often been contendecl. that this state of affairs is a necessary consequence of a com- petitive, or "capitalist," system of production ; but I hope to show that it is really due Co quite a different cause—to landlordism.

Land value, or ground value, or land rent, is the payment which must be made to the owners of the soil for permission to hire- on the earth and to make use of it.. It is a payment: which. as population increases, as inventiOns are made. as more and more efficient means of produc- tion are discovered, continually •increases. Thor°ld Rogers has said: "I could' show, if the nature of .my work required the proof, that land. for two miles round St. Paul's has increased, during the last hundred and fiVy years, a thous- andfold in value." And -there need be doubt that this is true of the country.. consid- ered .a.s.a. whole., Yet 'during' the whole of that period' which witnessed the great. develOpmenf and growth of modern industry. the wtiges of labour. rose .very little..To say that wages, in the course of that 150 years, rose fivefold' is pro- bably quite a fair estimate. But the value of land rose two hundred times as much. . Is it any wonder, then. that the ownership of 'capital has come Into the possession of a small minority? It could not Possibly be otherwise. From his scanty wage the labourer could not save and accumulate capital: the owner of the soil whose land continually increased in value through no effort of his own alone could. save and become a great capitalist.

div.head: MILLION RENT ROLL
div.p: MILLION RENT ROLL

The process still goes on continuously at the present. The workman may put by a few pence for a burial insurance, or some such object, but the Duke of Westminster, if he choose, can, from his rent roll of a million, easily save thousands or hundreds of thousands a year. If we talk abOut the rich becoming richer, and the poor poorer, surely here is the reason. And if the thing is finally to be put a stop to, then it is clear that there is no other way than to stop it at the source. The only means pf preventing this accumula- tion of capital into the hands of a few is to prevent these few, men from taking for their individual use the land values, which should have formed the collective capital of the people, since they are due to the people as a whole,- itind not to anything that the landlords have done. And the taking of land values in, taxation for public revenues would have consequences. even more important than the preventing of private individuals accumulating public earnings. It would enable the State to dispense with taxation levied on the food and homes of th( workers. Still- More important, by levying taxation on the value of land, whether used or unused, it would force the owners of land to put land to, the best use—either to use themselves, or to let it go into the possession' of others who could and 'would use' it--and so opening out wider and more -abundantly productive, oppor- tunities of employment would diminish the com- petition-of men for jobs and raise- wages. For. as Thorold IlogerS well .points out, the only cases • in which labour has been able 'to take advantage of inventions and improvements in the arts of producing wealth have occurred "when the distribution .of -employment lips become so exactly proportionate to the current demand for labour that demand has been always in excess of supply." It is this condition of demand for labour being always in excess of supply that the taxation of land values Will set up, because the, earth is the only thing from which wealth can be produced, and landoWners cannot hold it out of use if they are taxed on its selling value, and on that only. •

This is the line on which alone a solution can be found for this problem of concentration of capital. The labourer with higher wages, and with no taxes on his food, or rates on his home. may. if he choose, save and accumulate capital; on the other hand, .no one- will be able to accu- mulate capital out of the earnings of the nation: and so the present inequality—tyranny on the one side, dependence on the other—will dis- appear.

div.head: " TERRIERS " AT CHURCH. A Warning Against Sin.
div.p: " TERRIERS " AT CHURCH. A Warning Against Sin.

The 4th Batt: Prince of \Vales', Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment) paraded for Divine service at St. Paul's Church, Warrington, on Sunday. A good muster fell in at the Drill Hall, and, headed by the regimental band, marched to the church, under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel B. Fairclduel. 'About 50 members of the Army Service Corps, under Lieutenant H. Fairclough, also attended. Band- master Wainwright conducted the band, Which played the hymns in church. The Rev. 'W. Bracecainp conducted the ser- vice, and an eloquent sermon was preached by the Rev. Gardon' 'DOWsbn, curate of -HOly Trinity- Church-, -Walton Breck, Liverpool. The VICAR said they ,would have liked to have seen-more-Members 'present: The next time they:Would "meet would be in camp On the 24th inst. He Wighed them every sticeeSs in camp, and hoped they would have good health, plenty of exercise and hard work. As far as conduct was coneerned, they wanted them to do as they had done before. They wanted them to keep the good name they had always had. If they would do their dilly to the battalion and the brigade, they were assured of a good camp. Preaching from the text, "Be sure your sin will find you out" (Numbers xxxii. 23), the Rev. G. DAWSON said the text waA pre-eminently appropriate to the occasion, because it was spoken .by ,Moses to a section of a nation in arms, as a warning, and an incentive. He sup- posed a large number of those present. would be going to, comp for their annual period of training, and it was there that some of the usual and customary restraints of the ordinary civilised life ,would be lest. Whenever EEO was thp case, there were always temptations and trials to-beset Wan.

div.head: WARNING TEXT
div.p: A WARNING TEXT

The text was to be, taken generallY as a warning, and especially to those who were going to camp. :They should do their duty, even if certain restraints, which existed at home, were for the tithe. being loosened. Con- tinuing, the rev, gentleman dealt With the pun- ishment for sins coihniitted, and said that day follbwed night no more surely than, the penalty followed sin, whether that sin be great or small, habitual ,or through infirmity of the flesh. ,The truth of the text seemed to be ." when we had done with our sin, 'our sin would not be 'done Witn- us." No matter with what, good deeds they would try and hide,their sin, they would be tracked, and it would be made known to them that every evil done was evil to him who did it. He urged them pot to let their sin find them out, but they should find ,their sin out. and condemn themselves first. The beauty of the Christian religion was that they could take their hideous load .to Christ and he would for- give. At the close of the service the regimental band played the National Anthem.
