div.head: BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE BURIAL SOCIETY.
A Steady Increase in the Funds and
Lower Death Claims.
MORE MEMBERS WANTED.

The 42nd annual meeting of the Warrington Burial Society was held at the British Work- man Public-house, Horsemarket-street, on 'Monday. The attendance of members was ex- ceedingly good. The meeting was presided over by the President, Mr. Joseph W. Pomfrey, who was supported by the Vice-President, Mr. Wil- liam E. Clegg; the treasurer, Mr. James Parr; the trustees, Messrs. William Eckersley, James Gresty and Joseph Adams; the general secre- tary, Mr. Lawrence Weir; and others. The Chairman stated that-he Was pleased to meet them all that evening; he knew they had come to bear the _result .of their yearly stock- taking, and to have a just and true .account rendered to them of the work of the committee for the past year, and it was vers, gratifying. to him tti be able.to report the continued progress of the society. Their investments were of a sound and profit- able nature,and their thanks were due to Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co. for the efficient man- ner in which they had dealt with the committee and the legal portion of the business. He de- sired to compliment the permanent staff for their diligence. The meetings had at all times been of a• very harmonious nature, and it had been a pleasure to him to preside over them. They had in their secretary, Mr. Weir, a very able officer, and it was mainly due to his un- tiring energy that they were able to put before them such an encouraging balance sheet for the year. He exhorted the collectors to go. from that meeting with a determination to create a new, record both financially and numerically for the coming year. The General Secretary. Mr., Lawrence Woir, presented his annual balance Sheet, which showed that the society's funds now amourted to .t 5,007 10s. 21d., as against £4,744 10s. 24-d. the previous year, a. gain of .2263. The nnmerical condition was 1,581. as compared with 1.563 the year previous. The report further chewed that the society had mid away in death claims during the year .47 155.. as compared with 0f66 10s. the previons Year. The Secretary nointed out that the society had investor] on mortgage £4.555, and in the Corporation ..,1.150. INTEREST NEARLY PAYS EXPENSES.

He was pleased to say that the interest upon the total investments had, within a very small item, covered the whole of the working expenses during the year. The onlY drawback was the small quantity of entrants during the year, and though the competition was keen at present, he thought if the members put forth better efforts and laid themselves out for getting fresh business, there would be a different complexion in the numbers next year. The auditors, Messrs. David liarris and Frederick Massey, reported that the accounts and register kept by the General Secretary was correct, and, as usual, in perfect order; also the. books of the treasurer and 'collectors were correct and satisfactory. The bank books, Corporation bonds, mortgage investments and vouchers were produced for inspection, and the same were duly vouched. In the election of officers, Mr. William E. Clegg was unanimously elected president, and Mr. P. L. Edgar vice-president for the year. M. David Harris was elected auditor for the next two years.

Avery lengthy programme was gone through, the business chiefly effecting the general inter- est of the members as regards benefits. The following ,meinbers took part in the discussion: Messrs. John Haley, W. W. Ratcliffe, FrOstsk

div.head: SUFFRAGIST'S LITTLE HUBBY.
div.p: SUFFRAGIST'S LITTLE HUBBY.

In a police court in New York the magistrate had before him a little man named Lawrence Rupp, who was taken into custody on the com- plaint of his wife because he interrupted a speech she was delivering at a street corner on the suffrage. Mrs. Rupp said: " I have been married eigh- teen years, and always ,been a good wife. I was in the midst of my best period when my hus- band forced his way through the audience and shouted, 'Here is a woman who won't cook my supper, and won't put My children to bed because she wants to agitate for women's votes. What do you think of such womanf' Little boys began to hoot, and I caused- a policeman to arrest my husband for disorderly conduct." The magistrate, after severely telling the hus- band that he had no right to interfere with his wife's activities, dismissed him under suspended sentence.

div.head: HOLIDAY INSURED PATIENTS.
div.p: THE HOLIDAY INSURED PATIENTS.

The green ticket which entitles insured per- son§ to medical attendance whilst away from home on holiday has been a subject of corre- spondence between the Lancashire Insurance Committee and the Insurance Commissioners. The Lancashire Medical Benefit Sub-Com- mittee represented to the Commissioners that if any large number of insured persons made application there would be 51 pressure on the staff at holiday times which would be impos- sible to cope with. The Commissioners replied suggesting that the staff should be temporarily increased to meet emergencies of this kind. The sub-committee, however, have passed a resolution that they "Will try to make all necessary arrangements to supply the voucher to those persons who may require m!dical treat- ment during temporary absence from home."

div.head: SHUNTING ACCIDENT.
div.p: SHUNTING ACCIDENT.
Coroner's Strong Comments on recent
Sankey Fatality.
The inquest on the body of John Lee (46), 85, Fox-street, Warrington, was held at the Coroner's Court on Monday, before Coroner Brighouse.

There were present at the inquiry Mr. H. E. Brothers (inspector of factories), Mr. T. E. Knowles (for the relatives), Mr. Johnson (Liver- pool, for the L. and N.-W. Railway Company), ,and Mr. Sloan (managing director for the Mer- sey White Lead Company). . The Coroner said that the man was a general labourer ernployed by the Mersey White Lead Company. On Thursday afternoon of last week he was assiating a shunter named Burgess in shunting two waggons into a siding at the works. Deceased had hold of the brake, and when the waggon got near its destination he failed to let go, and was trapped between the Waggon and the wall. receiving injuries, from which he died at the Infirmary on Friday-. William Burgess, Si. Plumpton-street, said the siding down which they were shunting was slightly downhill to .the works. As the wag- gons appeared to be travelling rather fast, he shouted tO deceased, who was then working at a furnace, to put the brake on the first wag- gon, whilst he (witness) put, the brake on the second. Deceased lowered the- brake lever and sat on the handle.

The next witness saw was the deceased caught between the wall and the waggon. He seemed to get free, but before he could get away he was trapped by the second waggon. He was attended by Dr. Gandhi, and taken to the In- firmary.

div.head: NO CHANCE TO STOP WAGOON.
div.p: NO CHANCE TO STOP WAGOON.

Cross-examined: Burgess said there was no chance to stop the waggons by the use of one brake only; he had to obtain assistance. The waggons were travelling at the rate of abuut five miles per lour. There was a buttress on the side of the wall. Detective Holland informed the Coroner that the buttress was to be taken away that after- noon.

The Coroner: That is like locking the stable door when the horse t ird gone. Legislation ought to step in to prevent them putting lines close up to a building. In answer to Mr. Knowles, Burgess said that in order to stop the waggon effectively Lee had to sit on the brake. The destination of the waggons was about eight yards in front of the buttress.
By Mr. Johnson: lie gave instructions to the driver to put the waggons in motion, The Coroner: The accident would not have happened if there had been no buttress?-1t 'would not.
John William Jones, railway porter for the L. and N.-W. Railway Company at Sankey Bridges, corroborated .the last witness's evi- dence. •

Mr. Sloan said he did not think the speed of the waggons would be five miles per hour. The waggons Would not have done any harm if they had been allowed to run down. They only went a/few yards past the buttress. Lee was carrying out his duties by assisting the shunter with the waggons. It was his (witness) in- tention to have the buttress removed.

div.head: CORONER'S COMMENTS
div.p: CORONER'S COMMENTS

The Coroner said the crtilear nie whole case was that there was not sufficient space between the lines and the building. Perhaps when the next regulations were passed it would be laid down that there must be sufficient 'space between the waggons running On a siding and the building. If there were such regulations, it would tend to the -preservation of life, but, of course, they must kill a lot of people before something was done. He spoke from experience. In connection with the new docks at Bootle, they had rules and regulations, and he felt certain tfiat by passing such rules they had depreciated the number of deaths ,by 50 per cent. When a man went into employment it. was not right that he should be subjected to unnecessary danger. They appreciated the attitude of Mr. Sloan when he said they were going to have the buttress down at once. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." and expressed their sympathy with the .bereaved Telatives.

div.head: COUNCIL TO RECONSIDER MATTER
div.p: COUNCIL TO RECONSIDER MATTER

The wages question of the Council employees who do not come under the overtime clause was Tuesday evening, and it was discussed at the meeting of the Warrington 'all'elviegliedCthuanteliceolinsiderable number of employees were working under sweated conditions. The General Purposes Committee submitted the following resolution : position of the Mayor the com- mitteeOn ctohnesildneered the resolution passed by the Council at their last meeting, with reference to extra pay for Sunday work, when it was re- solved: That the following classes of workmen in the -employ of the Corporation, whose duties and remuneration are already fixed to cover Sunday work, be excluded from the scope of the resolution Passed by the Council on the lst July, 1913, with reference to the payment of a rate not less than time and a half for such work Caretakers and cleaners of municipal buildings and their staffs, caretakers of school premises and their staffs, resident engineers and other employees, hospital staffs and of Police force, Cemetery gravediggers dants, park keepers and a ee nr d r ne st si d, e n at n d members attendants, tt en o gardeners when acting as park keepers, fore- men, baths attendants, members of fire brigade (with 'the exception of the engineer and his assistant, when engaged in duties other than extinguishing fires).' " An amendment to refer the matter back was moved by Councillor WILSON. He said that he could not see why the workers named might not be paid overtime like the others. Caretakers had to do a tremendous amount of work, some of it on Sundays. The nurses in the hospitals were poorly paid, considering the long hours they worked, and the dangerous calling they followed. They could not get away, and were long periods on duty.

div.head: "A STAGGERING BLOW?"
div.p: "A STAGGERING BLOW?"

The figures in regard to the baths had been a staggering blow to him. The condition of the baths workmen was absolutely a scandal to the town. Some of the attendants worked 76 flours' a week for 28s. (" Shame.") The baths attend- ants at Manchester worked 531 hours and 541- hours. The boiler man at the baths at War- rington worked 78 hours a week for 255. (A Voice: " Goodness gracious !") There was a good case to be made out why the men he had named should be paid time and a half for Sun- day work. At the present time they had men working 76 and 78 hours a week, in one case— that of the boilerman—for less than 4d. an hour. -He thought he was asking a reasonable thing when he sought overtime for these men. Councillor OSBORNE said it was a perfect dis- grace that in an enlighten 'ed town like War- rington they should allow such an amount of sweating to go on.

div.head: SWEATED WOMEN.
div.p: SWEATED WOMEN.

lie was surprised to hear that the boilerman at the baths .worked 78 Lours a meek and was paid leas than 4d. an hour. It was not long since-there was. sweating of a deliberate charac- ter carried out in connection with the baths when women worked almost naked—wearing only a slight covering—while cleaning towels, and so on. He thought the men they were pleading for were unfairly paid. They should at least be paid a living wage. Councillor BROADHURST supported the with- drawal of the resolution, not because they were in conflict with the Mayor, who had introduced it, but because of the cases that had been brought to light. A glaring case was where a foreman, with 13 men under him, was paid 28s. per week, and received not a single farthing for the extra work he did. Councillor PEACOCK said that Messrs. Wilson and Broadhurst did not attend the General Pur- poses Committee, when the matter was under discussion. If the matter was referred back, would they promise to attend the committee? Would they attend and go into the details of "this twopenny halfpenny business"? (Voice: "Shame.") Councillor WILSON: It is not a twopenny ha'penny business, and I am not going to let you use these words. ("Order.")

div.head: " TUPENNY lIA'PENNY."
div.p: " TUPENNY lIA'PENNY."

Councillor PEACOCK thought they could not take up the public time by going into the de- tails. • They went thoroughly into it in the General Purposes Committee, and they thought they had come to a reasonable decision. Councillor WiLsoN said he had to -get his liv- ing and could not always be at the meetings of the committee, but no man had given more of his life to the town's service than he. "I know," he said, "the reason why it is thought a twopenny ha'penny affair; it is because it has come from ` tupenny ha'penny' Wilson." The MAYOR: You should not say that. You are raising ill-feeling and doing your case harm. Several councillors and' aldermen appealed for the matter to be re-considered. Councillor PEMBERTON : If you were giving a .2100 rise to an official with A:600 a year, nobody would say anything_ about it.

The MAYOR.' saielle-Ti-iWd justice to both sides, but not one-sided justice. There were two sides to every .point, and one side had as much right to be considered as the other. He did not intend to go into the matter that night, although he had answers to almost every point that Councillor Wilson had raised. He agrerAl to the matter being withdrawn.

div.head: TRADES COUNCIL RESOLUTION.
div.p: TRADES COUNCIL RESOLUTION.

The matter was referred to at a meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council en Tuesday night, and the following resolution was passed : " That this Council, representing the Allied Trade Unions of Warrington, protest against the exclusion of the. various Corporation em- ployees from the increased overtime rates. "-We are of opinion that these workers, bay- ing no rest day each week, are as ti.ucii mtled to extra remuneration as others, who are occa- sionally requestedato work on Sundays."

div.head: MOST LUCID SPEAKER.
div.p: MOST LUCID SPEAKER.
A Warrington Pastor Pays a Tribute to Mr. Lloyd George.
" LIMEHOUSING" MYTH.

Liberal enthusiasm is increasing in Warring- ton, and one had striking evidence in support of this statement at the weekly meeting of the Pro- gressive Labour League at Bridge Foot on Mon- day. A crowd of close upon 500 assembled, and were fully rewarded for any special effort they made to be present, for the speeches were of a most interesting and educational nature, the true note of progressiiie Liberalism being sounded by the Rev. H. Ogden (who occupied the chair), the Rev. Harry Ross, and Mr. E. Wynne Jones. At the outset, the CHAIRMAN said he belonged to that particular party which would give him Most; that party which would advance his ideals. "Was it possible," he asked, "that any party in this generation could give them as much as the Liberal Government had given them dur- ing the last seven years?" He ventured to assert, and , thought every fair-minded man would agree with, him, that there was no other party in the State that could possibly have carried out the beneficent reforms which they had had since the Liberal Govern- ment came into being. Dealing with reforms which were still necessary, the, reverend gentle- man said that the _school -age for children ought to be advanced. But people said: "We cannot afford to keep our children at school." In his (the speaker's) opinion, the man with 18s. per week and five little children was more a national asset than the millionaire with no children, and the man with 18s. per week should have the State help, in order that his children should have the education they deserved. Give them that education now, and it made easier of solu- tion the problems of to-morrow. He found himself on the side of the Liberal party because they were the ones who were active; doing some- thing very material now, for the present genera- tion. (Hear, hear.) They would move very much quicker if they could. If it was not for the fact that Lloyd George was hampered by an historic nation, things would "hum." (Hear, , hear.) After illustrating the worthlessness of Tory promises by instancing the promising of old-age pensions for 20 years, the speaker said that immediately the Liberal party got into office they set to work and got that great measure passed. The Old-age Pensions Act was the gospel compulsorily put into practice, the ser- mon on the Mount put into a national statute. In regard to the latest piece of legislation for the social amelioration of the people—the Insur- ance Act—he said that it was ti very good thing that Lloyd George could stand all the vitupera- tion which had been heaped upon him. One did glory in the fact that the brave little Welshman had withstood all the vituperation poured upon him, and had pursued faithfully and steadfastly the end and aim of the ideals he had in life. (Hear, hear.) One had a great deal of venera- tion for Gladstone, but he would venture to say that for his day Lloyd George was even greater than Gladdtone was in his greatest days.

div.head: MOST LUCID ORATOR,
div.p: THE MOST LUCID ORATOR,

Someone had told him that Lloyd George was a Limehouser, a Billingsgatite ; but he would state definitely. that the Chancellor was the greatest and most lucid orator to-day. The Insur- ance Act meant that the people should have an abundant share of the good things which God had provided; that the awful spectre of sickness, poverty and want were banished from every door. If they could only give the Chancellor 20 years of untrammelled operation he would make this land of ours really the Merrie England. Here, in Warrington, they could show their loyalty to the Government by giving Mr. Harold Smith the rightabout, and putting Mr. Crosfield in the House of Commons. (Applause.)

The Rev. HARRY Ross said we had come to one of the most interesting periods in the political history of the country. Similar to the process of the seasons; we had come quite close to the harvest time. The Liberal party had been striving to make the harvest the greatest and best in the history of the country. There was a magnificent crop ripening and waiting to be gathered. (Hear, hear.) They had set them- selves to remove the only obstacle which stood in the way of reaping a full harvest. They were out to secure the absolute veto of the House of Lords. It was not removed yet, but they had got the promise of it. and they had something of the poignancy of the promise. Some, of the seeds sown in years gone by, some sown in tears, bitterness, and blood, had sprouted, and there was a harvest waiting to be reaped, but what was interfering? Why was not the Home Rule Bill an Act of Parliament' at this moment? It was not because the people of England had re- fused to accept it. (Hear, hear.) Why was not the Church of England in Wales disestablished? It was because the people of Wales had not asked for it repeatedly, and by an overwhelming rnaiority. It was not because the British House of Commons had refused to grant Wales what they had asked for. They had not become laws because that unholy anaehronism—the House of Lords—had survived. (Hear, hear.) Instead of the Liberal doctrine, "Government of the people by the people for the people," they had substi• tilted "Government of the people by, those people who think they know and considered that they had a right to dictate to the people." The people had thought that they had won the fight with the House of Lords when they swallowed the Budget of 1910; reluctantly accepted the Old- age Pensions Act, and the Insurance Act, which no statesman dare pro/Km to repeal. (Hear, hear.) They had ewallowed them because they thought that .if they did not they would choke. (Laughter.) 'The House of Lords must be taught to spell tile word "Must," and for them to be taught thif lesson enshrined in that word depended on the staunchness and rigidity of the people.

div.head: MARVELLOUS ACHIEVEMENTS.
div.p: MARVELLOUS ACHIEVEMENTS.

The speaker then lucidly and interestingly dealt with the "marvellous achievements of the Liberal party in the financial and Imperialisa- tion affairs of the country." He said that the Liberals had paid off the debts incurred by the Tory Government in the quickest way that any Government could possibly do. (Hear, hear.) Dealing with Imperial affairs, he said that the true way to spell " Empire " was "Home." That was where they had the centre and the citadel of our British Empire. It mattered not what dominions we had unless the homes of the people were the castles of the Britisher. The homes of the workers should be secured to them, the people should have plenty of nourishing food, and the children should have plenty of fresh air and clean water. They might say those were parochial things, but they were very vital mat- ters, for, unless they had sound men and women at home, they could not maintain the Empire. It was not the multiplying of Dreadnoughts, not the bringing of our bpys and girls into the folds of, the National Service League, that brought us our security, but it was because of the principle of righteousness, which truly exhalteth a nation.

The Liberal Government had made history as glorious and as memorable as ever had been made in our long island story. • When the Chairman said he belonged to the party which gave him most he meant to say the party which gave us most, for there never was a Government which had done so much for the people as the present Liberal party. Amongst all the splendid things this Govern- ment had .done during the last seven years the greatest and best was that they had preserved us from the crass folly and unimaginable dis- aster of having Tariff Reform round our necks. Tariff Reform was nothing but a gigantic gamble —a big speculation. The only people who would benefit out of Tariff, Reform were those who could afford to pay ,21,000 to dine with the Duke of Westminster. He had once asked an audience what Tariff Reform was, and one man had slid, "Tommy Rot." "And," concluded the speOter, "he was right." (Applause.).

div.head: TORIES WOULD BE DELIGHTED.
div.p: TORIES WOULD BE DELIGHTED.

Mr. E. WYNNE JONES commented on the fact that they had such an extraordinarily large meeting, and said that the Tory party would be delighted to have such a large audience as that. (Hear, hear.) Much had been said that night (Continued :n next column.)

div.head: SCHOLARS MENACED.
div.p: SCHOLARS MENACED.
Some 350 Endangered by 100 Tuberculous Children.
COUNCIL DISCUSS THE EVIL.

Tuberculosis in children was stated to be proving a menace to scores of scholars in War- rington schools, and it has now been suggested that the Education Committee should assist in the work, in conjunction with the Council, in removing the menace. _ .

The matter was dealt with at Warrington Town Council on Tuesday night; when the Health Committee reported that they had had an interview with the Local Government Board on the subject of the proposed alterations and additions to Sankey Sanatorium.

Alderman JAMES w EVANS said that interview had taken place, and they had every reason to be satisfied with the results. They might in some measure, at any rate, congratulate them- selves that the way was now open for the com- pletion of theit work, so far as the sanatorium arrangements were concerned, or so far as the Health Committee contemplated. The Alderman said that the Health Committee had considered the question of the education of tuberculous children, and proposed that a sub-committee be appointed to confer with the Education Committee upon the ques- tion, and that the‘Chairman, the Deputy-Chair- man, the Mayor, Alderman Tinnion, and Coun- cillor Broadhurst be appointed a sub-committee.

div.head: VERY SERIOUS MATTER.
div.p: A VERY SERIOUS MATTER.

"This takes in another aspect of the tuber- culosis question,' said Alderman James Evans. "This matter, which is very serious, was tirst brought up by the Medical Officer of Health. He looks upon the juvenile section who are affected as' a very serious matter, and demand- ing some consideration from the Health Com- mittee. I may point out that between the ages of 41 years and 13 years, there are over 100 children that are in some measure affected with this disease, and it is for the purpose of pre- vention that the Medical Officer is moving in this matter. We think when our arrangements at Sankey are completed it will be compara- tively easy for the Health Committee to deal with the juvenile section?' (Hear, hear.) It was necessary that they should be able to deal with the whole of the population affected with consumption, and first, as a preventive measure, they should deal with the juvenile section, or they were only doing half the work. The committee thought, and were very anxious, that something should be done on those lines. (Hear, hear.) In carrying out the arrangements at Sankey, the Health Committee would render assistance to meet the particular requirements. It was an important matter on educational lines, so far as the Education Committee was concerned, and the committee would be delighted to have the cohesion and co-operation of the Education authority to help them to deal with the child- life of the town, so far as tubercular disease was concerned. (Hear, hear,)

div.head: SCHEME TO BE PREPARED.
div.p: SCHEME TO BE PREPARED.

They could not at present lay before the Council the scheme of the committee, but he would give an undertaking that before the com- mittee were finally committed to any scheme, that all its financial bearings would be laid before the Council. With regard to the interview with the Local Government Board, he said they would not insist upon costly buildings, but would give the Corporation some latitude :with rOgard to temporary buildings ,an 4 the question of deal- ing with isolation of smallpox. They gained a very great point altogether. Alderman BURTON seconded, and said he agreed with all that Alderman James Evans had said.

The MAYOR said he quite agreed with what the Chairman of the Health Committee had said about the -importance of tuberculous children being treated in co-operation with the Education Committee. It was more important from the fact that the diseases, such as diseased glands, were almost peculiar to children, and when they came to adult age they were ren- dered unfit for the useful work of life. It was common knowledge that children liable to these tubercular diseases were not liable to consump- tion of the lungs when they became adults. The danger was during childhood, and it was necessary that their bodies and minds should be treated at the same time.

div.head: NASTY PRACTICE.
div.p: A NASTY PRACTICE.

Alderman JAMES EVANS said there were 103 children known to be affected in the borough; and there were 350 school children in actual contact with those cases, out of the 13,000 children on the school registers. Councillor OSBORNE made a reference to the obnoxious practice of spitting on the streets, and pointed out that the Health Committee had resolved that the Town Clerk should pre- pare a by-law dealing with the matter. Round many of the public buildings, and par- ticularly with regard to one of the railway sta- tions, he said, it was very objectionable to sect people lounging about, spitting, causing incon- venience, with no doubt a lot of ill-health to people. He suggested that a notice after the manner of that exhibited outside public build- ings in America should be displayed, namely: "Ladies do not, gentlemen will not, and others must not-spit." (Laughtar ) • The minutes were adopted.

• MOST LUCID SPEAKER.—Coatinued. about the Empire, and he (the speaker) 'agreed with Mr.Wilj Crooks when he said "What's the use of talking about an Empire on which the sun never sets, when it never rises in your own backyards." The Liberal party were not of the Lord Ridley type. That noble scion, speaking on Tariff Reform, said that "Compared with the interests of the British Empire, the pros- perity of the working man was a side issue." The Liberals said that it was the welfare of the great mass of working classes—three-quarters of the population of the country—who ought to have first consideration. (Hear, hear.) They were the people who had the greatest stake in this country. The rich man, by bad laws and wicked customs, might have to go without some luxury, but the working men may lose all by bad laws. The Liberal party were striving to get the best and most beneficent measures passed, for the benefit of the masses of the country, and were, therefore, deserving of every support. The House of Lords had wanted to keep the Home Rule - and Disestablishment questions dangling before the electors, in order to turn their minds from the great social measures which had to be attended to by the Government of to-day. What had the Tories to offer as an alternative to Liberal proposals? Simply noth- ing. All their talk was "brag, bluster, and un- mitigated bluff?? (A Voice: "Why have the Tories not given Ireland Home Rule?") "All , they have done in regard to that," said Mr. Jones, "has been to toy with it for several years, but the Irish will get it before long." (Applause.)

div.head: LANDLORD'S TARIFFS.
div.p: THE LANDLORD'S TARIFFS.

Speaking of the latest Liberal project, Mr. Jones said that underneath our industrial pro- blem was the land question, and the Liberals were going to deal very drastically with that drag on the wheels of industry. They may talk about the foreign tariffs, but the tariffs the land- lord heaped against the people were worse than 'any coming from a foreign quarter. But the barrier must come dowp ; the landlord class was not to have the monopoly over the land, because if they gave people the power to monopolise land they gave them the power to monopolise life. No one had the right to claim that power, no mat- ter whether he be duke, landlord, or anything. (Hear, hear-)

The Liberal party was the only party in the State to-day who could do anything effective in the interests of the working classes, and they would, still go on with their excellent programme until we were really a happy and contented nation. (Applause.)
_ On Mr. Jones' proposition, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the speaker and Chairman.

div.head: LADY BOWLERS.
div.p: THE LADY BOWLERS.
Men Break Records—ln Language— When Women are on the Green. AN AMUSING DISCUSSION.

Lady bowlers on the Warrington bowling greens were, at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening, alleged to cause such a nuisance to the male players that it was proposed the ladies should have only the use of the greens three hours per week. It was iialso stated that the women trundlers caused the men to use unnecessarily• strong language, because they played into the men's lengths. The discussion arose over the following in the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee : , The head gardener submitted a report as to the, number of ladies using the bowling greens, and instructions were given that on all days, with the exception of those specially reserved for ladies, the bowling greens be re- served for men only." Councillor BROADHURST said it was deplorable that the committee should introduce such a drastic motion as that which only allowed ladies three hours per week on the greens. Why should lady shop assistants be debarred from a game at any other time but on a Thursday afternoon? They would only be allowed three hours a week in which to bowl, and for those with families and other iittle troubles—(laughter)--this recreation would pull them up more than anything else. Shop assistants, whose half-holiday was on Thursday, would be debarred for ever from en- joying a game of that description. He moved that the resolution should be referred back. Councillor DICKENSON : I won't withdraw it.
The MAroR,: You know the ladies cannot play bowls, as a rule, the same as men. They stop in the middle of the length. • Councillor BROADHURST : They will learn.
The MAYOR: It is a question of strength. Councillor BROADHURST : I am prepared to move a resolution if the Chairman won't withdraw it. Councillor DrcEENsoN : No.

div.head: NO DISGRACE.
div.p: NO DISGRACE.
Councillor BROADHURST : It would be no dis- grace to withdraw a resolution of this descrip- tion. ("No.") I propose this objectionable minute be withdrawn.

Alderman BENNETT seconded. He said they heard a good deal about injustice to women, and they were doing an injustice. Did they think if the Council consisted half of men and half of women they would pass such a resolution? (" No," and laughter.) Women should have the same opportunity for recreation as men, and the bowling greens gave the poorer women an opportunity for recreation. If it was the duty of the Council 'to cater for the male section, it was as necessary to cater for the female section. The latter required recreation as much as the males, and enjoyed it quite as much. It was a mistake to limit that to one sex, and they had not done their duty when they had planted a few trees and flowers for the women to admire.

The MAYOR: There is one thing that strikes me. The women cannot play at the same time as the men. The- only solution wpuld be to have separate bowling greens for the women, but that is for the committee to decide.
Councillor BIRTLES said lady shop assistants could only go on Thursday afternoons.
"JUSTICE TO WOMEN."

Councillor OSBORNE said that the committee's proposal was doing the women justice. It was not feasible or practical for the women to use the greens at the same time as the men. The women did not bowl quite as long lengths, and very often got into the way of the men who bowled. He thought the motion that the minute should be referred back ought to be with- drawn. It was passed after due consideration, and was entirely in the interests of women.

Councillor JENKINS suggested that one green in Victoria Park should be reserved for women on Thursday afternoons. He was sure the men would not be so selfish as to want both greens. Councillor lIENsnALL said that they contem- plated new tennis courts for women in Lovely- lane.
Councillor BROADHURST : For the Baths Com- mittee to jump to such a conclusion is prema- ture. Give the ladies a fair chance.
Councillor DICKENSON : I object to this.

The MAYOR: That is another speech. Councillor DICKENSON said he protested against Councillor Broadhurst and Alderman Bennett raising the question. Neither of them had ever visited the greens when the ladies had bebn bowling—(Councillor Pemberton: "Shame," and laughter)—or he did not think they would have brought forward such a motion.

div.head: "MORE FILTHY LANGUAGE."
div.p: "MORE FILTHY LANGUAGE."

"I have been on the green," ,continued Coun- cillor Dickenson, "when ladies have beep bowling —(Mr. Pemberton: " Ilkar, hear," and laugh- ter)--ind the accidents through the ladies bowl- ing into the crown of the green, and taking the whole green, have been the cause of more flithy language being used than. I have ever heard before. (Laughter.) There were two ladies bowlink continuously round the side of the green and the woods of the men were being knocked from place to place. I have never seen more than three or four women on the green at once." On a division. only Messrs. Broadhurst and Bennett voted for the withdrawing cf the minute, which was thus adopted.

div.head: CO-OPERATORS AND INCOME TAX
div.p: CO-OPERATORS AND INCOME TAX

In replying to a request of the Drapf;rs' Chamber of Trude that co-operative societies should be assessed for income tax on profits made, Mr. Masterman says the suggestion that co-operators escape the tax is based on a mis- conception.

div.head: CHURCHILL'S CRUISER.
div.p: CHURCHILL'S CRUISER.
Remarkable Vessel Passes Warrington
Outward Bound.
ARMED ON SHIP CANAL.
(" Examiner" Special.)

Silently and slowly on Sunday morning there glided along the Ship Canal, outward bound, past Warrington, the most remarkable vessel which has ever passed our doors. She has gone past on other occasions, out- ward bound to Australia, and inward bound to Manchester, but then she was a common trad- ing liner. On Sunday she passed out as an armed merchantman, the' third or fourth Of a considerable fleet of traders to be equipped with guns, and a gunners' crew, -under the scheme, recently introdtred by Mr. Whist, .:1 Churchill, to provide a new type of auxivAry cruisers. Thus her -outward trip of Sunday was of unusual interest.

The vessel was the ss. Shropshire, a ship of about 7,000 tons, and one of the largest which voyages along the canal. Somewhat of a record has been set up by the ship, as she was the first vessel to carry any type of gun that was ,equipped with the means for attack and defence at an inland port. Never in history has Manchester seen guns of a naval type mounted upon a ship in the docks.

.At the week-end a train laden with two powerful 4.7 quick-firing guns, of the kind which so materially assisted in the defence of Lady- smith, and carrying a large squad of naval armourers from Chatham, arrived at No. 9, the largest dock. at Manchester. Meanwhile a specially built armour plate of light character had been forwarded from SI-left-leld. Guns Speedily Mounted.

The armourers speedily got to work upon the vessel's quarter's, and soon the weighty guns were in position, along with the armour plate protection screen, which consists of hard, specially prepared steel, two inches thick. The guns have a wide range, and are most effective when firing astern. The shot can fravel four miles, and twelve rounds a minute can be fired. This novel vessel was visited !':f nytay inter- ested spectators on Saturiv. A special crew of Naval Reserve men, who are thoroughly familiar with the type of weapon mounted upon the Shropshire, have been engaged to man 'the ship. It is expected that some practice will be engaged in en route to Australia; whence the vessel is bound with a general cargo of Lancashire goods. "What is your opinion about this type of cruiser?" an " Examiner " representative asked one of the gunner's crew. "Well, they are as yet an experiment, and ,one cannot venture a guess what might •h-ap- pen if we actually came into contact with an enemy. I should think. hlwev,.!r, that we would be able to make good shooting."
For a Running Fight. "Against an enemy's Dreadnought?" ho was asked.

"No. It is scarcely likely, if ever the Shrop- shire had to be used in warfare, that we would tackle a battleship, or "a thoroughly armed cruiser. There are some people who think that our mission is to attack such warships, and they talk and write about our poor chance of escaping from such a battle. It is a• very foolish bit of imagination. The Shropshire, or any other armed merchantman, will not be engaged in that class of work. "Our guns, which would be useless against the heavier armament of a , Dreadnought or a cruiser, are mounted, so that _if war does take place, we could help to defend ourselves against attacks from torpedo boat destroyers and other small fry. In war time the small craft would be detailed to cut out merchant vessels. We could not run away from these ,greyhounds of the Navy, but if one or two attempted to chase us we should be in the position to give them a hot welcome.

"The destroyers of every nation carry guns of a much lighter type, and with a shorter range, than the 4.7 guns we thave mounted. Thus we could begin to pepper a pursuer long before she could get the ran.4e gif her guilt:, the possibility is that we could sink a destroyer before she could get near enough to strike us with a shell from her smaller type of guns.

A Chance of Escape. "'This would give us a chance to escape, where, without guns, we would be wholly at the mercy of the destroyer, or torpedo boat. "It is a good idea, but only actual practice can tell how. IL will operate. I hope we shall. not have, any occasion to learn from actual experience!' . "And the crew, will they make 'good fighters?" he was asked. Scanning a number of the men in view of the point of the deck upon which we stood, he answered :

"They seem a tough lot, and I reckon by the time they have done a few trips with us they will be well up to their new jobs. Of course, we, the special men, will man the guns." The Shropshire, with her guns wrapped in tarpaulin, and waterproof covers, passed War- rington on Sunday. There is a probability that some of her sister ships will be similarly armed when they arrive in the Ship Canal.

reached the road Lorrimer was bespattered all over. So was Leslie, for that matter, but it did not greatly trouble him. Soon after they struck into it several motors tore along the highway, and the white dust which whirled in the wake of them stuck in Lorrimer's hair, sprinkled his wet serge jacket, and clung to his damp skin. By-and-bye he sat down be- neath a hedgerow. "It's quite impossible for me to walk into the town like this," he said, and Leslie ad- mitted that it was at least not desirable. "You will have to go on and try to get a cab at the station. Then you can send it back to me." "The station," objected Leslie, "is more than a mile on the other glide of the town, and this isn't the kind of day on which one feels the least desire to walk any further than is necessary. Any way, I'll have a smoke first." He took out his pipe, and while they sat in the shadow a char-a-banc filled with excur- sionists went by. They gazed at the bare- headed Lorrimer with quite excusable curi- osity, and when some of them asked him deri- sive questions his face grew savagely red. It was a somewhat trying situation for a man who thought a good deal of his appearance, and was known as a leading member of a very ex- clusive yacht club, but Leslie felt that it was .probably good for him. Eventually a brilliant Idea ,struck the latter as a yan - with- an an- nouncement that the man it belonged to sup- plied the choicest bread and flour, came along. "Now," he said, "there's the very thing. I've no doubt he would drive you in." Lorrimer gazed at him in indignant astonishment. "Well," he said, "I suppose it's the only kind of suggestion one could ex- pect from you. No doubt you wouldn't mind driving along the promenade, wet through, outside a bread van, when everybody's about." "I meant inside," said Leslie. "Nobody could possibly see you." This appealed to Lorrimer, and he per- mitted Leslie to stop the van. The driver ap- peared to be a good-humoured person, and Leslie, who bundled ,his companion into the interior, took care to snap the hasp of the door so that he could not get out until somebody released him. Then he climbed up beside the driver. , "He'll give you half-a-crown if you'll take him into the town," he said. "You see, he's rather bashful, and doesn't want to be noticed." "No wonder ! " said the vanman. "I wouldn't either if I looked like that. What's he been doing?" "Well," said Leslie, in his dryest manner, "for one thing, he had a bathe." The driver laughed, and imitated a man raising a glass to his lips. "When I bathe," he said, " I like to take off my clothes." Leslie made no answer to this. He was quite aware that appearances were against Lorrimer, but that was no concern of his. The man, he decided, deserved no pity. Be- sides, he had reasons for believing that Mabel Carwardine shrank from him, though it was clear that he had her strong-willed mother's favour. By-and-bye they reached the edge of the little town, and Leslie, who was not a very conventional young man, bade his companion drive right on. "Where am I going to take you to?" asked the man. "To the Sea View," said Leslie. "That's where all the smart folks stay,", objected his companion. As a rule, my friend inside is one of the smartest of them.', "If you hadn't told me, I'd never have be- lieved it," said the vanman. In due time they approached the hotel, which stood back on slightly higher ground, with a stretch of garden between it and the promenade. The big, shady verandah in the front of it was a favourite lounge on a hot afternoon, and Leslie was not astonished to see Major and Mrs. Carwardine and Mabel still sitting there. A number of their ac- quaintances were also sitting close by. " Which door?" asked the driver. "The front," said Leslie, carelessly. "Go straight up the drive." The van had, however, hardly reached the steps when a man in resplendent uniform strode out of the hall, and waved his hand. "The other entrance for all tradesman's stores," he said, shortly. " Stores ! " exclaimed the driver. got a man who's staying here inside." Then he pulled up, and it became evident that most of the party on the verandah had heard him, for they gathered along the balus- trade, while Major Carwardine strode to the head of the stairway, and beckoned to Leslie whoa ne got dow4 "Will you explain what you mean by this?" he asked, standing very upright, and growing red in the face. "Well," said Leslie, quietly, "I had to bring Lorrimer home, and there wasn't a cab about." " Lorrimer ! Where is he?" and Mrs. Car- wardine ,joined her husband now. "He's in the van," said Leslie. Then, while Carwardine followed him down the steps, he ran round to the back of the van, and heard a muffled scuffling inside. " Let me out! Where are we?" a half- heard voice cried. Leslie cautiously opened the door an inch or two. "You're at home," he said. "At home ! " said the voice. "What do yon mean by home? I don't live within„ sixty miles of here. I want to be taken to a little quiet pub—up a back street somewhere—you besotted imbecile ! " Leslie turned round and saw Major Car- wardine standing close behind him very grim ia the face. "Yes," said the latter, "that explains it! It's the most fitting place for him. It's a pity you didn't fall in with his wishes. It would at least have saved him from being turned out of the Sea View." "What are you talking for?" cried Lorri- mer, from behind the door. "Let me out if it's a quiet place. If not, drive on. Can't you hear?" It was evident to Leslie that his companion was very, angry, and did not know, where he was, but just then a clerk came out of the the hotel and walked quickly up to the van. "We can't have any disturbance here," he said to the driver. -" Get ,up on your box and drive away, at once. , - - "I've got one of your. guests inside," said the man. "He seems kind of violent, and won't come out." The clerk was evidently startled, which was, perhaps, not astonishing. He had seen guests arrive in motors cabs, and station 'buses but this was the, first ' time one had ever been driven there inside a bread van. He looked round as though uncertain what to do, and Leslie noticed' that Mrs. Carwardine stood at the head of the stairway, while her daughter leant on the balustrade not far away, and apparently half the guests in the hotel had flocked out upon the verandah. Just then, however, Lorrimer apparently lost his patience, for the door of the van flew open with a crash, and he came out back- wards, then stood still a moment, apparently dazzled by the change from darkness to the bright sunlight. He did not look very much drier than when he got in;' his garments clung creased and wrinkled about his limbs; and there was now flour all over him. In another moment or two he evidently saw the interested audience watching him, - and Car- wardine's grim face. Perhaps he also saw that - Mrs. Carwardine had turned erimBon with anger, and that Mabel was studiously looking away from him. Nobody could have fancied that she was anxious to claim him as an acquaintance. In any case, he swung round suddenly, and striding along beneath the verandah vanished through a little gate in the wall of tlo garden. Then the clerk looked up at the drivel. "Are you going, or must we telephone for the police?" he asked. "I'm waiting for my half-crown," said the man. Leslie gave it him, and then warked into the hotel with Carwardine. • Nobody, saw tile latter, WO= expect very much from you, but I don't think you need have managed the thing so abominably untactfully." Then he turned and looked at the younger man with disconcerting steadiness. oat presume you both had some refreshment?" "One half-pint of very poor lager, sir," said Leslie. That was my share." Carwardine turned away abruptly and left him, but they sat down together at dinner an hour or two afterwards, and when they rose the manager came up to the Major. "Mr. Lorrimer has sent for his things," he said. "There's nothing else in the message, but it suggests that he means to leave, and, in any case, I think you will not` blame us for giving up his room to another guest. It might, however, perhaps be a little more deli- cate' if you gave him a hint to that effect." Carwardine smiled very grimly. " I can't take any exception to your decision. You. Continved in next column.
"I've

LORRIMER'S MISADVENTURE.—Continued. however, neea have Tfo uneasiness about kr. Lorrimer coining back while I remain. In fact, I'll engage to see that he doesn't." He said nothing further son the subject, but during the rest of the, evening Mabel was, for no evident reason, very gracious to Leslie, and when his friend Hodson arrived by-and- bye Mrs.' Carwardine was distinctly less cold to him than she had been on previous occasions. . .

"After all, I have no great objections to Mr. Hodson, and I must admit that I have been cmelly deceived• as to Lorrimer's charac- ter," she said to her husband. "Although he seemed- greatly struck with Mabel, and had everything one could reasonably wish for to offer her, the man is, of course, quite im- possible.' Carwardine laughed. "I let you have your way, but I thought more of Hodson all along," he said. Any way, it's certain that he won't disgrace you like the other fellow." In a few days Hodson had become one of the party, and Lorrimer might have vanished the earth for all that was heard of him.
