div.head: PUBLICAN PUZZLE. Is a Licensee a Servant of the Brewers? STIPENDIARY'S DECISION
div.p: A PUBLICAN PUZZLE. Is a Licensee a Servant of the Brewers? STIPENDIARY'S DECISION

The puzzle, which has baffled many, as to whether a licensee of a public-house is a ser- vant of the brewers, and, should come under the‘provisions of the Shop Hours Act, has been solved by the Liverpool Stipendiary, in a case in which Peter Walker and Son, Limited, were summoned for not specifying on a Shops Act notice, exhibited in the public-house, 2, lice- lane, Walton, the day on which a certain shop assistant was to take his statutory half-holiday. The assistant was John Moorhouse Todd, the licensee and manager of the house. The Stipendiary said evidence had been given that the premises were, and had been for some years past, the property_ of the company; that Todd was the holder of the licence, and was on the Parliamentary and parochial register in respect of the premises; that all liquors sold there were the property of the company; and that Todd carried on the business for the sole benefit of the company, and took the takings to the company's office, after making deductions for wages, &c., for himself and the other people employed at the house. It had also been given in evidence that the company paid the rent and rates for the house, and was entered in the rate-books as the "occupier." In considering the case, the Stipendiary proceeded, it was important to ob- serve that no definition of the word "occupier" occurred in the Act, and it became necessary for the Court to put upon the word its ordinary interpretation. He thought it was clear from the evidence, and he -found as a fact that Todd was merely the servant of the company, and that it was in the discharge of his duties as a-servant that he held ! the licence.- Todd was required under an !agreement_ to live on the premises, and he had no right •to reside there other than by 'virtue of his position as servant or employee of the cOm-

div.head: COMPULSORY .00CUPATION
div.p: A COMPULSORY .00CUPATION

The Stipendiary said he found, withoUt hesi- tation, that the company was the occupier, for Todffs occupation, if he could be said to have any occupation at all, was a compulsory occu- pation in his capacity as the servant or-agent of the company. . "I am quite unable, under the circumstances existing in this case," said the Stipendiary, "to distinguish Todd's position from ,that of the manager of any ordinary branch shop of any big trading company which carried on the busi- ness of selling goods at a number of different shops, and I 'don't -think that the fact that the premises in this case are licensed premises makes any difference." It was clear, he continued, that a very big distinction was drawn between a shop assistant and an occupier; and there could be little doubt that, whatever the strict interpretation of the Act this might lead to in special cases, it was the intention of Parliament to use the word "occupier" in the sense of "employer," or, at. any rate, the belief of Parliament .that an occu- pier would be an employer. • TENANT NOT OCCUPIER

He did not think the Act contemplated the pos- sibility of a person who fell within the category of shop assistant falling also within the cate- gory of occupier. It was clear in the present case that Todd was nothing more than a ser- vant, and himself a shop assistant, and in no betteronor worse position in any respect. than his fellow shop assistants, the two barmen. In those circumstances it was manifestly im- possible for Todd to be a person who was to decide as to the kind of holidays his fellow- assistants were to enjoy. If Todd, were to be regarded as • an, occupier, the .absurdity would arise that Todd, as a shop assistant, was en- titled to have his name included in the pre- scribed form of notice for a holiday, and if he did not include himself,, or take .such holiday, he. as occupier, would be liable to a fine. The Stipendiary accordingly convicted the defendant company. and imposed a nominal fine of ss. and costs:. He was mate: aware that his decision might 'cause considerable • ineOnveni- mire to the company,. and he. was willing, and desirous to give every Mei* to assiSt. them get his decision reviewed by a superior Court.

div.head: BAPTIST BOYS' BRIGADE. Latchford Youths' Camp.
div.p: BAPTIST BOYS' BRIGADE. Latchford Youths' Camp.

The camp party, numbering 26, who have been spending a fortnight under canvas at Whitley, on ground kindly lent by;Mr. J. R. Wilkinson, returned home on Saturday evening. The lads were in high spirits, and appeared to be in the pink of health, their brown 'cheeks bear- ing witness to the almost unbroken sunshine they had enjoyed during the whole fortnight. The weather conditions had been perfect and had more than made up for the disappointing experience of last year's camp, :during which it rained almost continuously. The beginning QI each day was announced by the sounding of the Reveille at six a.m. The greater part of the forenoon was spent in dril- -ling.exercises, and delightful marches along the beautiful- c'otintrylanes, and the altetnoOns And evenings were devoted to cricket, bathing, and all manner of healthy and haplay outdoor acti- vities. The time for evening .prayers and the "Last Post" at 9.30 always seemed to arrive far too soon.

_ 'On 'Sunday, the 3rd inst., a drum-head ser- vice was held in camp, conducted by Mr. J. B. Wilkinson, in the absence of the chaplain, and was largely attended by visitors from the sur- rounding neighbourhood. In the evening the company attended service in the Whitley Wes- leyan Chapel'. On Thursday, the 7th inst., a visit was paid to the camp by. the Girls' Guild, who, to the number of about 70, including officers; Were conveyed to .and from the ground in omnibuses.. The afternoon was a mosr:enjoyable one, for, both the campers and the Visitors The .The -girls started for home at eight- p.m. and. were eseofied part Of -the way i?'y the p.m., Bugle -Band.. ":- • •

. During the whole camp y the 'conduct of the boys has been 7exemplary and has called forth the warm .commendation of many of the resi- dents in the neighbourhood. The officers in charge were Colonel Alfred Grounds (who has been appointed Commanding Officer of the recently-formed Warrington Battalion, Free Church Boys' Brigade), Quartermaster-Lieut. H. Appleton,' Captain A. ,Appleton and Lieutenant A. Banks, along with the Chaplain (thelley. J: S. Chedburn);

div.head: Colborne Street Company.
div.p: Colborne Street Company.

The 'company of the Boys' Brigade in connec- tion with the Golborne-street Baptist Church went into camp on Saturday, in a field adjoining Stretton Hall, by the kind permission of \ Mr. Faulkner. The company, twentS, strong, are under the command of Captain T. S. Davies, assisted by Lieutenant E. H. Jones and Sub- Lieutenant W. H. Michael. The 'Chaplain (the Rev. H. Ogden) was also present until Wednes- day, but had o leave on account of his marriage on Thursday - of this week; with Miss Wright; The weather was favourable. The cooking arrangements have been in the hands ‘• of Mes- dames Davies and Savage (members of the church), and this has added .much to the effi- cient feeding of the camp. The kindness of Mr. Faulkner has been beyond praise, and he has done his utmost to Meet the needs of the camp, and rendered every assistance in making the camp such a success as if has been.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913. WARRINOTON BRIDGE SQUABBLE.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913. WARRINOTON BRIDGE SQUABBLE.
Alderman Smethurst Indignantly Trounces the Critics
for their Attacks.

div.head: IS GRASS DESTROYED BY NOXIOUS VAPOURS?
div.p: IS GRASS DESTROYED BY NOXIOUS VAPOURS?

With the exception of a little "breeze," the meeting of the Warrington Council on Tues- day night was bright, brief, and brotherly. The question of the Bridge was raised, and Alderman Smethurst indignantly denied alle- gations made by critics. Thoughtless public, he alleged, chiefly contri- buted to any traffic confusion that had arisen. They did not help the police. Interrupting Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Pemberton created a bit of stir, but ended the incident, after he had made his point, by apologising to the Alderman. Alderman Bennett alleged that noxious fumes were killing the grass, as well as trees, on the bowling greens at Manchester-road. He thought drastic action should be taken. The debate on the question of slot meters was not started. Members were reported on holi- day, and had not time to consider the matter, so the question was left in abeyance.

There was a solemn note struck at the com- mencement of the Council on Tuesday evening. The MAYOR made reference to the death of Dr. E. A. Fox, who had, he said, lived the whole of his professional life in Warrington. Dr. Fox had rendered great public service, in addition to his work in connection with the In- firmary. He was an able, capable mat in the healing art, genial and cheery in his manner, and of the utmost rectitude of character. These were not platitudes from him, as he had not the slightest doubt that Dr. lift's professional ser- vices were instrumental in curing many of those under his care, and his kindly manner and words soothed the last moments of those who were beyond human aid. No one could speak more strongly from the personal point of view than he could. _ _

His acquaintance with Dr. Fox began when he (Dr. Joseph) was barely 19 years of age. They were students together at the same college. Their lot was cast in Warrington, and, although they were professional rivals, it never interfered with their friendship, and they were close friends all through. He had the pleasure and privilege of his close friendship practically the 'whole of his life, and now he mourned one of the most loyal friends anyone could have had. He moved a resolution to the effect that the Council re- ceived with deep regret the announcement of the death of the doctor, a worthy and respected townsman and; a Justice of the Peace for the borough, and desired to express condolence with the family in their bereavement. Alderman JAMES EVANS, in seconding, said most of the members of the Council knew something of the life and character of Dr. Fox. It had not been his privilege to have been associated very closely with him, but whenever he had come into contact with him he had found him to be one of the most kindly, sincere, and genial .citizens of the town. The resolution was carried by the members silently standing.

works to the town and increase Warrington's prosperity, that no obstacle ought to be thrown in the way by any other committee. The land had been offered for sale by auction some time ago, and the reserve price was not reached. The committee had then fully made up their minds to sell it.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT.

The MAYOR moved a resolution appreciative of the work the Chief Constable and his staff per- formed during the Royal Visit. He said he could not help expressing the thanks they owed' to the Chief Constable and his staff for the able and efficient manner in which they maintained order on the occasion of the Royal visit. Grati- tude was also due to the public for the manner in which they conducted themselves, for they made it comparatively easy- for the police to perform their duties and maintain proper order. (Hear, hear.) Alderman FORSHAW seconded, and the resolu- tion was adopted. Alderman BENNETT proposed thanks to the Mayor for the excellent'•arrangements .he had made. He said he had- -net heard a single dis- sentient voice raised against the arrangements. (Hear, hear.) Everybody seemed to be thor- oughly satisfied. He had always felt that the King would be willing to open the bridge, al- though it was not coMplete, and they had evi- denced that -fact, and the opening gave the crowning touch to an historic occasion. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They certainly owed a deep debt of gratitude to the Mayor for his con- duct afterwards, and they were all delighted to see the ceremony repeated again at the various picture houses. He-cotild not-help feeling .that the films repre- senting the visit should be preserved and kept at the Museum, or at some other suitable place. His Worship's activities throughout the arrange- ments for the visit of the King and Queen were absolutely untiring. It was, of course, impos- sible to please all, although the "Mayor did his best to do so, and he succeeded even beyond his most sanguine expectations. (Applause.) 1 Alderman JAMES EVANS seconded, and said he had heard nothing but praise for the way the Mayor had made the arrangements, and for the way he threw himself so zealously into his task. The Alderman added that he had seen some pub- lic processions in Warrington, including the re:. joicings at the proclamation of peace after the Russian War, but he did not know of any recep- tion which had been so well carried out as that in connection with the recent Royal visit. (Ap- plause.) Alderman SmrfaunsT said he quite endorsed all the previous speakers had said. Alderman FORSHAW said there was no doubt the arrangements were -carried out in a perfect manner. (Hear, hear.) • The resolution was carried unanimously. .

Acknowledging the vote, the MAYOR said there had been -a great deal of anxiety and reSponsi- bility.. He received valuable assistance from many sources. He felt that he had the confi- dence of his colleagues in the Town Council, but, at the same time, there was a responsibility, and, being of a somewhat sensitive and worrying nature, that responsibility took it out of him a great deal more than it would in the case of other people. He had no doubt that the open- ing of' the bridge had largely increased the his- toric value of the visit—the visit would have been much more an ordinary event but for that singular ceremony. - He thanked Alderman Bennett for the sup- port he gave him at Preston, where they met Lord Derby, and mentioned-the matter to him, and he believed that Alderman Bennett encour- aged and helped him in that respect. He ten- dered his best thanks to the Town Clerk and staff, the Borough Surveyor and staff, the Direc- tor of Education, the teachers and many others, whom he could not for the moment enumerate, for the admirable assistance rendered to him, without which he could not possibly have carried out the work. (Applause.)

div.head: ENCOURAGING NEW INDUSTRIES.
div.p: ENCOURAGING NEW INDUSTRIES.

It was reported that an application for the letting of the Mersey Bedstead site, in Knuts- ford-road, was considered by the Street Improve- ment Committee, and it was decided that the site should not be sold until the widening of the road had been completed: Councillor PEACOCK said the Towns Committee were doing all they could to get new works to come to Warrington, and that was one of the sites the committee had in view of allowing some firm to take on a rental; or to buy. (Hear, hear.) When a new firm applied for that site they should not have the door bolted in their face. He hoped the Street Improvement Committee would bring the matter forward and see if some- thing could not be done. They should do all they possibly could to encourage any new indus- tries. Why had the committee refused to enter- tain an offer? - _
The MAYOR: The application was for letting, not for sale. ' The committee want to sell, not to let.

Councillor PEMBERTON felt very strongly on the point. The resolution said the site was not to be sold until the widening of the road had been completed. If they passed that resolution they 'would not be able to sell the land, if an appli- cation came, say, in a month, before the matter had been before the Council again. The passing of that resolution would tie the hands of the committee, and he moved that the resolution be sent bacir. He thought that when one committee was doing its utmost, in every way, to bring new

div.head: BATHS FOR WORKERS.
div.p: BATHS FOR WORKERS.

Criticising the following resolution passed at a meeting of the Street Improvement Com- mittee: That the Water Committee be re- quested to consider, in the interests of public health, the advisability of discontinuing the charge for water for baths in all houses below the rateable value of £20," Councillor Pemberton said that they heard a lot of garden city move- ments in the town, and they had a lot of people who went about preaching on health, and yet when it came to doing the actual and material thing, the Corporation were the first people to put an obstacle in the road. Take an ordinary house assessed at -£9, the water rate was Bs. 2d. If a man went to a house where he was'assessed at £2O he had to pay £1 is. Bd. without a bath. On the top of that they put a 10s. 6d. bath rate, and if that was not penalising cleanliness he did not know, what was.
Councillor iIENSHALL seconded Councillor Pem- berton's amendment that the first resolution be sent back.
Alderman BENNETT said he thought they were carrying the resolution too far. When the scheme was completed it would enhance the value of the land.

Alderman BURTON said he would vote for the amendment. He did not like things being done in such a way. Alderman BENNETT : It is not of public interest to bring the matter up. Alderman JAMES EVANS suggested that if there were matters of urgency the resolution should be withdrawn for the committee to further con- sider and bring the matter before the next meet- ing of the Council. Councillor BIRTLES said he could not see where they were drifting to in connection with the matter., It was a private matter entirely, and it was a very important question for them to answer and deal with.

Councillor PEMBERTON said, that Councillor Birtles must be mixing two properties up. Councillor BIRTLES :I am not. We may deal with two things at once. • Alderman BENNETT : I am quite sure it is in the interests of the town as the matter stands at the present moment, but if the Council de- sired, he would withdraw the resolution.
The MAYOR: As seconder, I agree with that. The resolution was withdrawn.

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT'S COMPLAINT.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT'S COMPLAINT.

Councillor DicxEssoN moved, and Councillor HALLIWELL seconded that the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee be adopted. Alderman BENNETT called special attention to the following minute: "That the head gardener had reported on the damage' to grass and shrubs at the bowling green in Manchester-road, and a report by the public analyst on the probable cause having been read, it was decided that the Town Clerk should call the attention of the manufacturers in the vicinity of the -green, and that the attention of the Inspector under the Alkali Acts be drawn to the matter." The Alderman Said that vegetation was Suffering', and he did not think the Council realised how serious the matter was. Unless something was done, an asphalt open space would have to be resorted to. Trees in the neighbourhood were dying, and on the extreme end they were managing to main- tain a precarious existence. -No one wanted to interfere with legitimate industry, but the fumes which escaped from some of the chimneys were infinitely more harmful than black smoke. If mild remonstrances were not enough, then more '-Ira stic aetion should he taken. It was possible , that the nuisance could be reduced to a minimum if not abolished altogether. The MAYOR was rather surprised at the atti- tude of Alderman Bennett. He had previously spoken of the ill-effects of black smoke, but had not before alluded to noxious vapours. (Laugh- ter.)
Alderman BENNETT declared that he had. The IfAvoß : Yon have not the candour to ad- mit you are converted from black smoke to noxious vapours.
Alderman BENNETT : It Is not want oi candour; it is want of conviction. There were. he con- tinued, acids which were fur worse than the smoke. Smoke was bad, but the noxious vapours were worse.

The MAYOR said he had recently seen a bean- Will specimen of a carnation which was grown within a hundred yards of Bewsev Forge. Alderman SMETHURST, complaining of bloek smoke, said that a .week aro he.had to .nnt,the pane* down. in the house, because he could not see for smoke.

div.head: AUTOMATIC METER RATES:
div.p: AUTOMATIC METER RATES:

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Gas Committee, Alderman JOHN EVANS referred to the statement prepared by the Assistant Sec- retary to the Gas Department with reference to the consumption of gas through slot meters and ordinary meters, and asked that the consideration of the question should be deferred, as some of the committee had been away on holidays. Councillor Gough had consented to withdraw the following motions, which he had intended to submit that evening: "That all slot meter gas consumers in the borough be allowed sd. per 1,000 cubic feet on all gas consumed ,on and after the -30th September, 1913; that .those in the borough pay a rent of Is. 6d. for each three-light Meter, and for each five-light meter shall pay rent -of. .3s. per annum. The ,discount allowed by the •Corporation to the. consumer shall he returned each quarter or each time • the slot meter is emptied of money. The meter rent shall be paid each quarter, or a quarter's rent kept out of the discount allowed by the Corpora- tion by the collector each quarter. or each time the meter is Pmntied ; that all slot meter gas pansumers in the borough, on and after the 30t' September, 1913, shall pay a rent for all slot cookers or grillers supplied by the Corporation, who have not purchased them."

Councillor 6SBORNE said it was his intention to criticise the Assistant Secretary's statement. He would, however, defer s‘ich.. criticism until the next meeting-. He hoped that the figures would not be taken into account for the present, as he thought they were incorrect and did not give a true state of the position of affairs. at any rate Iso far as it appeared to him. He did not believe there was a deficiency on the side of the slot meters. (Hear. hear.) The Council decided not to discuss the matter that nighty

div.head: IMPROVED WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: IMPROVED WATER SUPPLY.

In. moving the adoption of the minutes of the Water Committee, Alderman JOHN EVANS said the committee had been Considering a very im- portant scheme for improving the water supply for manufacturers. They hoped to lay the whole scheme before the Council at the next meeting. Councillor JENKINS seconded the minutes, which were confirmed. Councillor BROADHURST' said that the whole of the ratepayers would be pleased to see the reso- lution where the Water Committee were pre- pared to consider the matter of no charge for baths in houses of the rateable value of £2O. Formerly, the matter had been one of grievance to-ratepayers in general. He thought they were dealing with the question in a splendid manner. The minutes of the Electricity and Tramways Committee were confirmed, on the motion of Alderman SMETHURST, seconded by Councillor WILKINSON.

div.head: MOTOR 'BUS SERVICE.
div.p: MOTOR 'BUS SERVICE.
Alderman SMETHEIRST said the new motor 'buses were being well patronised. There was no doubt the 'buses were filling up a long-felt want in the districts which they served.

Alderman BENNETT was glad to hear of the success of the motor 'buses. They were a great public need, and he would like to ask if there had been any accidents. Referring to the need of a waiting-room at the Sankey tram terminus, the Alderman said that it often happened that the weather was cold and wintry, and people

had either to stand out in the rain, or shelter in an adjacent public-house. Alderman JAMES EVANS said that when the Sanitary Works Committee were seeking out sites for tubercular accommodation, birth was given to the idea that waiting-rooms should be provided at the tram termini. He hoped the project would be carried out harmoniously be- tween the two committees. ,
Councillor HENSHALL hoped that in making such provision the Council would not forget Latchford.

div.head: BRIDGE CONTROVERSY.
div.p: THE BRIDGE CONTROVERSY.

Councillor PEMBERTON asked what was going to be done to make the traffic over the new bridge more convenient? A single line for the trams was intolerable, and he could not under- stand why doable lines had not been laid down. The state of things which uxisteci now -was absolutely intolerable and danw.mvis. Ti‘o- thirds more of the bridge had to be built, and at the present rate of progress it would be four years before the bridge would be completed. When winter came the condition of the bridge would be both dangerous and intolerable. It was a great pity that all these questions were not submitted to the General Purposes Com- mittee. The traffic generally was on the w:ong side of the road. Whoever could have thought of the existing plan he did not know. He should be surprised if they had no accidents during the winter months. The MAYOR: My experience is that accidents don't happen. at-. dangerous places, as care is exercised there: The accidents generally occur at places which are supposed to be safe. Pre- cautions are taken 4at dangerous places. I have no fear of accidents at the ,bridge. Councillor PnuraToN: It is wonderful'. how accidents are avoided. The outside public who don't know the conditions have to go on the wrong side of the road. . . The MAYOR: They are getting educated now —they will soon know.
Councillor PEMBERTON : It is very dangerous. 'Councillor GOUGH : Do you intend to put double lines? Councillor WILEINsoN : We shall do that when the bridge is finished. •

div.head: CRITIC CRITICISED.
div.p: CRITIC CRITICISED.

Alderman SMETHURST confirmed Councillor Wilkinson's statement. He had been very anxious that accommodation 'should be provided at each end of the tram route, and if they could join with the Sanitary Works Committee, it would be strength added to strength, and he hoped they would be able to get the shelters put up soon, as well as conveniences for ladies and. gentlemen. They had not had a single accident yet, and since the introduction of the electric cars, no fatal accident had occurred on the tramways. (Applause.) _ _ _ _

A letter in a local paper, in which a corre- spondent suggested that for the present, owing to the great traffic over the bridge, the present motor 'bus service should be discontinued, and the 'buses run instead of the trams, one to Latchford and the other to Stockton Heath, caused the Alderman to comment that some people, if they had their way, would deprive half the town of the privilege of using the !buses just to make it conYenient•for those who went over Warrington Bridge. He went to the bridge once or twice every day, and spoke to the policemen on point duty. He always asked if any accident had occurred, and there was always a reply in the negative. He wished the public would help the police by keeping on the right side of the road, but they would not always do so. One man had deliberately walked in front of the car, and if he had been killed the wiseacres of the town, who talked about the tram traffic, would have blamed the accident on the Bridges Committee. He thought the bridge would be finished in far less time than Councillor Pemberton had said. He wished he was 'as safe of living as the bridge was of being built in two years. If it was not built in twelve months he would be astonished.

Alderman SMETHURST moved the confirmation of the Bridges Committee -minutes, and 'Coun- cillor HEN'SHALL seconded. Councillor PEMBERTON said that it was a scandal that only one-third of the bridge was actually opened. Where was the business man in that Council who would tolerate such delay? The MAYOR: What if he could not help it?

div.head: "GO AS YOU PLEASE JOB."
div.p: "GO AS YOU PLEASE JOB."

Councillor PEMBERTON : If he had had any such experiences he would take good care they did noc occur again. The Warrington Bridge con- tract was a disgrace to. the .town—the whole bridge ought to have been finished long ago: Councillor WILKINSON: That is your opinion. Councillor PEMBERTON : It is the opinion of the engineers. It is in the contract. It seems to be a go-as-you-please sort of job. The Corpora- tion ought to stick up for the ratepayers instead of for tne contractor. What was the job going to cost them? A few thousands were nothing to some of them.

It was in a very heated manner that Council- lor BROADHURST replied to Councillor Pember- ton's criticism. He (Councillor Broadhurst) was as honourable in his work as a representa- tive of the ratepayers of Warrington as he was in connection with his own business, and for Councillor Pemberton to lay the charges he had done at the doorstep of any member of the Council was abominable. If it were left to some one to say who had had the most experience in bridge-building, he (Councillor Broadhurst) 'would not Come off second best, as he had had five years' experience in bridge-modelling. Coun- cillor Pemberton must be absolutely blind when he knew what had been done, or he would not have made the charges he had made that night. He was wilfully misleading the people of the town and trying to make people believe that something was going on which ought not to go on. 'On occasions like- these Councillor Pember- ton would always find him opposed to him when he made such base. charges. He (Councillor Broadhurst) believed that the Bridges Com- mittee had worked in the best interests of the town. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that Councillor Pemberton would in future think twice before he opened his mouth once. (Laughter.) They wanted beautiful things in Warrington—and the bridge would be one of them—and he only wished they had a few more Alderman Ben- netts to stand up for things beautiful, which would please the people. They were looking forward to the day when the drab buildings of Warrington would be wiped away.

div.head: " EH!" AND WHAT FOLLOWED.
div.p: " EH!" AND WHAT FOLLOWED.

In reply, Alderman SMETHURST said he had heard similar speeches from Councillor Pember- ton before. He wished the members would go to the bridge and see the men working down in the bowels of the earth.

Councillor PEMBERTON : Eh! (Laughter.) The sMAyoit : That is not -a Parliamentary ex- pression. • Councillor PEMBERTON : I was surprised at their going down into the bowels of., the earth to the foundations. _ _
The MAYOR: I think you ought to apologise. Councillor PEMBERTON : I do apologise, but I was surprised. The MAYOR: It is an ordinary expression of Alderman Smethurst's.

Alderman SMETHURST : You will find it is so. Those who had so much to say about only part of the bridge being finished, should go to the spot and see what work had been carried out. They had put the whole of the three training walls up, and were finishing the fourth, and men were working 30ft. below the level of the street. They would be driving piles for another month. These minutes were also confirmed.

div.head: WORKED FOR 80 YEARS.
div.p: WORKED FOR 80 YEARS.

A remarkable record of longevity in one parish comes from Glynde, Sussex, the ances- tral home of the Brands. An old lady 'has just died aged 93. • Her hus- band, who predeceased her, was 92, and he worked on the Glynde estate for 75 years. Joe Ede, the woodman, is still 'living, aged 88. He has worked- for the Brands 80 years. In a row of six cottages at Glynde there are people liv- ing whose ages are 90, 87, and 80 '(two cases), and over 70.

A striking family record is reported from Ness, in the Island of Lewis, where seven mem- bers of one family are drawing old-age pen- sions. They are the three sons and four daughters. of the late John Gunn Lionel. They are all married and have had large families.

div.head: PRINCE'S STOLEN CHEQUE.
div.p: PRINCE'S STOLEN CHEQUE.

Prince 'Rodenburg was the sufferer in a dar- ing cheque theft at the Hotel Cecil, in the Strand, on Tuesday evening. He had recently arrived from South America and placed an open cheque for ze2oo drawn on a' Lancashire bunlc on the hotel cashier's desk:

• Several people were standing about at the time, and when, after a few moments' inatten- tion, the Prince turned again to the desk the cheo.ue ' had disappeared. A telegram was at once sent to the bank stopping the cheque, so that the net loss is the penny Government stamp. _

Charles Wilson, an Ardwick man, was at Manchester sentenced to three months' impris- onment for stealing 7.11 b. of rubber, valued at 365., from the works of Messrs. David Moseley, Chapelfield Works, Ardwick, in whose employ he had been for nine years.

div.head: PIRATES OF THE CANAL.
div.p: PIRATES OF THE CANAL.
What Might Happen if Captain Hydd.
Reurned to Life.
VESSELS WITH UNTOLD WEALTH.
[" Examiner " Special.]
Captain Kydd and his pirate boys returned to life they need not search the Spanish Main for plunder.
They need not go further than the Ship Canal, near 'Warrington, to capture and possess themselves of untold wealth.

Untold wealth literally steams past Warring- ton every day, plunder, undreamt of by Cap- tain Kydd and his pirate crews, goes along the Ship Canal. If he who used to despoil the Spanish galleons, and his crew, could return it is certain that Captain Kydd would do nothing else, in these modern days, than come to War- rington. Just let us try to\imagine what he would do. Scouts he would have all over the Mersey estuary to keep him filled with useful informa- tion; his spies would evade the police at the dock gates of Manchester, and would prowl about, picking up the value of cargoes and other knowledge, useful to the chief of the plundering gang. Perhaps he would be enter- prising enough to have a series of wireless tele- graphic stations rigged up, so that he could receive intelligence with Marconi-like rapidity. Mysterious Movements. In the dusk of evening men in mysterious clothing, with sheath knives and an array of pistols, would be seep hiding amongst the shrubbery.of the canal banks. Another batch would be busy rigging a boom across the canal, other villains would be lurking in armed boats amidst the shadows of the banks, all watching the waterway carefully. , Away below the railway bridge flickers a light. It is the masthead lamp of a vessel. Soon her port and starboard lights appear. Captain Kydd gaps steadily at the vessel through the night glasses. Quite unconscious of the terrible fate which awaits them, the offi- cers keep the ship moving slowly, but steadily, over the water. Kydd grins and passes along his orders. • Bump goes the vessel into the boom. Boats shoot out from all directions. Their crews make fast to the merchantman and swarm upon deck. Revolvers are pushed into the faces of the officers and crew, who, taken by surprise, are quickly herded into the saloon, and kept prisoners under a powerful guard. The hatches are lifted, and the pirates swam into the holds. The derricks are soon at work, lifting the selected plunder to the deck. The Pirates' Spoil. What a motley mixture it is, this spoil! Rare-- articles of virtu from- Japan and China.; models of idols, elephants, birds, temples and other things, worked in solid gold and silver, from India, have been unearthed and laden into the pirates' boats. The ship is thoroughly ran- sacked, and all valuable articles are removed. Then the pirates slip over the ship's side, enter their boats and vanish in the night. The stillness, instead of stir, on deck, informs the imprisoned crew that the cut-throats have departed, and, with a desperate effort(, they break out of their place of confinement. An officer grasps the wheel, the engineers start the engines, and the plundered merchantman hastily heads for the port of Manchester to report this daring attack upon a peaceful vessel voyaging over the ocean—the canal, it should be said. The good people of .Manchester are horror- stricken at the outrage; Parliament must be asked to send a fleet to ferret out and -punish the highwaymen of the sea—canal, I mean. Valuable as Gold. Hastily Kydd and his men dispose of their plunder in their secret lairs; once more they take up their favourite positions. Stately another vessel ploughs her way through the jet-black waters. The lookout must have slum- bered at his post, for he sees not the silent stir,, or the-movement of quick, sculled boats. The pirates are -aboard before he can raise an alarm.

The plundering commences with renewed vigour, fore hold, stern hold, midship hold; quickly are emptied of their more precious con- tents. Captain Kydd smiles- complacently as he makes a mental note of the pillage. There are piles Of the finest ham and bacon, literally worth . their weight in gold in these times of bacon scarcity. There are kegs of butter. which is selected from amidst the barrels of margarine, the latter being cast contemptuously overboard. There are boxes of eggs and juicy joints of beef and pork. . A Liquid Find. A clink of glass makes the captain's eyes- flash out the tires of pleasure. He eagerly looks in the direction of the sounp. He guesses what the clinking *leans. "What have you got there?" sternly demands Kydd. _ _
"Cases of Irish whisky and Dublin stout, sir," comes the answer. "Shall I stow them in the boats, sir?"

"Aye, aye! Below, take care of the precious cargo," shouts Captain Kydd. The pirates gloat over the alcohol and stow it In the boats with infinite care.' "What the deuce have you got here, ,Lieu- tenant Jones?". cries Kydd, as his second officer drags forward a screaming woman. "A purty Irish wench- as ever ye set eyes on, sir. Caught her below. Vixen to fight," replies the officer. "Luck's with us, Jones. Leave me the wench and get below for anything valuable." •Jones departs and :Kydd seizes the Irish girl, who is. it passenger on the Irish boat just taken. Death Preferred. "Yes, you are a comely wench. a kiss to begin with," Kydd says. "Never, never, villain! I would rather face death than such dishonour." "I'll soon break your Irish pride, my beauty!" Kydd makes a blow at the girl, who wriggles from • his grasp, climbs the bulwark, and plunges into the water, to—swim ashore. . Cursing his 'fate, the pirate captain calls to his .men to make haste, as the first peeps of dawn are appearing, and he knows not what other craft may hove on the scene, and frustrate his nefarious game. Hurriedly the boats get away, with their booty weighing them down to the gunwales. The plundered ship is at last free of the pirates' clutch, and steams .on full speed ahead to carry the tidings of the outrage to the port of Manchester. At the news the good citizens-- are awestruck, and more urgent messages are dispatched for the aid of the British Fleet to clear the canal. of the daring outlaws. • Cruiser's Revenge. \Vhen the wireless flashes the message into the office of the Admiralty, a pleasant-faced man reads it eagerly. "I'll do them to-night," he ejaculates, and sends forth a message to hasten - on the arming of the ss. Swiftshire, one of the armed merchantmen attached to - the British Navy. In a few hours a'sPecial train, laden with big guns, small -quick-firers and cases of rifles and ammtmition, arrive at Manchester Docks. horde of arsenal workers rig up the guns, and by nightfall the ss. Swiftshire sails. steadily the armed merchantman ploughs her way over the waters, until she arrives at the pirate-infested spot, marked carefully upon the vessel's chart. Then she comes to a stop. From the shOres there shoot out a flotilla of small boats. The captain of the Swiftshire smiles and quietly passes on his orders. The Pirates' End. "Boom, boom," crashes the fr big guns- "rip- rip-rip," snarled the quickfirers, while rifles, from how to stern, bark angrily. Shot and shell fall like hail around the pirates. Their day has come to an end; they are wiped out.
I must have
Of course, this being all imaginary, the bodies of Captain Kydd and his villainous crew are never found, and the Lancashire and •Cheshire coroners do not need to sit in inquest upon them.

div.head: Dear Sir,

Having been a sufferer from Deafness for many years, I resolved to try the AKOU-VIBRA ELECTRICAL TREATMENT, and am pleased to report I find a great improvement. I can now enter into conversation with greater ease than for many years past, and I shall take every opportunity of recommending this treatment to anyone who is deaf I consider I have made rapid strides and that I shall be quite cured.
Yours faithfully, PETER KNIGHT.
MR. SUMMER, the Inventor of this wonderful Instrument is visiting Warrington for a short time, and invites all who are Deaf and who have Head Noises to call for a full DEMONSTRATION and Test Free.
Arrangements have been made for suitable cases either to undergo a course of Treatment at these rooms or to have an Instrument on Hire and Trial at home.

The Scientific Press endorse the principle of the AKOU-VIBRA TREATMENT, including The Lancet, Chambers Journal, (Science Notes), Science Siftings" dm. Truth states : This treatment is efficacious in many forms of Deafness."

THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913,
THEIR DAYS "NEARLY NUMBERED."

On the Ileport Stage of the Mental Deficiency Bill in the House of Lords, the EARL or SELBORNE made tk.sPeech which was notable for the con- fession that "he supposed the days Of the House of Lords as at present composed were nearly-numbered." He would appear to cherish no illusions as to the light in which a hereditary Chamber, whose proceedings are characterised by an invariable party bias and tenderness for class privileges and interests, is regarded by the overwhelming majority of the nation. Probably LORD SELBORNE remembers the complaints of Tariff Reform candidates at the last General Election, that it was hopeless for them to appeal to industrial constituencies if they were saddled with the obligation to defend a hereditary Chamber. The discussiop of the Mental Defi- ciency Bill itself was extremely perfunctory. That it reached the House of Lords so late was largely the result of an almost single-handed struggle, stubbornly maintained in Standing Committee,. with the object of hampering its progress as much as possible. But it was absurd for LORD SALISBURY to pretend that any other Government would be more successful in dealing with obstruction of this kind.

LORD SELBORNE followed up his denunciation, ; in the House of Lords, of the debate on the , Mental Deficiency Bill as "a farce," with a 'lengthy letter to the "Morning Post," in which he contended that the Parliament Act had deprived the Peers of all power. What the Parliament Act has really done is to take from the, Peers the power of condemning a Liberal House of Commons to plough the sands

through the whole lifetime of a Parliament, but - to give Vtem the opportunity of revising legisla- tion by means of negotiation and arrangement. That there is plenty of scope for the House of Lords to perform such a function under the Par- liament Act appears quite plainly in the case of the Scottish Temperance Act. When, on the Contrary, the Lords simply set themselves, in a spirit of perversity and impotent malice, to reject the measures of the Commons up to the last, hour which the, Parliament Act allows, they cease to be a revising -Chamber at all. But it is their own term* which they ought to blame as the cause if they consequently else to count seriously in legislation.
TENNIS, CROQUET, CRICKET &.- Other outdoor Games.-4. S. GARLAND, 51, 53 & 55, Bridge- etreet, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: PROTECTION AND ENIPLOVNIENT.
div.p: PROTECTION AND ENIPLOVNIENT.

When the "raging, tearing, campaign" of Tariff Reform propaganda was at its height, the workers of this country were exhorted to turn their eyes upon the Elysium which Protection had created in the United States for the Ameri- can working man. In a country protected by a "scientific tariff," it was declared, a period of trade depression did not spell unemployment. Factories were not closed, nor blast furnac,..2s damped down, because the surplus goods for which there had ceased to be a home demand were dumped upon these shores, rendered defenceless by Free Trade. The recent Report on the Conditions of Employment, in the Iron and Steel Industry in the United States, by the Secretary of Commerce and Labour, tells a very different' story. While the •American worker has serious complaints to make of excessively long hours andof the failure of wages to keep pace with the increase in the cost of living, his main grievance is extreme irregularity of em- ployment. Nearly half of the employees in blast furnaces were discharged during the panic of 1907. Complete recovery was not reaChed till August, 1909, and then again at the: end of 1910 over 33 per cent. were discharged. But in times of depression the rolling mills and steel works'shut down before any great decrease is made in the production of the 'blast furnaces; Even in a prosperous year the average employee loses, through causes over which he has no control, at least 13 per cent. of the total. That is the "regular employment" which Protection has to offer the worker.
THE BOONS OF NATIONAL INsen-

div.head: ANCE.
div.p: ANCE.

Mr. LLOI'D GEORGE made- a spirited defence of the Insurance Act last Saturday at Sutton-in- AShlield. lit his vivid treatment figures were translated into concrete and living realities. But even the mere figures themselves •tell an impressive and . moving story. Under the Insurance Act :

500,000 sick workers, male and female, are receiving medical treatment, free of charge, every week. 270,000 are in receipt of sick benefit every week. 24,000 workers have been treated for tuber- culosis in sanatoria, at dispensaries, or in their own homes., 500,000 persons have received the maternity benefit since the Insurance. Act came into operation.

Under the Amending Act which has just been placed on the Statute Book persons over fifty will receive exactly the same benefits as those who are younger in years.: Mr. LLOYD GEORGE concluded with the reminder that for social reform to be thorough and effective it must move on an extended front. The Liberal Govern- ment has already attacked the poverty, of the aged worker; they have/started their movement against sweating; intemperance is being attacked. The Liberal Party, Mr. LLOYD GEORGE added, is " now about to march against the central position where land monopoly is entrenched."

div.head: HOW TARIFFS RAISE PRICES.
div.p: HOW TARIFFS RAISE PRICES.

The "American Economist," which .is the organ of the high Protectionists in the United States, is, 'unlike our Tariff Reform League, always absolutely honest in its admissions that import duties raise prices. Its object is to see that there are protective tluties, and that prices are so raised to the consumer. Here is a para- graph from its leading article on July 25th last :

On July 1, 1912, the amount of goods in bond in New York was 45,000,000 dollars. The great increase has taken place within the last few weeks. The importers are storing up .the goods, and are taking out of bond only enough to fill orders that come in from day to day. . . . There are bonded warehouses in every port of entry throughout the United States, and if New York warehouses should have one hundred million dollars of held-up imports, by- the time the law is passed and goes into effect, it is safe to assume that the bonded imports in other warehouses will add another fifty million dollars to the sum total. It must be borne in mind that this 150,000,000 dollars represents foreign values, and with an average addition of 50 per-cent. for duties, the 150,000,000 dollars would now become 225,000,000 dollars of displacement of equivalent American goods in the American market.
FLAGS, STREAMERS, BUNTING.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, 53 and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.

mittee can provide a cheapened supply without infringing the private citizens' rights, they will confer a boon to inanufacturers that will be appreciated as much as it will be beneficial to the trade of the town.

VEGETATION AND SMOKE. In a discussion at the Warrington Council on Tuesday 'about the destruction of vegetation in some parts of the borough by noxious fumes and smoke, the Mayor stated that he had seen a beautiful carnation grown within g, hundred yards of Bewsey Forge. In that pail or South Staffordshire known, as the Black Country ex- cellent vegetables of all kinds flourish, while the young children languish and die. Fumes are good for neither vegetable nor animal life when too pronounced, and the fact. that vegeta tion in the Manchester-road distrtet does Dot -thrive calls for careful investig•rion on the lines urged by Alderman Bennett.

div.head: PASSING WEEK.
div.p: THE PASSING WEEK.
To-MORROWS MUSICAL FESTIVAL

_ To-morrow, the weather being fine, will wit- ness the fifth open-air. Musical festival, held in the Park, for the benefit of the Infirmary; in the event of adverse conditions, shelter frctm the rain will be sought in Parr Hall, so that, in any event, the festival will take place. The pro- gramme that the mixed choir and Crosfield's Band will render is set forth in another column, and will be found to be of a very high order, and suitable in character for a Sunday after- mion. It is to be hoped that the unselfish devo- tion f the Working Men's Committee will be duly rewarded by substantial takings, and to this end it would be keenly appreciated if men of good and. ofliCial position would patronise thee'festival by their presence. For those who find it impossible to be present, there is the alternative plan of sending donations, which Mr. Hampson will .be pleased to receive any time, at the Infirmary. It is of interest to note that the fonr preceding festivals have pro- duced £134. • The last two were held On a Sunday and produced £7l; the first two were held on a Thursday, and produced £62, figures which are slightly in favour of the Sunday fix- ture. It is also an interesting fact .that many of the members of the great choir that will do duty to-morrow are member& of the Male Choral Union,. that has done such Valuable ser- vice on this occasion in the past. We shall all wish the Working Men's Committee all the luck and all the success they deserve.

div.head: GAME U.
div.p: THE GAME U.

We are inclined to think the game is t.p. The Governinent have decided to give Home Rule to Ireland; but Mr. Harold Smith, .M.P., while too modest to claim that he has initiated the idea, has been telling the world that the Warrington Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform League have undertaken to shelter the women and children of those men of Ulster who will take the field, should they be called upon to fight on Le passing of Home Rule. It is a dreadful prospect, but if the Warrington Women Union- ;ts have- decided that they will offer this suc- cour, there must be something behind. It sounds far more serious than that famous, but non-committal, telegram to Sir Edward Carson. It is more serious even than' the speeches when Sir Edward came to Warrington to acknowledge the telegram, and when the rockets that were :taken for signals of distress went up in the neighbourhood of Winmarleigh-street. But it is said that a certain undesirable individual finds mischief for idle hands. The Warrington Women*s Unionist and Tariff Reform terigue have -evidently nothing to do for the lost cause of the Tariffs, so they are concentrating upon the Unionism section of their title. They have let go the tariff question in honour of the if fte Hheyome will consult the same author- Rule qUestiOn they would biCieioelsown'uisie peso,lC th though they would be somewhat dis- concerted. We Sincerely hope the Government will not collapse when the news of what the Warrington Women Tariff Reformers fire doing. has reached their ears.

div.head: REGISTER
div.p: REGISTER

We would remind our readers that the last day for making claims for a vote is next Wed- nesday. It is the duty of every Liberal who is entitled to a vote to see that his name appears on the Register. The next election, which may come suddenly upon us, will be a rnonrmt:ols one, and locally every vote will be of the high,- est value. Apathy might result in a set-back to the progressive cause, and give enconraele- ment to the reactionaries to attack. the 'advance posts which the Liberal party have established upon the road to social refOrni with so much courage and deletmination since 1906. Mr. Sanders. at the Liberal- Club. will be deligh!od to give the necessary.assistanee to any Liberal who may require information. We must get our forces at full strength, aria the ciefeat the re-actionaries will be certain.

div.head: ROM- VISIT .CONGRATULATIONS.
div.p: ROM- VISIT .CONGRATULATIONS.

- It was appropriate that the Town Council should have extended its congratulations to the Mayor, at the first meeting after the Royal visit, upon the success which attended the event. ,In doing so, the Council only voiced the general opinion of the community. Upon that auspicious occasion the Mayor had no easy task to fulfil., Prior to the. visit he was deeply in- volved in making harassing and patience-try- ing arrangements. Subtle plans had to be de- vised, and it was his duty as Chief Magistrate to see that they were carried out in entirety. As the first town in the tour, Warrington was looked upon by other boroughs to set an ex- ample in management, and in the fulfilment of that etiquette which necessarily surrounds the visit of a Sovereign. The Mayor performed his part' with a grace and dignity, which not only set a good example, but brought fame to the event. For what he did he was worthy of the hearty congratulations bestowed upon him, and so was the Chief of Police and his staff, who so ably managed the crowds with a complete absence of any trace of friction or officiousness.

div.head: INDUSTRY AND CONSUMPTION,
div.p: INDUSTRY AND CONSUMPTION,

It is to be hoped that the manufacturers of Warrington will weigh to the full the sugges- tions that have just been placed befOre them in ,t circular from the Tuberculosis Care Commit- tee. Now that the Insurance Act is-, at work it ...111 be worth the while of eniployers to note the incidence of illness -among their workpeople, especially with a view to the checking of any industrial causes Of disease. • There has been 4,g00d deal of talk about malingering, but it has got to .be realised 'that now Working :men will go to the doctor for minor ailments. From the standpoint,of public health this will-eventu- ally mean a great economy, for it is obviously easier to check a disease in its earlier than in its later stages. In dealing with tuberculosis early diagnosis is of the utmost importance. A slight case of' tuberculosis promptly treated in a sanatorium has excellent chances of ultimate recovery if suitable employment can be found after treatment. That is just where the em- ployer can give a helping hand, if he will take some pains to see the problem as a whole, and I be prepared to put himself to some trouble and I slight saorifice. At any rate, the Tuberculosis I Committee is trying to ascertain the extent of the after-work problem, after the employer has done his best.

div.head: NOURISHMENT AND BEDDING.
div.p: NOURISHMENT AND BEDDING.

Another point raised by the committee is that of the provision" Of nourishment and extra bed- ding when necessary. Probably there will always be a certain number of tuberculous patients in excess of sanatOrihm accommoda- tion, and =it is very necessary that they should be properly fed at home. Many, of course, are not insured people, and it: is, by no means a simple -question as to how provision should be made .for patients who cannot pay their way. Sooner or later, the whole problem of the feed- ing of the wage-earners will have to be faced. There would be fewer tuberculous patients if every home had enough suitable food, properly cooked. .

div.head: WATER FOR TRADE.
div.p: WATER FOR TRADE.

The more Warrington Council lays itself out to cater for the trade of the district, the greater development will the borough witness. Of our town it can be truthfully said: "We live to trade, and we trade to live." Evidently the Water Committee have taken .that to heart. as their motto, for they are preparing a scheme, whereby manufacture will be fostered by the conceding of an Unproved water supply. The proposals are not complete, but a report is pro- mised for the next meeting of the Cokincil, and it will be awaited with interest. There is one thing, which doubtless the committee will keep in mind, and it is that trade must not be fostered at the expense of the consumers of water for domestic purposes. If the corn-

div.head: LADY BOWLER-S' GRIEVANCE.
div.p: LADY BOWLER-S' GRIEVANCE.

The lady bowlers must be as indignant as only women can when they feel slighted. The Council has passed a mandate that they are to be' allowed upon the bowling greens only three hours in the week, and doubtless the fair bowlers are nursing' their wrath ,at this slight to give it vent when the November elections come round. FUrther, they must feel Vexed with the Councillor who alleged that the pre- sence of the ladies on the greens was provoca- tive of very bad language—on the part of the men. Now, iS it fair to lay the blame for that language at the' door of the ladies? The,man who. first discovers a fire is not *necessarily an incendiary, 'and it is not logic to say, because the ladies have been on the green, that they are entirely responsible for the men using naughty language. However, the Council has decided upon thive hours per week ,for the ladies, and that. decision. will be as Immovable as the law of the Medes mid Persians. It must be remem- bered that some woman have votes for Council elections !

div.head: MOTOR 'Bus SERVICE.
div.p: THE MOTOR 'Bus SERVICE.

There were some pessimists, who, when the motor 'bus scheme was announced, saw such a service run at a loss. Their predictions, like most pessimistic forecasts, have proved untrue. Alderman Bennett, at the meeting of the Coun- cil on Tuesday, announced that the 'buses were proving a financial success. These are satis- factory tidings, and it is extremely gratifying to note the way the new motor services are sup- pOrted by the public. It proves they have come, if somewhat late in the day, to supply a public want. There is no doubt the motor 'bus is the vehicle of the future, and it will gradually drive the track trams off the streets. Thus Warring- ton, in introducing motor 'busei on the Gorsey- lane and Bewsey routes in place of laying down trams, has acted evidently with an eye to the future. The 'buses, beyond the price of the vehicles, cost practically nothing, whereas a mile of double tram track costs anything above £lO,OOO. From this it will be realised the ad- vantage motor 'buses possess over trams, and it only seems a question of time when a stern economical law will end the reign of King Tram.

div.head: " COOL " SUGGESTION.
div.p: A " COOL " SUGGESTION.

We note with pleasure, and especially in view of the oppressive weather we have been experi- encing of late; that a correspondent, writing from Stockton Heath, suggests that the traffic difficulty on the new bridge might be satisfac- torily solved by the use of our motor which might be withdrawn from their usual routes. Warrington should, briefly, rob its own districts of their conveniences to 'oblige the 'coy" damsel, who is still telling WarringtiTh to keep at a distance—except, it seems, for .the concession of 'buses!

div.head: Tlif NARROW WAY:
div.p: Tlif NARROW WAY:

"It is not the narrow way ; it. is the people who tread it." In this Cryptic sentence was sunintA up tritely the position at the Warrington Brithlp about the •congestion said to exist. The opinion of those who have studied the problem is that it is not so much the new part of the bridge which is at fault as the people who make use of it. They pay little attention to the instructions of the police, and,, because of this neglect, con- gestion arises. For this the police are unfairly blamed, and the controversialists point the fin- ger .in every direction but the right one. A Manchester police official, with a wide experi- ence in controlling heavy traffic in congested areas, seems to have touched the true spot when he said to an " Examiner " representative this week: "The drivers of vehicles must, if they dis- obey the policeman on point duty, be handled sternly, and such a method' will soon regulate the little congestion which I saw existing at the Bridge. Drivers and cyclists, if they will not do so voluntarily, must be taught to obey the police -signals. I think the constables on duty are doing excellently, but the driving public do not assist the officers as they might:" Will drivers and cyclists take the hint and act up to it, thus ensuring their own and other people's safety and prOgress?

THE BRONTE LETTERS. So long hast thou been dead, brave heart, So long—that we forget— Whose prying words lay bare thy smart— Thy spirit may be yet As near as if thou'dst died but yesterday, And round thy body still the watchers stay. Then, as we chattering stand, "0, hush !" they
say, She yet may hear : rather fold hands and
pray." So soon shall we be dead, poor heart, So soon—let us be dumb, Nor voice Love's sorrow even in part,

To voiceless winds. that come And go—and come again in alter years To blow our soul's dead trust in alien ears. Rememb'ring that our turn must come some day, Ask nothing more: rather fold hands and pray. ROSA E. CLADDING.

div.head: TRINITY INFANT SCHOOL. Transfer from Cairo-street Satisfactorily Arranged. DIFFICULTY SETTLED:
div.p: TRINITY INFANT SCHOOL. Transfer from Cairo-street Satisfactorily Arranged. DIFFICULTY SETTLED:

• The attention of parents is called to the fact that the infants' School in. Cairo-street has now been .closed, and that the Head. Mistress (Miss Bullen) and staff will, on and after Monday next, be located in the Trinity School in Museum-street, where a new infants' depart- ment has been created. - Those who followed the discussions at the meetings of the Education Committee when this matter was being arrangedovill be aware that it has resulted from the depletion of the Trinity School, after the opening of the new Council School. in Evelyn-street last midsummer, and from the fact that the premises in Cairo-street have for many years been adversely reported upon by the Medical Officer of Health: The arrangement seems to be h sensible and sound. one. The infants could not be allowed to continue in premises which had .been con- demned on sanitary grounds, but there was ample accommodation for them (subject to some rearrangement of the rooms) in a neighbouring school. The only possible source of difficulty might have been caused by the fact that the Trinity School is a denominational one, whilst the Cairo-street School was an' undermining- tional one, but this has been effectively removed by the agreement into which the managers and the Education Committee have entered, whereby the infants department is to retain its unde- nominational character. The instruction of the infants under the new conditions will, there- fore, be precisely the same as it was at Cairo- street,- and it will be given by the same staff.

div.head: From Everywhere.
div.p: From Everywhere.

Warrington magistrates were puzzled by a carter stating that he had removed some furni- ture to a " beast " market. After much ques- tioning it was elicited from the carter that he Meant a cattle mart.
A Fine View.

Trippers arrived home from Southport at Warrington Station on Saturday. One of them was overheard to say that the view she was most interested in was that of the town clock, which she could see from the bedroom window. Southport' 's advertised attractions will not feel flattered.

A Moon A-piece. The moon was shining at Stockton Heath on Saturday night, when. a youngster boarded the tramcar. At Bridge-street the moon could be seen still shining, and it impressed the nipper, who remarked upon the phenomenon to his parent thusly: "Dad, 1( see they have Also got a moon in Warrington."
Not in the Ark.

A Mr. Veal has married a Miss Lamb, who was given away by Mr. Hare, and Mr. Fox looked on. This wedding did not happen in the Ark, but in London. It recalls a matrimonial union near Warrington, of a Miss Summer, Who became Mrs. Winter. Another marriage we remehiber was a Scotch .lassie named Death, who entered into conjugal joys with Mr. Heaven.
Never Came -Back.

Fowls will wander into other people's gar- dens. A pair of suburban neighbours met at a boundary fence. "Do you know," quoth one, "your hens come into my garden?" "Thought as much," retorted the other. "Why?" questioned the first. "It needs only a simple bit of deduction to find that. out—they have never come back." The suburban gar- deniteS are reported now to be upon terms of very distant acquaintanceship.
Blind Athletes.

Captain Crosfield, at the bowling prize pre- sentation on Saturday, told of a blind golfer who played the game guided by a caddy with a bell. We once saw two blind association foot- ball teams play rather an kciting game with r football draped with small bells. It was one of the most wonderful sights to witness how, guided only by sound, they were able to manceuvre the sphere and score goals.
Peat Fuel.

Peat is cut at Risley to make bedding material for horses. The day may come when it will be utilised to.drive our engines in Warrington. A Swede has invented a process whereby peat is ground to powder, and, through the medium of a cheap, special apparatus, can be burned in boilers,. A ton and a half of the peat gives a better heating power than a ton of the best coal. Perhaps tile day may comq when we will not need to fear a coal famine like that which beset us in March of 1912.

King and Music Halls.: After visiting Warrington in July. the King was present at a music hall entertainment at Knowsley. His Majesty seems to have taken a liking to this type of amusement, so -long chiefly patronised by the working class. He has now promised to attend a performance at a London theatre of varieties, and the show is not to be run ,by all stars. Lesser luminaries of .the hail stage are to be on the programme.
Perhaps when the King next visits Warrington he will patronise our local hall: More un- expected things have happened since he came to the throne to be "the workers' king.'!

A Tale of "Bray." . A local man, just returned from a holiday in Germany, has related to some of his Warring- ton friends the marvels he discovered in "de Fadderland." At railway stations there, he says, they have gramophones which shout out the station name when a train arrives. We know of a station in Ireland where they have a donkey tethered upon the platform, and, when a train arrives, it gives a prolonged blast upon its vocal organ, and thus announces the name of the station to strangers. The official title of the station is "Bray." -

Only Bees. A swarm of bees, invading a signal lamp on the L. and N.-W. line north of Warrington, held up the main express trains for some time. A Warrington resident; 'some years ago, had --a still more curious experience, the train he was travelling in being brought to a stop on a steep incline in the highlands of Scotland by myriads of gnats settling on the rails. The engine wheels crushed the flies into oil, find the train could not climb the incline until the passengers and guard had covered the metals with a thick 'coating of sand. Millions of tiny flies sacrificed their lives by stupidly remaining on the rails.

Salt 4d. per lb. A reader, interested, by the article in the last issue Of the " Examiner " about the expensive price of food-stuffs during the Franco-German War of Is7o-1,- states that. a more remarkable thing happened during the wars this country waged with Napoleon. From old records he found that salt. rose steadily in price until it reaChed'£3o per ton, and was sold retail in this part •of Lancashire at 4d'. per lb. • The only reason he can ascribe for this famine price of salt was that the "press gangs" had pressed the salt makers as soldiers, and the production was left to unexperienced women and children, while the demand was great, in order to supply salted beef to the troops abroad.
Rather Green.

We joined him in the train as it was speeding from Warrington to Manchester, and we talked. lie said that he was a native of Canada, and never, had set foot in the Old Country before. Pointing to the fields of green corn, grass, and potatoes, just outside Padgate, he remarked: "Fine little fields these, nice and fresh. Guess you never get a two-day drought, else they would be burned up. In Canada a week with- out rain makes everything dry yellow." When he was informed-that we had experienced nearly a month of rainless weather, he was incredu- lous. " Gee-whiz," he ejaculated, "your far- mers must have had a busy time with the water can to keep these patches so green. We were too Wile to tell the Ganadian that his know- ledge of our agricultural methods was rather "green."
Humour in Court.

A defendant hi the Police Court asked to get ,away, as he had never been in that court before; "What abciut being in the court in the Buttermarket?" questioned the Chief Con- stable. The accused man admitted a visit to the old place and confessed himself Outwitted.

The police, strange fact, but true, admitted that they were partially responsible for a man appearing on a charge of drunkenness. He was fined on Saiturd'ay, and got time in which to pay the fine. "He was back in the cells the same evening.

"ft takes Me a week to get properly right after a booze," quoted a man, charged at Tues- day's Court with being drunk. "you should be nearly through ,the week now," answered the Chief Constable, "for fast Thursday you fell through a window." - A new constable was giving evidence againsf a man charged with drunkenness, and the% accused denied the offence. "'Although you' come from Scotland," said' the Chief' to the officer; "you know a drunken man when' you see him?" The constable adinitted that he did'.

div.head: PRESTATYN CAMP.
div.p: PRESTATYN CAMP.
Warrington Children's Last Week by the Sea.
UNBROKEN PLEASURES.
By a Correspondent.

Those of our readers who are accustomed to their annual fortnight's or month's holiday •at the seaside, can hardly realize the joy which a week's seaside holiday brings to the children of the "deserving poor" of our town. As all know, voluntary contributions are relied upon to support this movement, and if the Warring- tin public could only see the children in camp, many more would be willing subscribers. Let us accompany the second detachment of boys during their week's sojourn. After meeting, as usual at the Drill Hall, 120 lads cheerily made their way to Bank Quay Station, and there boarded the train for North Wales. Prestatyn was reached at 11.30. a.m.

Sunday was observed by holding a brief ser- vice in camp, the address being given by Mr. Appleton, one of the -officers. On no occasion has it been necessary to remain under cover. During the 'fortnight the camp .has been visited by Warrington people and others, all being greatly interested. On one occasiOn the visit- ors suggested that they should give a concert to the lads. NO fTme was lost in putting this suggestion into practice, and for an hour and a half the lads were entertained with songS.by the visitors, officers .and fellow companions. The item of chief inTerest, judging 15y applause, was a ragtime competition, in which the-lads ex- celled. One youthful instrumentalist, charmed us all with his wonderful "mouth organ" solo. So much for indoor ,pleasure. . Of all outdoor amusements, the most thor- oughly enjoyed were the sports. These con- sisted of sack, boot, three-legged and obstacle races, in addition to the usual flat races, to suit all ages. The entries for the events were taken previous to the commencement of the sports, and every lad in the camp was given an oppor- tunity of winning a prize. Our esteemed hon. secretary, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, came over on Thursday, and was thus able to be an inter- ested spectator of the full programme, gener- ously volunteering to give four copies of his book "How Tom Jeffrey saw the World," to four of the first prize-winners.. Several Pres- tatyn visitors witnessed the sports with keen interest, adding considerably to the prize list. During this last week of camp life, the children have been under the care of Mr. W. H. Hough- ton (superintendent), ably and willingly, assisted by Inspector Wainwright and Messrs. Jones, Appleton, Farrar and Mee.

From what can .be gathered, both the boys and girls who have been lucky enough to spend a week at the camp, have had one of the best times of their lives. Let us trust that fortune will favour them to such an extent that they will always be able to have a seaside holiday. In any case, the pleasures of this week's holi- day will be firmly 'implanted in the children's memory, and. will be something to look back upon.

div.head: OUR DEARER FOOD.
div.p: OUR DEARER FOOD.
Prices Equal to the Early Eighties ; not so High as in the Seventies.
WORLD-WIDE INCREASES.

Statistics issued by the Board of Trade con- firm the facts mentioned in the special articles, which have appeared in the " Examiner " during the past two weeks, in regard to the rise in the price of food. "The level now reached," says the Blue Book, "is, however, no higher than in the early eighties, and much below that of the seventies, when prices were exceptionally high.". We have not yet reached the tenpenny- loaf stage, as we showed, in last week's special article, existed in the seventies. ' The information set forth .by the Board of 'Trade shows that rents, taking the country as a whole, had increased, between 1905 and 1913, about 1.8 per cent., retail prices of food and coal had increased by 13.7 per cent. Wages, al- though increased in certain trades, have not advanced to any appreciable extent. The up- ward movement of prices has, of course, been world-Wide, and in many of the chief commer- cial countries the rise in food prices has ex- eceeded that in the United Kingdom. , During the first six months of 1913, the level of-retail prices in the United Kingdom remained fairly stationary, it is reported. The practical conclusion from the data available is that dur- ing 1905-1912 there has been a rise in the cost of clothing, probably not much less in proportion than that of food and coal and rent combined, the rise taking the 'form either of increased price for the same article, or a lower quality for the same price.
A Bacon Trust.

Taken all round, there has been an increase in food. Bacon has jumped up tO a record figure, and, as was indicated in a previous article in the. "Examiner," there is a suspicion that the rise in price is artificial. America, which suppties a large quantity of our ham and bacon, has been nobbled-. by .a bacon trust, who have almost swept the market,. - . In fact, in consequence of. the- manceuvres of the bacon trust, lite price of this commodity in America is now higher than What it is in England, where a Certain amount of competition from Irish' and English rearers has had a beneficial effect. In the United States bacon has vanished almost as a breakfast dish. In the past six years bacon has advanced in Warrington about twopence per pound, and our retail dealers cannot be blamed for that, as they have to buy in a whole- sale . market, where prices have reached record level.

Coal, clothes and other necessities have ad- vanced. In some towns' the increase has been less than in others. Curiously enough, Che- shire furnishes a striking illustration. In Macclesfield the cost of living has only advanced 10 per cent., while in Stockport it has gone up 20 per cent. Why there should be this marked difference in prices in two almost neighbouring towns is .ft riddle no man or woman under- standeth, but the fact remains.

Theory of Mr. Ilarold Cox. There is a cause for the increased cost of the necessities of life, and while others are groping round in the dark, 'vainly seeking it, Mr. Har,-}:d Cox, the Free Trade economist, seerns to have hit the right nail on the head when he says:— "I think one good reason for the rise in food prices is the fact that wages have been rising throughout the world, for it is more a world matter than an -English question, especially among the poorer classes and the more back- ward races.

"It must be remembered that these Classes are eating more and dressing better than they did 10 or 15 years ago, and the fact of this in- creased demand is the cause of the increased prices. It is, you see, a question of supply and demand; ive always get 'back to that. "To sum the matter up in an instance, you can say that because the Poles, who formerly lived on rye bread, are now demanding wheaten bread, we have to pay more for our wheat." Another puzzle is : • Where are our Tariff Reform friends? They are lacking in enterprise I not to grasp this question, and bellow from the housetops of Warrington, and elsewhere, "See. your food has cost you more." The present silence among the shrewder section of the " Reformers "is significant. If a free, open British market shows rising prices, a food-taxed market, would double the cost. Germhny, France, the U.S.A., so' oft quoted as heavens ander Protection, now feel the pinch of increased food more than Britain. Perhaps that is why I the Tariff Reformers are silent.
