Mr. F. Pendlebury represented Warrington golfers in the Ramsay (1.0. M. golf tournament on Tuesday. He finished sixth in a large field of competitors.
Athlete Wins Handicap. #
At the Football Players' Union sports at, Leeds on Saturday, J. Long, of Warrington, won the first place in the half-mile handicap. He started from the 45 yards mark.

div.head: Grouse Duly Came
div.p: The Grouse Duly Came
Grouse duly arrived in Warrington on Tues- day, the "Twelfth," but the birds were to meet Private orders. The price was stated to be about 7s. 6d. a brace. They came from the South of Scotland.

Week-end .Weather Prospects. With the barometer fairly high and steady, there are prospects of another week-end favour- able to holiday-makers. The wind may remain westerly, or north-westerly, and may blow in occasional showers from the Atlantic, but gener- ally the, weather may Drove favourable.

div.head: Increase in Cheese Prices.
div.p: Increase in Cheese Prices.

Makers of cheese in the Lancashire and Che- shire districts around Warrington are delighted at the marked rise in the wholesale market. The increased prices are said to be due to the develop- ment of a cheese boom. Foreign demand is the cause. So far, the retail price has not been affected to any appreciable extent.

div.head: Yesterday's Fatality at RN lands'.
div.p: Yesterday's Fatality at RN lands'.

A shocking fatality occui:re7;e-sle-i7da-Tafter- noon at the Dalton Bank Works of Messrs. ltylands Bros., Ltd., Church-street, Warrington. At 2.39 p.m. Martin Lane, furnaceman, 22, GandyLstreet, was caught by the handle of a crane, and was struck in the stomach. He re- ceived serious injuries, from which he died.

The Progressive Labour League. The Warrington Progressive Labour League is performing a valuable educational work, and another of tile League's interesting meetings will be held on Monday night at Bridge-foot, starting promptly at 7.30. The speaker, Mr. H. Garside, Xianchester, usually has some in. teresting topic to discuss, and is a speaker worth hearing.

div.head: Died at Work.
div.p: Died at Work.

A sensation was caused at Messrs. Rylands Bros.' wire works, Chiirch-street, on Monday night, when a youth, named Albert Taylor, 16 years of age, living in General-street, died sud- denly. Deceased, who was a block minder, was winding wire, and it is. supposed that death was due to nis chest having been pierced by a piece of wire.—The inquest is to be held this morn- ing at 11 o'clock.

Births in Warrington. The population of Warrington was slightly in- creaseu last week, the nunwer of births being 23 more than the deaths. Births numbered is (15 males, one of which was illegitimate, and 22 females), compared with 36 in the same week last year. The birth-rate was 26.7, as against 27.0 last year.

div.head: School Playground By-law.
div.p: School Playground By-law.

To prevent intruders not desired in school Rua who often prove a source ot sihe Warrington. Town Council have annoyance,ptilciao3p'geu new by-law, and official notice of the fact is published in our advertising columns. The by-law ordains that any person, other than teacher, child or manager, or otherwise author- ised, who refuses to depart from 'a school play- ground on request, will be liable to prosecution.

div.head: Pavement Advertising to End.
div.p: Pavement Advertising to End.

The cneap method of 'securlA4 an advertise- ment by coalking an announcenienr-upon toe pavements and footways is to -be put an end to W arrington. The Town Council announce the passing of a by-law to the enect that '` no person shall, for the purpose of advertising, deface tile footway or roadway of any street by writing or.otner marks." Tne penalty, for such. an offence will not -exceed •

div.head: Coming Agricultural Show.
div.p: The Coming Agricultural Show.

_ • The event in the local agricultural world, the WarringtOn blioW, will be held .at Walton Hall on 'Thursday. It is expected that the 'exhibi- tion of KLOCK will be equal to the best seen at any of the previous 23 shows. Strong features will be found in the hunter, jumpers, and shire horse sections, and a large display is expected in the class, devoted to turnouts. The judging commences at 9.30 a.m., and from then onwards there will be a steady procession of interesting events. The musical programme will be ren- dered by the crack band of the Cheshire Yeomanry.

div.head: " " System.
div.p: The " " System.

The Shop Assistants' Union has commenced a campaign against " living-in " conditions, and are urging all assistants to refuse to accept board and lodgings as part payment of wages. A minimum wage, scale is also being drafted, and meetings in support of the union's scheme are to be held in this part of Lancashire and Cheshire in the autumn. The "living-in" sys- tem is not so general in Warrington, however, as in other towns.

div.head: Deaths from Diarrhcea.
div.p: Deaths from Diarrhcea.

The summer plague, diarrhwa, a sequel to. the warm weather, nas made itself apparent in War- rington, and the Medical Officer reports two deaths from this cause. The death-rate last week was 10.5, compared with the average of 9.6 for the previous six weeks, and 17.0 , for the corresponding week in 1912. With the exception of Bootle, Warrington had the lowest death-rate of any large .Lancashire town last week. Five new cases of scarlet fever were reported, and 55 patients were in the hospitals.

div.head: Latchford Garden Society.
div.p: Latchford Garden Society.

The outdoor exhibits in connection with the Latchford Elower Show, to be held to-day, have been adjudicated upon with the following re- sults :—Class I, front garden: 1, Mrs. Davies, Lower Wash-lane; 2, Mr. 'Jowett, Lower Wash- lane; 3, Mr. 'lledditt, Knutsford-road. Class 2: 1, Mr. J. Sykes, Lower Wash-lane; 2, Mr. J. lee, 11, Enville-street.; 3, Mr. H. Smith, Knuts- ford-road. Class 3 t 1, Mr. 'Cadkys, Grappen; hall-road; .2, Mrs. Hatton;. Tunstall's7row ; 3, Mrs. Williams. Class 3a, allotments or kitchen gardens 1, Mr. Philip Johnston, Victoria 'Park allotments; 2, Mr. H. H., Drury, Victoria Park allotments; 3, C. Foster, Manor Locks, Latch- ford. The cult of flowers is a strong feature with.. the Latchford 'Garden Society, and the show this zear is being eagerly anticipated. This takes place to-day at the Wash-lane Schools, and in the Park, lent by Mrs. Broad- bent. An excellent programme, calculated to please all tastes, has been arranged, and Mrs. Broadbent is to perform the opening ceremony at 3 p.m.

Women Liberals' Picnic. This annual event, which takes place on Monday, September 29, to Belle Viie, is adver- tised in to-day's "Examiner," and details as to times and prices will be found on our first page. The inclusive charge in respect of members, non-members and children covers fare, admis- sion to the Gardens and tea. There will be the usual attractions, with a special display of fire- works in the evening. Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Crosfield will be present, and will speak; and it is expected that other well-known Liberals will attend. Mrs. Osborne, the lion. Secretary of the Women's Liberal Association, will be in attend- ance at the Junior Liberal Club, Horsemarket Cllambers, every afternoon between 2 o'clock and 5 o'clock from Thursday, September 18, to Thursday, September 25, for the purpose of issuing tickets. Tickets will not be obtainable after the latter date: It is expected that this ever-popular everit will be exceedingly well attended, and it would be a convenience to those making the arrangements if applications for tickets were made as early as possible.

div.head: " Sir " John Holden, 4%0M., K.D.H.,
div.p: " Sir " John Holden, 4%0M., K.D.H.,
Provincial Grand Chamberlain.

This is now the. full R.A.0.8. title of Mr. John Holden, in Bufialoism, in which he has been a very active worker for a number of years. On Tuesday of this week he had the honour of knighthood conferred upon ltim at the "Samuel Waxefield " Lodge, the ceremony being per- formed by " Sir " Thomas Davies, K.0.M., K.D.H., in a manner quite worthy of the occa- sion. " Sir " John , Wolfenden, K.0.M., K.D.H., was Brother Holden's sponsor. Mr. Holden was initiated in November, 1909, and was raised to second degree a year later. He is treasurer of the widows' and orphans' fund. At the inauguration of the Alexandra encamp- ment of the knights of the Golden Horn, he was knighted by "Sir " John Gordon, Past Grand Knight Commander, Knight of the Shield, and was also elected first scribe and purge-bearer. He is a founder of the ` Alexandra ' Lodge, and was elected its first primo. In his propaganda work he has had the unique experience of occu- pying the chair as Worthy Primo for upwards of five months, and at the first raising to the second degree he was chosen by the Provincial Grand Lodge to he installing officer. He has been the recipient of many decorations.
LOCAL INTELLIGENCE—continued.
Billiard League.
The annual general meeting of the Warring- ton Billiard League takes place at Rylands Bros.' Recreation. Club on Monday at half-past seven.
Sale of Valuable Furniture.

" Leckonby," Lymm, the home of the late Mr. James Gregson, is on Thursday to be the scene of a sale by auction of a valuable collection of furniture, and a number of outside effects. Messrs'. A. H. Clive and Co., the auctioneers, have timed the sale to commence promptly at 1.30 p.m.

div.head: DRINK OR ENVIRONMENT?
div.p: DRINK OR ENVIRONMENT?
The Greatest Obstacle in the Way of
Social Reform.
TOO MANY BREWERS.

"The rents of the houses and farms in the kingdom could, have been paid by the money which was .spent in strong drink last year." This startling 'statement was made by Mr. W. E. Boreland, of the United Kingdom Alliance, Liverpool, who was the principal speaker at the weekly meeting of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League and U.K.A., at Cornhill on Wednesday evening. Mr. WILLIAM WRIGHT, who presided, said we Were 'spending more than £160600,000 per an- nuiri in strong drink, and, as 'a country, we were not in a position to spend—or, he should say, waste—so much money on intoxicating liquors. Temperance workers contended that if anything like half the amount of money spent in strong drink was distributed in channels of production, it would be of great help to the people, and we should have a far different', state of things obtaining than we had at the present time. The country would be far more prosperous and -the people happier and more contented in every way. We were net only wasting this money, but. we were destroying a large proportion of the lives of our fellow-men who were using it. (Hear, hear.) When there was some question as' to how they were going to find the money for old-age pensions, he felt ' that surely if we Could spend so much money in drink,-we could find .the Xs.d. in order to help those who had fought the battle of life to gain rest and happiness in their old days. Drink was interfering very much with the many social problems of life. Some people said Lacy. were doubtful as to whether environment caused poverty, or whether drink was the greatest cause of poverty, but he was certain that one greatly affected the other. If it was not for the drink curse there was no doubt that many. of the social evils against which we had to con- tend would be wiped away. (Hear, hear.) If they were to solve some of the social problems In life, they must lay hold of the greatest factor against them, that of strong drink, which affected them in every quarter. Strong drink was filling the workhouse, asylums and gaols; it robbed the child .of its birth-right, and the facilities it. should have, to make its way easler in the world. How could they expect any boy to make his way in the world when he was dragged' down by those who indulged in strong drink?. They wanted .to get. the Children inter- ested in the question, for they were to be the men and women of to-morrow, when a sober, sensible people would be needed. (Applause.) Mr. BOBELAND said they should do their level best to induce the people to keep away from the. public-house, and then use all the powers they possessed to keep the drink away from the people, His experience of temperance ex- tended since. 1869, and it had acted very well in his case. During that time he had given the pledge to 30,000 men, Women and children—(ap- plause)—and those who had stuck to it had never regretted it, far their homes and lives Were brighter and better in every way. After men- tioning the large number of public-houses which had 'been closed in Liverpool during recent years, the speaker asked, "Have you ever dosed a public-hotise in Warrington?" to which Mr. Wright answered, "Not many." "I suppose," continued the .speaker, "you dare not; there are too many brewers about." (Hear, hear.) Speak- ing of the evil-effects of strong drink on the child life of the 'country, the speaker said that .the reports of Dr. Barnardo's Home. Waifs' and Strays' Society, and .the N.S.P.C.C., told. the awful tale of how many.child_lives were being clestrdyed lay the drink traffic. It. was the child life they bad to save, and when they did that they could rest assured that the nation :of the' future would. be a great credit. (Applause.) Votes of thanks to the speaker and Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: Examiner Team's Success.
div.p: Examiner Team's Success.

The " Examiner " rink hockey team beat the Whitecross contingent in the final game of the Works Medal Competition at the Empire Rink on Saturday. The Whitecross men pressed hard at the outset, but the ball ora..; quickly got away, and, after a most exciting inarrt!i, tl,e P :•.;4s.nen won by three goals to one. After the match the Medals, which are of silver, with gold facings, were presented to the winning team. •
A Pretty Wedding Ceremony iS Solemnised at
Golborne-s treet Church.
THE REV. H. OGDEN WEDS MISS ANNIE WRIGHT.
BRIDAL PARTY LE
VING THE CHURCH.

A marriage, which aroused a large amount of interest, was solemnised in Golborne-street Bap- tist Church, Warrington? on Thursday after- noon, in the presence of a large congregation. The function was of special interest, in that the bridegroom was the pastor of the chapel, the Rev. H. Ogden, who is one of the most popular ministers in the borough. He is a son of the late Mr. Edward Ogden, of Todmorden, York- shire.
The bride was Miss Annie Wright, daughter of Mr. William Wright, Palmerston, Cross-lane, Grappenhall.
RECEPTION AND PRESETS.

- . The ceremony was choral, and was conducted by the Bevs. T. N. Tattersall, London; G. Cur- tis, Hill Cliffe ; and J. S. Chedburn, Latchford. The music was provided by Mr. S. Bickers, the organist of the Golborne-street Baptist ChurCh, and amongst the appropriate items he rendered were "0, love divine," and "Since Jesus freely did appear to grace a marriage feast." The bride, who was escorted to the altar and bestowed upon the happy bridegroom by her father, was charmingly gowned in a cream cloth costume, with a Tuscan hat, trimmed with ostrich feathers to match. She carried a deli- cately Pretty bouquet of white roses and lily of
the valley blossom. The only ornament was a cameo brooch.

Miss Wright was attended to the altar by Miss Mary Wright (her sister), who wore a pale blue cloth costume, Tuscan hat with black ostrich plume, 'and her single ornament consisted of a gold bracelet, the gife of the bridegroom. She carried a pretty bouquet of sweet peas and streamers.
The duties of best man were efficiently filled by Mr. A. E. Elliott, of Warrington.

After the ceremony the happy -couple, their relatives and friends drove in motors to Atkin- son's Cafe, Bridge-street, and after the luncheon the Bev. and Mrs. Ogden started for the honey- moon, which is to be spent in London, Brussels, and other parts of the Continent. The bride's travelling dress consisted of a navy blue serge costume and black velure hat, with feather mount.

The couple received 'a large number of valu- able wedding presents from their many friends. The bridegroom's gift to the bride consisted of a handsome music cabinet and stool; and the bride gave the bridegroom a pretty and useful travelling case and bag. The motors which conveyed the guests to and from the church were supplied by Messrs. Patterson's, Latchford.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. ROYAL COURT. THEATRE.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS. ROYAL COURT. THEATRE.
"THE GAMBLER."

The sporting fraternity who patronise the Royal Court Theatre have had a. regular feast this week, for "The Gambler," from the pen of Sheila Walsh, is 'full of exciting incidents, deal- ing with the turf and the pasteboards. The story of the Spendthrift: happy-go-lucky bus- band's ruin through cards and horses, and his ultimate reformation, is extremely well enacted, and plenty of local colour is introduced in the scenery. As a climax we witness an intensely exciting race at , Goodwood, in which three thoroughbreds run as fast as they can for the cup, in full view of the audience, a revolving mat making this possible. An abundance of wholesome Irish comedy is introduced to advan- tage, for it relieves the heavier aspects of the play to an appreciable degree. As Dick Ran- dall, the spendthrift, Mr. Cecil W. Parke is a decided success. In the scene where he de- cides to uphold the family motto, "Death before dishonour," his acting is highly emotional, but in no way overdone. Mr. Dane Clarke gives an impressive delineation of the character of Burton, the butler, his gestures and facial ex- pressions being very fine. Mr. Charles H. Mortimer is a scheming Captain Cyril Stanley, and is awarded his quota of hisses from the " popular " 'parts.. Miss Sheila Walsh plays the part of Lady Paula Ware, Stanley's accom- plice, in a capital manner, infusing the part with plenty of spirit. Mr. George Portius is a typical racing tout, and as Snig Fowler he is very successful. Mr. George Scully, as Danny Ryan, the head groom, convulses the audience with his quaint Irishisms, in addition to pro- viding an admirable connecting link with the play. Miss Maisie Hanbury is a clever actress, and as Helen Randall ha S ample scope for her emotional powers. Miss Jennie Clare adds to the comedy parts as Rosie Ray, and the part of The Cherub, the .apprentice jockey. who rides " MoYa " past the post, is in the abTennds of Mr. E. Josiah.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME

Everyone has heard of Chung Ling Soo; and his marvellous tricks, but it is only on rare occasions that one has the chance of witnessing such a great and finished artiste. Warrington people have been fortunate this week, and the numerous patrons of the Hippodrome have been mystified, yet delighted, by Soo's per- formance. Amidst, Oriental surroundings, and assisted by Miss Sure Seen and a large staff of Chinese assistants, the conjuror peilorms the most weird and mystifying illusions. Soo is an exceptionally smart sleight of hand artiste, and in addition to many big attractions, he intro- duces numerous manipulation tricks, which bewilder and amuse. Soo gets through an ex- tensive repertoire each night, and one cannot help but admire the unostentatious and rapid manner in which each illusion is performed. Amongst the most notable feats which he in- troduces is "Asleep in the air." A beautiful Chinese maiden is sent .to sleep on a couch, and after Soo has passed the magic fan over her form several times, the lady gently rises, stretched at full length, and, in a minute' or two we see her in mid-air. flings are passed under and over ,the body to Satisfy the audience that no wires are suspending it, and this illu- sion is one of the most baffling in the whole performance. "The Magic taiffdron " trick is also very cleverly executed. A large cauldron, in which buckets of water are poured, is placed upon a fire, and after the water has boiled, Miss Seen jumps out of the steaming pot, from which also emdge live rabbits, pigeons, &c. _

--The Chung Ling Soo matinee on Thursday was well attended, and another matinee will be given to-day. At these performances Soo is the only'artiste, and he presents the whole of the programme. In addition to repeating his nightly performance, he introduces many special illusions. The other items are of an exceptionally high standard, and the representation of "Captain Careless, V.C.," by George Sheldon and Rawson Buckley's company has been thoroughly appre- ciated. Rich. Taylor is a clever ventriloquist, and scores a decided success in a novel whist- ling and singing ventriloquial scena. In an artistic dancing and musical act, Mignon and Frosettis are highly successful, the dancing of the juvenile member of the trio being exceed- ing graceful. Rene Ralph is a dainty character nedienne, and sings in a captivating man- ner.

div.head: "THE LIFEGUARDSMAN " NEXT WEEK.
div.p: "THE LIFEGUARDSMAN " NEXT WEEK.
There will be quite a diversion from the ordin- ary programme at the Hippodrome next week, when Mr. Walter Howard will present the

Photograph by Warwick Brookes. MISS FLORENCE CHEVERTON., who will play Dorine in Walter Howard's popular drama, "The Lifeguardsman," at the Warrington Hippodrome next week. Miss Cheverton has had experience Of repertory work under Miss Darragh at the Gaiety Theatre, Man- chester, and has played in a romantic sketch by Stanley Houghton on the music halls.

romantic play, "The Lifeguardsman," twice nightly. The play was first produced by Walter Howard at the Junction Theatre, Manchester, some two years ago, and proved such a huge success that it was played to packed houses nightly for six weeks. It met, with equal suc- cess on tour, and finally, at the invitation of the New Middlesex Theatre management, Lon- don, it was turned into a twice-nightly show, and drew large houses in London. The play is a stirring one; with plenty of living incidents, and a considerable amount of. humour. !Hs a pro- duction that will grip* the audience from stant. to finish.

div.head: THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: THEATRE ROYAL.

"The Red Villa Affair," an exceedingly inter- esting picture, delighted big audiences at the Theatre Royal in the early part of the week, and patrons have been loud in their approba- tion of "-The Curse," which has been shown since, and will be included in the programme to-night. Other pictures, of a humorous and pathetic nature will also be shown. The chief pictures for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next will be ." The Changeling" and "Child of an Indian Brave." For the remainder of the week "A. Guilty Love." and "The Little Child" will occupy premier position. The Two Countees will also appear as har- monising duettists.

div.head: PICTUREDROME.
div.p: THE PICTUREDROME.

Exclusive rights for this district have been obtained by the management of the Picture- drome for production of the best animal picture ever shown, "Alone in the Jungle." The pic- ture will be displayed all week at each of the three performances daily. It is a most thrilling and sensational animal masterpiece, and is a story of Central Africa. For Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday only the special comedy picture, "The Magic Wand," will be shown.

div.head: BRIDGE TRAFFIC.
div.p: THE BRIDGE TRAFFIC.
Cases in the Police Court.

Two cases concerning traffic over the • bridge were heard at Warrington Police Court on Thursday. A fine was inflicted in one and the other was adjourned. Henry Challoner, contractor; Wash-lane, was fined I.os. and costs 'for driving a horse and lurry over Warrington Bridge, to the common danger. Sergt. Edwards said .that defendant did not stop when P.C. Tolley put" his hand up. De- fendant, he said, was a very obstinate man, and a source of trouble to the police 'at times, _ _ _ _

Defendant: I did not see- the 'officer put his hand up. Sergt. Edwards: He did see him, because he laughed at Tolley. Marcus Cuthbert Dromgoole, " Sprayhurst," Boundary-road, St. Helens, Was summoned for having driven a motor car over Warrington Bridge at a speed dangerous to the public. Reuben Martindale, Royal Automobile Club inspector, said that he saw the defendant driv- ing a small car over the bridge at the rate of. 12 miles an hour. There was a good deal of traffic about, and, a large number of pedes- trians were going over the bridge on their way home from work. Defendant came suddenly from some more traffic, and Witness and a policeman had to jump out of the way. The officer shouted, but the man went on up Bridge- street. At the time a speed higher than walk- ing pace would be dangerous. • In the absence of the policeman, who was seriously ill, the case was adjourned, for four weeks.
LABOUR M.P. T. TORY M.P. THE COUNTRYSIDE
Remarkable Sequel to Walker's Brewery Labourers' Strike.
MR. J. R. CLYNES' CHALLENGE.
Colonel Hall Walker's Counter
Challenge.

There has been a remarkable sequel to the strike of the labourers, a few months ago, at the brewery of Messrs, Peter Walker and Son, Warrington. Mr. J.•ft.. Clynes, the Labour M.P. for one of the itliancheater Divisions, and secretary of Mt Lancashire District of the Nationt4 Unitoop of Gatsworkers and General Labourers,, has challenged Colonel Hall Walker, AP. 'for Wielmm to meet in public debate, and discuss some questions which have arksen since the strike.

How the challenge came to be issued is detailed by Min Clyna in a letter received by Mr. Charles Dukes, the secretary of the War- rington Trades and Labour Council, on Thurs- day. The Labour Member states that he was desired by his executive 0 communicate the letter. He adds :

"The union, in March last, sent to Messrs. Walker and Son, brewers, Warrington, an ap- plication for advances and improvements in the wages and conditions of a number of the work- men. The firm declined to discuss it, and refused to see anyone on the men's behalf. Sev- eral workmen were picked out and dismissed. A strike followed. But before and during the dispute the meh acted without any advice from me; the union carried out the decisions of the men."'

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS' SCENE.
div.p: A HOUSE OF COMMONS' SCENE.

Mr. Clynes alleges that, after the men tendered notice to cease work, Colonel Hall Walker spoke to him in the House of Commons for submitting the men's claims, and, as a result of what trans- pired, Mr. Clynes says, he reported the matter to the executive of the union, and a letter was sent to Colonel Walker, inviting him to name any date and time suitable for a meeting, in either the constituency of Widnes or Warring- ton. "lie did not reply," writes Mr. Clynes, In concluding his epistle, Mr. Clynes. says he objects to be challenged "for seeking to get better conditions for the men," and,. in turn, challenges Colonel Walker to meet him "in pub- lic at any meeting he (the Colonel) wishes to call to debate the points at issue." The position thus created is rather remark- able and is one of the greatest interest to the workers. It is a decided novelty for one M.P. to challenge another to debate outside the House of Commons, and if such a meeting could be arranged there would be a large "gate," the proceeds of which could, be devoted to some charity, either in Widnes or Warring- ton.

div.head: COUNTER-CHALLENGE.
div.p: THE COUNTER-CHALLENGE.

We made inquiries of Colonel Hall Walker at Gateacre as to whether he intended to. accept Mr. Clynes' challenge. We received the fol- lowing reply by wire "I challenge Clynes to give any working men as comfortable a billet as Peter Walker and Son do to their men.—Hall Walker."

div.head: JUNIOR LIBERALS.
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERALS.
The Renewed " Activity" of Women
Tariff Reformers.
MR. H. SMITH'S "LATEST."

There was a large attendance at an open-air meeting held under the auspices of the War- rington 'Junior Liberal Association on the Flags, Knutsford-road, last night. The principal speaker was Mr. T. H. Garside, of Manchester, and the chairman was Mr. E. A. Sanders. At the outset, the Chairman referred to what he termed "Harold Smith's latest." fn view of the passing of the Tariff Reform League, he was forming one called 'Help the Women of Ulster League." He had invited all symriathisers with the poor oppressed people of Ulster to take the wives and children of Ulster into their tiornes, whilst the ,men fought. Mr. Smith and his leaders would* be far froth the 'field" of battle. More probably, they would be superintending the carrying out of soup kitchens for the poor homeless 'ones. Mr. Smith might venture to write 'a new play "Mad as a Mardi Hare," and give the proceeds to the cause. (Laughter.) Mr. Harold Smith wound up his heartrending appeal by saying that already 6,000 members of the League, headed by Lady Greenall, were tumbling over each other to take in these in- teresting lodgers. In conclusion, Mr. Sanders said that Mr., Garside would deal more fully with this silly appeal at Monday's Meeting of the Progressive Labour League. Mr. Garside dealt extensively with the land question, and said that we had to-day 20,000 men who had made application for small hold- ings, and they could not get them. The land was there, but the landlords would not let it go. They 'said, "My price, please." They had not the slightest right to fix a price on land, because the land belonged to the Nvthole of the people, and not to any individual landowner.

div.head: CQUNTRYSIDE—continued.
div.p: CQUNTRYSIDE—continued.

that the warm air is full of buzzing insects— solitary bees flittering from flower to flower, in search of nectar and pollen, or the active little yellow and. black bodied sand wasps seek- ing young caterpillars, or spiders, to store up for their growing grubs. Over yonder, flying in and out amongst the herbage, is a large black and yellow robber-fly, more than an inch long, stalking for prey. Now and again we disturb a moth from its hiding-place, where it waits for the twilight hours. At our feet numbers of bright, burnished green and blue metallie col- oured beetles are running about the plants. Away out of sight, until sought for, lurking at the roots ot plants, and in all sorts of odd corners that afford shelter,are numberless smal- ler insects of many kinds. On the bare patch of sand to the left is an agile little Sand Lizard, scuttling out of our way, so like the sand in colour as to be invisible until alarmed. It is only its movement that separates its form from its surroundings. Under a heap of large pebbles, and other flotsam further.along, several Natterjack toads, with their olive green skin and a bright yellow line down the centre of the back, were dislodged. It is very pleasing to note that this interesting little toad still survives in good numbers, and is not yet sacrificed on .the altar of golf.
G. A. DUNLOP.

div.head: Pt A Meditation on the Scottish Sandhills. –
div.p: Pt A Meditation on the Scottish Sandhills. -
PLANT BOUND SHORES.

Sandhills are. of particular interest to the naturalist, and many little surprises are in store for the observer. There the coast is found protected from erosion by the sea by plants binding together the loose sands. The description of how the sand-dunes are formed and finally prepared by Nature for the grow th of vegetation is of particular interest.
During the past week I have had the oppor- tunity of renewing acquaintance, after many years, with a particularly interesting stretch (- sandlulls, or sand-dunes, as they. are more p

perly called, on the Ayrshire Coast. No paris of the British coast-line are so full of interest: to the Nature lover as the sand-dunes. Whether the dunes on the Lancashire and Cheshire sea— board, extending from Grange to West Kirby, or those. on the Welsh Coast at Prestatyn, or the Ayrshire coast-line from Saltcoats to the Heads of Ayr, the problems they suggest are. always the same. The particular part of Uicse Ayrshire sand-dunes that I am now referring to, extend from high-water mark to about a thiril of a, mike inland, where they merge gradually into cultivated land.

A long fine of irregular sand-dunes follows the Curve of the coast. . Immediately above the high-water fine, there is a sudden rise in the surface of the ground. The rising slope ot. loose, shifting sand culminates in a ridge, cov- ered with a sparse growth of the Marram Grass. After a slight dip the land gradually rises again; and then falls into a long, receding shelf, until it passes to more or less undulating hillocky ground. Except in a few places here- and there, where the Golf Club have made "putting greens," the sandy waste is entireljr unspoiled by men, and here can be seen ant studied the forces which are making, altering, and re-making .the land. For the loose sands are continually in motion, the winds from sea: and land blowing the sand about, first here Anti then there, and back again, the contours of the dunes. undergoing incessant change. Indeed, it is only the vegetation which prevents the sand being blown away altogether. In many parts of the world, including our own land, the coast is only saved from erosion by the ravages of wind and sea, by the plants which bind together the loose sands 'composing the shore. The name conditions are present on a sand-dune coast-line„ everywhere, those on the Ayrshire or the Wirral Coast are essentially similar.

Interesting Formations. Altholigh the formation of the sand-dunes is- an extremely interesting one—and one which may form the subject of a later article—their fixation and retention by means of vegetation, besides being interesting, is of considerable economic importance as well. Nature's ways are indeed wonderful. Let us see how she pro- ceeds in this case. Mention has already been made of the ridge of the dunes being capped with growths of Sea Marram Grass (Psamma ,arenaria). This grass has long, spreading underground stems, with fine fibrous roots, a system most admirably adapted for holding the loose grains of sand. The persistence of the ridge is due to the binding qualities of the plant, which, to a great extent, .resist the drifting action of the wind. Moreover, the dense mass of decaying grass gives more humus to the ground. This addition cf organic matter to the soil soon makes it possible for other plants to obtain a sustenance, and we find plants like the Cats-ear and Best-barrow joining the Lyme Grass. The advent of the Best-harrow is a very important one on the new plant association, for it brings with it the well-known nitrogenous properties of the natural order LeguminosEe. As generation after generation of Best-harrow wither and die, valuable constituents Are added to the soil, and as it. becomes richer in chemical_ contents, many other plants like Ragwort, Hawkbit, Hawkbeard, arid the Dwarf Willow are added to the company. When the Dwarf Wil- low once gets a good hold of the sand, quite a small army of other plants enter into occupation. of the adjoining ground, such as maritime grasses, the seaside violet, ladies' bed-straw, sea plantain, sea campion, bird's-foot trefoil, ' sea. spurge, hound's-tongue, and a host of others. These are all more or less plants with fleshy, or large leaves. They in turn add greatly to the nutritious matter in the soil. In this way a succession of plants is formed, leading up to a dense tangle of -the little burnet rose. Stilt further inland, grasses have taken possessions and made the land fit for cultivation.

Adaptation. . A little further examination will show that the flora has, a peculiar character of its own, and one which is exactly adapted to the condi- tions of the soil. The principal difficulty whictx the plants has to contend against, owing to the porous nature of the ground, is scarcity of water. It is therefore necessary, seeing the substratum is poor in water, that the plants, in order to obtain a living, must be adapted to resist transpiration as much as possible. This is done in two ways—(l) by the leaf surface being reduced to a minimum; or (2) by the leaf being of a thick, fleshy, succulent nature. Most of the plants growing in very loose sand belong to the first group, the leaves are narrow and ex- pose Very little surface. In the Murrain Grass, —which may be examined on the Museum flower table—the breathing pores are all on .the under- surface of the leaves, and the edges are so rolled over that the pores open into what is practically a'closed tube. The air in the tube is saturated with vapour, and hence the transpiration is minimised. The other group is found where the addition of the humus of decaying vegeta- tion has added to the water-holding nature of the soil.

Two or three other points of interest may be found by anyone curious enough to examine the sandhills and their plants. For instance, it will be found that the layer of decayed organic matter only forms a crust from six to,ten inches in thickness; below that is pure sand. Also that it is this " crust " which is principally concerned in holding the moisture upon which the vegeta- tion 'feeds. Until recently more attention has been paid to the nutritive value of this layer, rather than its water-holding capacity. Mr_ A. D. Hall has pointed' out the importance of this latter factor. He has shown that it is of more value to the plants, and is dependent on the size of the particles composing the soil. For instance, in clay, where the particles are .very minute, a very largc quantity of water is tamed at at the surface. If, on the other hand, the particles are coarse, as in sand, a very small portion of water is retained. Most of the water comes from rain showers, and, owing. to the relatively small particles in the humus layer, it is held longer tlfrin in the larger grains. of sand. Sand, however, has a certain amount of water raising and retaining power. At a depth or twelve to fifteen inches, just below the direct- influence of sun and air, a considerable quantity of moisture 'will be found.

It is still further interesting to note the pecu- liar adaptation of the roots to the various con- ditions in which they grow. Many of the long- rooted plants, such as Cat's-ear, send their roots • and rootlets straight down to the moisture zone in the sand, but where they occur in the humus, water-holding layer, a dense growth of side- • roots and root-hairs are produced just on that part of the root which passed through the layer. These side-roots are absent on that part of the tap-root which extends into the pure sand below. Nature is full of infinite sugges- tiveness to the inquiring mind, and she reveals many of her secrets to the seeing eye.
Animal Life. In our walk over the sandhills, not only the plant life is interesting, but the animal life as well. For we shall not have failed to notice - Continu3d in preceding column.

div.head: CRUELTY TO GOATS.
div.p: CRUELTY TO GOATS.

Sir,--The barbarous practice of tethering ill- kept, neglected goats to famish by the wayside, without *titer, food, shade front the burning sun, or shelter frotn wind and rain, seems to be on the increase in our villages. If destined to give milk, goats need the most careful feeding, and also must be groomed every.l:,y, otherwise lice will fall into the pail. One Shudders to realise that these frowsy. unkempt animals may be providers of vermin-haunted milk for the children and in- valids of the community!

.... . Thi. whole question of goat keeping for this Purpose. in this country, is a, doubtful one, and the we!kneaning persons who encourage Me custom among cottagers should bear in mind hoW liable to abuse it is. 'Certainly the pro- pinquity to human dwellings of goats, noisome Er.'" neglect, must be highly insanitary..
JUSTICE.

TEMPERANCE AND ITS WORKERS. Sirt—My attention has been-drt ,vrt to a letter, aPPeal'ing in your columns a week or two ago, complaining about the apathy of temperance workers in the . town,- to which charge I am " bound to a certain extent to plead guilty. I am very much pleased at the efforts tieing made la, IV IV friend at Ellesmere-street, and gratified "v' 9 find he is taking an active part in propa- gating temperance principles. Let me point out to hint that there are two _organisations in the to continually propagating the temper- ance cause. The Sons of Temperance meet at Bewsey-road fortnightly, and have both adult and juyenile branches, and the Good Templars meet at Buckley-street every week. The Good Templars have an adulrlodge and a juvenile temple, both of which meet ever y% Wednesday night; the temple 7 to 8, the lodge 8 to 10. ,The members of this fraternity would be very , Pleased to welcome your correspondent among _ them to help in the /good cause. I admit that temperance workers are no doing all they might dpr to advance the common cause. and I again cordially invite him .to come and form one of the circle in our fraternal home, and give us hiS counsel and help in improving matters.
A TEMPLAR.

STOCKTON HEATH AND AMALGAMATION. Sir,—_ la your "Passing Week " 'column refer- ence was Made to the above question; and, if YOU will pardon me saying so, erroneous state- ments have been made. The consideration of the matter did not arise from the growing pres- sure of county rates, as you assert; but so far as I and the other two candidates who issued a joint election address are concerned, amalgama- tion was advocated from the standpoint of " mutual benefit." The committee formed to consider the matter was the outcome of a reso- lution passed at, a parish meeting, asking that an inquio be held. I repeat what was made clear at that meeting, namely, that it should not be a matter of..rates.so much as. public requirements, and the POint, becomes, how best to provide them.,

The Mop was correct when he said that there was tt' community of interests between Warrington and its .suburbs. Those interests can best be served by both sides accepting their responsibilitirs, despite a probable increase in rates. Stockton Heath may enjoy lower rates the people are not thereby assured lower rents. The public service provided by Warrington are just as necessary to Stockton Heath as to War- rington herself. We should not consider this matter from the standpoint of commercial barter, but from the view point of public enter- prise.
CHARLES DUKES, Member of the Parish Council.

div.head: WHAT IS LOCAL OPTION?
div.p: WHAT IS LOCAL OPTION?

my correspondence, as well as in. public discussion, I aim to present what I con- CelVe to be the truth, Without attributing insin- cerity to those who differ from me. If my last letter, to which your correspondent., jr. Ed- ward Tucker, takes exception, , oversteps that rule, l,malie haste to apologise. I have no copy of the letter, but if it inferred, as I fear that Mr. Tucker was wilfully. misrepresenting the facts, I unhesitatingly withdraw that part of it.

As regards the substance of my letter. I have nothing either to withdraw, or for which to apologise. It is perfectly true, as Mr. Tucker, points out, that Clause 2 of the 1908 Licensing Bill makes provision for a prohibitory resolu- tion only, and enacts that on the requisition of one-tenth of the parochial electors a poll shall be taken, and the resolution ”shall be deemed to be carried on a poll if a majority of the votes are in favour of the resolution."

It is quite inc:OnTe-ii;a-bTe.lll7iluch• a poll wOuld be demanded unless in that area there was an application for a .new licence. The poll would in effect deide "No licence," or, "Licence." and .the Majority would be the determining factor. It Would naturally follow that "although a majority Voting against a prohibitory reolu• lion. could not demand that new licence "as of right." yet .sheh would be the effect. The law of England with regard to the drink traffic is prohibition—with exceptions. The number of those exceptions is determined by the, Licensing .Bench. We want the vote of the majority in the areas affected to be an instruc- tion to the magistrates to refuse or to grant such a licence. That, I submit, is the obvious mean- ing of Clause 2, Sections 1 to 4, of the Licensing Bill of 1908.

If the majority defeated a prohibitory resolu- tion the magistrates could do (and accepting the principle of local option, would do) what they would otherwise be prohibited from doing. With this "gigantic evil" still to be remedied. it is surely too late in the day to demand thrit the option "to prohibit or not to prohibit". should be altered to "grant or not to grant." The effect would be the same, but the principle behind the Bill of 1908 is the .right of a com- munity to protect. itself from the gross wrong of having a licence thrust upon it against the will of the majority. That is Local Option.
THOS. D. LESLIE, k.
August 11th, 1913

RATING REFORM. • Sir,—The second reading debate, on the Ttevenue Bill in the House of Commons draws • attention to the urgent need for Rating Reform. •' In speaking of the necessity for deducting the -value of improvements in the valuation of agri- cultural land, in order that a true valuation might be arrived at, so providing the necessary basis Of any real rating reform,. the Chancellor of the Exchequer said that although he did not, pretend to have any definite view on the sub- ject, one thing was quite clear, and that was that the present rating system did to, a certain extent discourage improvements in town and country. fie did ,suggest that it was worth while considering whether improvements should not, sorbehow or Other, become an element in the qUestion of rating to a larger extent than 'was the case at present. . It is to be hoped that, in view of the corning , land campaign, Mr. Lloyd George will bring forward proposals for empowering local author- ities to levy rates on land values, .and exempt improvennts. Land reformers throughout the country, embracing practically the whole body of the supporters of Liberalism, are looking eagerly for the embodiment of the rating of land values in the Chancellor's proposals. The demand for that has been made with most complete unanimity by Liberal , Con fe re n t '0 after' Liberal Conference throughout the eauntrV. The •Liberal PartY is pledged, over and over again, to carry

the rating of land values at the first opportunity. Even in a Tory House of Commons theprinciple was affirmed on the second reading of a Bill for the rating of kind values, by a large majority. As Mr. Runciman pointed out in the House of Commons, the present method of assessment

penalises disastrOusly the small holder. For example, prior to the purchase by the Small Holdings Committee of the North Riding, the assessment on the SkidbY Estate was £583. It is now assessed at £1,012. There are many similar examples that could be quoted. It is not only in rural affairs that the present rating system acts so disastrously in hampering, and impeding productivd effort. .It acts simi- larly in all branches of . industry. Concrete examples could be furnished, but the fact is so patent that is it unnecessary. That the present rating system must be dras- tically reformed is admitted on all sides. Mr. Lloyd ciporge and other Liberal leaders have pointed out how the rating of improvements penaliges industry and restricts progress. If the problem is to be tackled in a radical manner, proposals must necessarily be brought forward for the unrating of improvements, and, consequently, for the rating of land values. SIDNEY J. PHILLIPS.

div.head: PILGRIMS' AFTER THOUGHTS. The Prime Minister and the Women's
div.p: PILGRIMS' AFTER THOUGHTS. The Prime Minister and the Women's
- Cause. LOCAL OPINION.

The women's pilgrimage has already had important results. In the first place, the Home Secretary received, a deputation from the National Union Of Women's Suffrage .Societies, who laid before him the inadequate protection given to women in certain places in the *Mid- lands and South against attacks- by bands of roughs. The members of the deputation pointed out that the inhabitants of the towns and villages, through which the pilgrims passed, were anxious to give the women a fair hearing, and were generally sympathetic; but that in several places organised attacks had been made by a band of men, who followed the pilgrims from place to place. The police, in spite of warnings, took no extra precautions, and though they rendered what help they could, their numbers were often totally inade- quate. No effort had been made to punish offenders and no arrests were made. The /lint of the deputation was to destroy the idea in some quarters. that women suffragists were fair. game.

Mr. McKenna said that he was grateful to the deputation for laying definite facts before him. They had as much right to adequate pro- tection as any other organisation. He 'prom- ised, on full information being supplied him, to make representations where they were needed, and he expressed appreciation of the constitutional efforts of the National Union and the courage of Rs Members. But more striking still is the fact that the Prime Minister, who has steadily declined to receive deputations on the woman suffrage question (for example, one from Scottish town councillors and one from clergymen), eonsented last Saturday to receive a deputation from the National _Union, led by Mrs. Fawcett. "I felt," he said. "that the request stood on an entirely different footing. In the first place, the request had come from a body, which I believe repre- sents practically the whole of the constitutional organisation working for women's 'suffrage. In the next place, it came immediately after the very impressive .demonstration (of the pil- vrimage). and further, Mrs. Fawcett told me that as the result of the experiences during that pilgrimage, she thought there were new facts. or, at all events, new evidence which could be adduced for me to consider."

div.head: ADVANCE OF OPINION
div.p: ADVANCE OF OPINION

Miss Margaret Robertson, the first speaker. of the deputation, instanced the rapid advance of opinion atuong working men during the past five years. It was deplorable that the chivalry and common sense; which, working , men so continually showed in their- reception of ._suffra- gist speakers- and arguments, should be so entirely ignored by the Press, whilst the doings of a few hooligans were published from the housetops. The most important suggestion was made by Mrs. Fawcett. After reviewing the Parliamen- tary- history of the suffrage movement during the last few years, she pointed out. that nothing less than a Government measure would be of any use. All parties have been divided. on great and momentous questions before they have been definitely adopted into the party pro- gramme. Her suggestion was that the anti- suffrage members of the Government should follow the precedent of Mr. Goschen in 1880. Mr. Goschen stood aside because of his deter- mined opposition to the enfranchisement of the agricultural labourers. . •

Mr. Asquith, in his reply, expressed regret at the Speaker's Tilling on the Franchise Bill in January last. "It. is quite impossible, if the Liberal party, by a substantial majority, is in favour of a great measure, such as that you are advocating, for a minority to obstruct or to prevent the realisation of it."

div.head: DEFINITE PROMISE.
div.p: A DEFINITE PROMISE.

"I will promise to communicate to my col- leagues tile very important gild serious facts, some of them new facts, which you. have brought before me. I was particularly inter- ested in what Miss Robertson told us about the attitude of working men and women, and also in the evidence that the public are beginning to draw distinctions between the • militant. sec- tion, which is a very small minority, and those who, like yourselves, have been content with undramatic But thoroughly honest and 'con- stitutional methods of advocacy. It is a most regrettable thing that so much prominence should be given .to those repellant incidents which bulk so largely in'the_puplic eye, and it is iic:eonsequence of. that, that the real work, which is _being done in aupporl,:of what even opponents. must -regard' as in n -honourable and worthy -cause,. is: kept out of sight and,ignored. " Frepeat that it is a matter -which, in the final resort, must be decided by the people themselves. If you can convince-you say you have and you may be righl7—the judgment and conscience of the people, that it is a bene- ficent charge, there is no combination in the world which can prevent your success, and no political party will attempt to do it. If I might offer one word of counsel, it would be: Pro- ceed as you have been 'proceeding, and con- tinue to the end. I am perfectly- certain that if you succeed in persuading the judgment of the people, your most determined opponents would be the first to how to it, and to make the change as beneficial as is possible. •

Territorials Going to Camp. . It is expected that the greater percentage of the officers and men of the 4th Batt. South Lancashire Regiment will go to the, camp at Denbigh, The advance party of 20 rank and file, under Lieutenant and Quartermaster G. H. Ingram, will depart from Warrington this morning. The battalion parades at noon to- morrow at the Warrington Drill Hall, and will, under the command of . Colonel Q. Elgood, en- train for Denbigh. The Newton detachment, in charge of Capt. G. R. Crosfield, will join the main body en route. The camping ground at Denbigh is reported to be one of the most in- teresting ever visited by the battalion. Thee inhabitants make the visitors welcome, and the North Lancashire Brigade report that Denbigh is the best camping ground they have ever attended.

div.head: FRESH AIR FOR PICTURES
div.p: FRESH AIR FOR PICTURES

The necessity of fresh tar for 'pictures is a consideration that is causing the authorities of the picture gallery of the Louvre some anxiety. It has now been discovered that the shutting out of air from the canvases by covering them with a glass, has had a distinctly bad effect on some of the most valuable paintings. Leonardo da Vinci's "St. Anne" has been found spotted with a vegetable parasitic growth. Further, the condensing of vapour on the inside on the glass, added to the varying temperature of the gallery, is disintegrating the colouring matter. Experiments are being made .vith a glass mounted in a metal frame and so arranged that.the air can circulate behind it.

The village folk sacrificed to the goddess of pleasure tins week. They did not go in for rushbearing, but rushed to the seaside. A few, however,-kePt Up the practice handed down from pagan times. Boys sold bullrushes, and on Saturday night there were lively doings at the Cross. The "nuts" patronised Blackpool in large numbers, and they sought to paint it "nutty red."
Picture postcards flowed back to the stay-al- homes, and .the postmen were kept busy. A little Lymm lass was taken to sea the sea for the first time in •tier life.
At. Blackpool she was laßen to a point where a good view of the billowy ocean was avail- able.
She gazed upon the scene, and ejaculated : "Is that the sea, daddy?" "Yes !" was the reply. "Then," quoth the lass, "it's nothing but water."

SPECIAL TRAIN TO THE RESCUE.-111 r. C. E. Cow- per, in addition to giving, his employees of the Booth's Hill and Rush Green cutting shops a holiday on Tuesday, generously provided them with a trip to Southport. Favoured with lovely weather, the ppi:ty spent a pleasant time in ‘Garden City," ample enjoy- mentn the " City " and on the n hlboin.iaee. gnd' 8 Unfortunately, suppliede a Seaside bo I the return train did not make the expected connection, and, to avoid a long wait, Mr. Cowper ordered" England's a special train, which soon conveyed the party to Lymm.

kimabde MERRYMAKERS AT RRYL—Another Monday trip w y the, Congregational Sunday "Sunny Rhyl " their goal. During recent years great improvements have been made at this resort in the interests of day trippers, the grounds surrounding the Marine Lake having been transformed, and fur- nished with the most up-to-date mirth-provok- ing contrivances. It was this Marine Lake Pleasure Park that was the scene of much merri- ment for the Lymm holiday-makers, thought the sands and other attractions of this "Children's Paradise " were also appreciated.

TRIP TO NEW BRIGHTON.—Monday morning also saw the departure from Heatley Station. en route for New Brighton, of between fifty and sixty scholars, parents and friends connected with the Broom Edge Sunday School. After the difficulties of Passing through Liverpool and party lost no time in entering into the en- crossing the river Mersey had been negotiated, the ioyments provided at this Cheshire resort. The Tower, the manner party with its fair ground, in which are all of nttractions, appealed equally to those With refined taste and cultured mind, as to the others whose bent in the pursuit of of pleasure was of a more boisterous nature. Some members of the party extended their out- ing ;to an inspection of the Liverpool Exhibi- tion. All, however, .had tea fOgether, and the return journey . was commenced from New Brighten Pier Pt 7 o'clock, arriving back at Heatley • soon after 10 pm. RUSII-REARING "%ITEM—Whereas Whitweek is the great holiday time (if the year for Man- chester, the people of Lynam ma-lie rush-beitring week the season of their coming under the spell of the goddess of pleasure. Though the old customs which once surrounded this festive season have to a large extent disappeared, there still exists .a few reminding features,. such as the band, which). carried out a good programme at the Cross last Saturday night, and the boys going round selling bullrushes. A goodly num- ter of people went for their holidays on Satur- day, but it was on Monday that the real holi- day-making commenced. Most of the shops and works were closed, and, owing to the patronage of the various trips of the day, the village in the morning had quite a deserted appearance: in fact, it looked as if the Pied Piper had paid Lymm a visit and had not only spirited the children away, but the adults as well. How- ever, the afternoon arrival of the usual mothers' Monday outings brought a 'little more life into the locality.

EAGLE BROW' SUNDAY SCHOLARS' SPORTS.—The scholars of the Eagle Brow Sunday School held their summer treat on Tuesday, in the field kindly lent by Mr., Peter Warburton. In•the afternoon a variety of outdoor games were en- joyed, and keen appetites prepared for the ex- cellent tea which followed. After tea an inter- esting programme of sports was carried out, which resulted as follows :—Class 7 race: 1, Edith Cook; 2 Nellie Beatty. Class 6: 1, Cissie Tonge ; 2, William Sharpies. Class 5: 1, Stan- ley Knowles; 2, Joe Thornicroft. Class 4: 1, Nellie Mairs ; 2, Edith Ackerley. Class 3: 1, George Davies; 2. Harry Cheetham. Class 2: 1, Bessie Cross; 2. Elizabeth Appleton. Class 1: 1, George Appleton ; 2. Arthur Appleton. Girls' three leg race: Nellie Ma irs and Mary Broadey. Boys' three leg race: George Davies and , Charles Percival. Wheelbarrow race: George Davies and Charles Percival. Consola- tion race: Edward Griffiths. Owing to the generosity of :Mr. H. Champ and other teachers, a supply of prizes had been obtained, and were presented to the 'successful competitors by Mr. G. •L. Welford. • .

GIRL'S EXCITING ADVENTURE.—The Wesleyan Sunday scholars; with their teachers and frisk's, to the number of Seventy, left Lymiii by the 77.48 train on Wednesday morning, their destination being New Brighton. In reserved compartments the railway journey provided a foretaste of the Pleasures that awaited them at its termination. The short sail across the river, though beneficial in the case of most maladies, is apparently in- effectual where the passengers are badly smitten by holiday fever, and it was a merry and healthy party that disembarked at the New Brighton pier. Seen in their quest for pleasure, they invaded the sands, Tower Grounds, &c.,. drinking the cup of enjoyment to the dregs. Walks and rides along the fine promenade through Liscard and Egremont afforded splendid views of the shipping in the estuary. Some excitement was caused when one of the girls, as she was wading, stepped into a hole and got wet through. She was speedily rescued and her needs attended to. Tea was catered at the Lifeboat Restaurant, and was heartily appreciated. As is the habit of good things, they are over too soon, and it was with regrets at having to leave the seaside that the return journey was commenced, the party eventually arriving at Lymm after a happy day's outing.

EXODUS TO Ihric.EPooL.--..The annual excursion to Blackpool, organised this year by the Primi- tive Methodist Sunday School, with Mr. W. T. Moss as hon. secretary, was as popular as ever, and, despite the prospect of gloomy weather, a large number of people were assembled on the Lymm Station platform by 6.15 a.m. on Monday morning, for the purpose of journeying by the special train. Though the Lymm Tradesmen's Association was not officially attached to the trip, a number of the members and their families joined the excursion. The employees of Mr. J. H. Holt also went for their annual outing to Blackpool, a saloon on the same train being reserved for their use. On arrival at Talbot-road Station, the excursionists soon became merged in the large number of visitors at this popular resort, and were left to enjoy the day according to their respective tastes. The sands afforded a great attraction for the young folk, whilst the allurements of the 'rower, Winter Gardens, Piers and South Shore pleasure beach, with its collection of amuse- ments, supplied a continuous round of pleasure. The weather, apart from a brief shower at noon. was excellent, and even the "sad sea- waves" were equal to the occasion, the sea being excep- tionally calm, and a lovely sunset was witnessed before the return train was due to depart. It was fortunate for the excursionists that on the homeward journey the railway company's by- laws 'relating to passengers' luggage were not enforced, for nearly every person appeared to possess one or more parcels, presumably. souvenirs and presents. Lymm was safely reached shortly before 11.30 p.m. Quite a num- ber of persons are utilising the long and short date tickets. which were also issued in connec- tion with this trip.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH
Township Tittle-Tattle.
There was an exciting fight in the Square on Saturday night.
A fiery terrier and a strong built collie dog were the combatants.
The fire bell was not rung; nor the police sum- moned to the fray.
A dog whip, lustily wielded, proved effectual in ending the scrimmage. In the dry, thirsty weather, some " Heathens " have blessed Warrington licensing regulations.
After the Heath hotels were closed at ten, it was so easy to step into Warrington and imbibe for an hour longer.

Manchester is grievously offended with Stock- ton Heath for insinuating that the city is responsible for the canal odours. Despite the Manchester denial that it is responsible, the perfume remains a menace to the health of Stockton Heath.
"Soup a la Ship Canal" was a dish on the dinner menu at the Manchester Municipal Officers' annual picnic on Monday.
If they secured the water for the brewing of the soup out of the Canal at Stockton Heath, no thickening or masoning ingredients would have been required.

HARVEST PROSPECTS.—The cereal crops are ripening rapidly, and harvesting operations will probably commence within the next ten or twelve days. The rain came opportunely for the parched crops. -Provided the weather is suitable, farmers are . hopeful of successful results.

THE CANAL °HOLUM—The Ship Canal is again ". speaking" in an odorous sense, and the allega- tion has been made that sewage from Manchester is responsible. The Stockton Heath complaint was brought to the attention of a member of Manchester's Sanitary Authority by an " Exam- iner " representative. "There is no truth," he saki, "in the statement that sewage from Man- chester goes into the Ship Canal. The River Irwell is purer now than ever it was, but ic might be made better, arid will be improved. It is the Mersey which is the chief offender, and it does not touch Manchester at all. The chief fault seems to lie with the industries of Stock- port and other places on the Mersey." Despite this denial, Stockton Heath still has the smell.

WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The annual trip of the scholars, teachers and friends took place to Overton Hills, Frodsham, on Thursday. The scholars assembled at the Schoolroom at eight o'clock in the morning, and proceeded to Vic- toria-square, where special cars were waiting to convey them to Bank Quay Station, from whence they proceeded by train to Frodsham. Dinner and tea was supplied in the spacious rooms of Mersey View Pleasure Grounds, and this was provided by the teachers and officers of the school. The day was spent by the children Playing rounders, .football, cricket, and many of the seniors enjoyed a game of bowls. Others visited "Jacob's Ladder" and the "Caves." . The races in the various classes provided much amusement, especially the races for the young ladies' and married men's classes. The Rev. W. A. Beckett paid a visit to the trippers, and his presence was much appreciated by the officials of the school. The party returned from Frod- sham by special train at 8.20 p.m., Stockton Heath being safely reached shortly after nine o'clock.

div.head: AMERICAN HONOUR FOR A NATIVE
div.p: AMERICAN HONOUR FOR A NATIVE

Mr. James Whitley, chairman of the Stockton Heath Parish Council, has received a letter from his son, the Rev. John Edward Whitley, that be has received the degree of M.A. froin•the Harvard University in America. June- 19 was the great day of the year in the University. Hundreds of -graduates in different departments of the University wore cap and gown and walked in dignified procession to. the hall, *here - the different degrees were conferred. I The Rev. J. E. Whitley has spent two years in post graduate study in the School of Arts and Sciences, and be now holds thrge dezrees, as follow: 8.A., Drury College, 1897; 8.D., Yale University. 1900; and M.A., Harvard University. 1913; and his degrees now are 8.A.. LL.B., M.A. His church is at Cambridge, Mass. Mr. Whitley received his early education under that re- spected master, the late Mr. John Grinrod, St.

SERVICE OF WARRINGTON BRIGADE. The terms upon which the Warrington Fire Brigade were to be available for fire outbreaks in Stockton Heath were mentioned at a meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday night. The charge recommended by the Fire Commit- cee was £75 per annum. Alderman Burton said the committee had given careful consideration to the application from Stockton Heath, and he thought that .115 per annum was a reasonable charge. They had arrived at that on the base of the rateable value of Stockton Heath, so far as it related to the upkeep and proper maintenance of a fire bri- gade, as compared with , the rateable value, for that purpose, of Warrington. He thought they were asking a fair sum, and if Stockton Heath wanted the service and bene- fit of the Warrington Brigade, it was only reasonable they should pay a proportion towards the maintenance of the brigade. The report was approved, and now the matter rests with Stockton Heath to say whether they shall accept the terms offered by Warrington.

UNDESIRABLE VISITOR.—Thomas Herbert Wil- liams, of Warrington, no settled address, pleaded guilty to loitering with intent to cora- -mit a felony in London-road, Stockton Heath. Shortly after -midnight on Aupst 7th prisoner was -seen by P.C. Cronipton loitering about the. road and standing in a -gateway. He went up Opening•and was caught- by Constable Worth- ingtmi. • A 'conple of. Stones . were- found in his possession, and when questioned about these he said: "Well, I haven't any tools, and I must have something to break in with. If you hadn't caught me I should have been in somewhere ' before very long."—P.C. Worthington gave corroborative evidence, and Supt. Ennion said prisoner was sent to a reformatory school in 1909, and, was bound over in May this year for loitering.—Williams was sent to gaol for three months.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

_ ASYLUM EzoLorEgs' CLAIM.—In the House of Commons on Monday, Lord Wolmer asked the President of the Board of Trade whether he was aware that the employees of Winwick County Asylum were much dissatisfied at being compulsorily insured under the National In- surance Act, and whether, in view of the fact that these men were practically permanently employed and objected to paying contributions from which they could not expect to derive any benefit, he would-. grant an exemption to' them under Section 107 of the National Insurance Act.—Mr. Robertson: in an 'application, for the exemption under Section 107 (4) made in July, 1912, on behalf of the employees of this asylum by one of their number, it was stated that the services of the. employees could be terminated by notice' given by 'the medical superintendent. It is not the practice to grant exemption under this section unless 'the power of dismissal rests with the governing body and not with any in- dividual officer or officers. Subject, however, to the fulfilment of this condition, the Board of Trade will be prepared to reconsider the anpli- cation in respect of the employees in question, if. as I assume, they come under the provisions of the Asylum Officers' Superannuation Act, 1909.
