div.head: RISLEY.
div.p: RISLEY.

ODDFELLOWS DINE.—The annual dinner of the members of the "City of Refuge" Friendly Society, Loyal Order of Oddfellows, was held at the Noggin Inn on Saturday. Bro. Pimblett, who presicted, referred to the success of their society, and impressed upon the members the necessity of keeping more in touch with each other, with the object of furthering the inter- ests of the lodge a.nd themselves. Several new members were enrolled, and it was resolved to have an annual parade, a fund being started for that purpose.

FEARNHEAD INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHURCH.— Anniversary sermons were preached in the above church on Sunday by Mr. J. Crumblehulme, of Southport,. who gave two eloquent sermons. He spoke from the words, "I went with them to the House of God with the voice of joy and praise" (Psalm xlii.; 4) in the morning, and in the evening from Eph. ii., 4: "But God, Who is rich in mercy for His great love wherewith He loved us." The anthems, "Go, labour on," and "0 0 Daughter of Zion," were expressively ren- dered by the choir. In the afternoon Mr. Crumblehulme gave an inspiring reminiscent address. Solos and recitations were given by members of the school. Mr. Percy Bate pre- sided at the organ.

div.head: GRAPPENH ALL.
div.p: GRAPPENH ALL.

LIBERAL CANDIDATE'S VISIT.—AIL open-air meet- ing was held at the corner of Knutsford-road Post Office on Thursday evening, when addresses were delivered by Mr. Philip M. Oliver, the pros- pective Liberal candidate for the Division, and Councillor J. Middleton, of Oldham. The chair was occupied by Mr. Tomlinson, Mr. Oliver dealt at great length with the Home Rule Bill and the Reformation of the House of Lords. The last, he said; must undoubtedly be one of the main issues at the next General Election.

DEATH OF MRS. W. ECKERSLEY. Mrs. W. Eckersley, widow of Mr. W. Eckersley, and mother-in-law of Mr. Henry Greenall, died at the home of her son-in-law, Hill Cliffe, on Monday. Mrs. Eckersley, who was in her 74th year, was a resident of South- port, but, through paying frequent visits to Mrs. Greenall, her daughter, she became well known in Warrington. The remains of Mrs. Eckersley were laid to rest in the Grappenhall Parish Churchyard on Wednesday afternoon. 'There was a full choral service, Mr. Arthur Down presiding at the organ. The hymns "Peace, perfect peace," and "On the Resurrection morning" were effectively rendered by the choir. The officiating clergy were the Revs. H. V. Pigot, J. Collins and the Hon. and Rev. C. F. Cross. There were a large number of floral tributes. Amongst those sent were wreaths from: "Edith and Henry," "Jack and Duse," ".George and Peggy," " Lil," "Myles and May," "Kitty and, Ireland," "Violet and Teddy," Anne," "Helen," Mr. and Mrs. F. A: Frost, Capt. A. H. and Mrs. Hervey Talbot, Mr. and Mrs. C. Shepherd Cross. Major Greaves .Banning and Rene. " Marion and Godfrey." "The Office," "Grey Friars, North- wieli," Mr. and . Mrs. W. P. Rylands, Mr. Richard Gorton and family, Mrs. and Miss Nor- riss. Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, Elizabeth and J. Taylor.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

HARVEST COMMENCED.—Harvest commenced in the Padgate district yesterday, when a small field of oats was cut. It is expected that next week will witness a general start with the har- vesting operations, oats being now nearly ready for the reaping machine.

RAILWAY GARDENS.—The railway men have some neat little, gardens for a distance from Padgate along the sides of the Great Central line, and this is a feature which is much admired by train travellers, who often express their appreciation of the railroad men turning waste land into such use. Vegetables are chiefly grown, and they are grown well. Beetroot seem of excellent quantity and quality. Such railway side cultivation is a decided credit to the men concerned.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

A STUDENT'S SUCCESS.-111T. J. Hepple Dodds, third son of the late Mr. James Dodds, of Pen- keth, has been awarded the degree of 8.A., with fourth class honours, in the Final School of Modern History, Oxford University.

div.head: AN ELECTION SURPRISE.
div.p: AN ELECTION SURPRISE.

SOLICITOR-GENERAL TO CONTEST A , MANCHESTER SEAT. The Conservatives in North-West Manchester received a_rude surpriseyesterday morningovilen they learned that Sir John. Simon, M.P., the Solicitor-General, was. relinq.uishing a safe seat at Walthamstow, in order to regain the Man- chester seat- for the Progressive cause. Sir John, in accepting the invitation of the Manchester Liberals, wrote to Sir Arthur Haworth, as follows

"The invitation which you conveyed to me from the Selection Committee of the North-West Manchester Liberal Association to become their candidate at the next General Election is one which, flattering as it is, and attractive as a keen Free Trader like myself must feel it to be, has vall'ed for 'very anxious consideration. To leave my, old constituency is no light matter, but after full consultation with the Prime Minister, and with his approval, I write to say that I am prepared to undertake the enterprise to which you call me, and I will do my best.',- With the exception of Mid-Lothian, no seat in the country arouses so much interest in a con- test' as this of Nth-Ur-West Manchester. From 1900 to 1906 it was considered a safe Tory pre- serve, but in the Free Trade election of 1906 Mr. Winston Churchill plucked it from the Tory grasp. When the Arch Apostle of food taxation, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, at Highbury, received the figures of that election over the telephone from a Birmingham newspaper, he was asked by the writer what was his opinion of the Tariff Reform defeat. In the treble voice of the Unionist Statesman there flittered over the wire the answer: "Well, we are not downhearted !" Thus was the well- known political phrase of "Are we down- hearted?' coined.

The division remained Liberal until the by-elec- tion in 1912, when, through misrepresentation about the Insurance Act, it was again captured by the Tories. There is a large Jewish elector- ate, and in that by-election their fears about the working of the Act were played upon to such an extent that they voted Tory almost en masse. Since then the Jews have learned to appreciate the benefits of. insurance, and in the future their votes will be cast for Liberalism, and with their aid Sir John Simon should win the seat.
STRONG LANGUAGE. $

Mr. McKenna, in the House of Commons, in reply to Mr. W. Thorne (Lab., West Ham, S.), said there could be no doubt that the language which Mr. Lansbury had used was a direct and effective incitement to crime, but if he received an assurance from Mr. Lansbury that he would not in future be guilty of such criminal incite- ment he would be glad to consider favourably the remission of his sentence. Mr. Thorne: Was the language used by Mr. Lansbury any stronger than that which has been used by the member for Dublin Unix, er- sity and by the Member for one of the Divisbns of Liverpool? Mr. McKenna: I must have notice at that. (Laughter.) I do not know which language in particular the hon. member refers to.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1 913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1 913.
THE CASTLES OF NORTH WALES.
Some Points of Interest for Holiday Study.

div.head: THEIR ORIGIN, HISTORY AND MEANING.
div.p: THEIR ORIGIN, HISTORY AND MEANING.
North Wales is happy in the possession of artificial adornments such as few countries can show; of castles beautiful for situation, and now the mom beautiful because of the softening touch of time.

It is one of the little ironies of history that these attractive piles of masonry were the gift of an enemy, and built not for her safety and strength, but for her threatening and subjection. It was King Edward the First who took Wales in hand, and who reared the fine chain of castles from Flint to Aberystwyth. They stand to this day, shapely and beautiful, at Flint, Bhuddlan, Conway, Beaumaris, Carnarvon, Criccieth, Harlech, and Aberystwyth.

HOW THE CASTLES CAME INTO BEING. Edward had been proclaimed King on the death of Henry in 1272, and among those who were called to render homage to him was Llewelyn. But Llewelyn did not appear, and Edward decided that Wales should be placed in subjection. His camp was pitched at Basing- werk in July, 1277, and Llewelyn was obliged to yield. The country, as far as Conway, was taken over, and the King began to superintend the building of castles at Flint and Bhuddlan. Edmund, the King's brother, marched an army to LlanbEidam, and began to build the Castle of Aberystwyth. Thus from each end began the chain of fortresses, and four years ,)f peace gave Edward an opportunity to malie' good progress. But in 281 Llewelyn pounced upon the castles. His brother, 'David, surprised the castle at Hawarden, and destroyed the garrison', after- wards joining Llewelyn in the siege of Flint 4nd Bhuddlan. Edward came to the rescue in 1282; Llewelyn was destroyed in battle,, and David was taken and slain as a traitor..

By the "Statute of Bhuddlan," the King for- mally annexed Wales to England in 1283, and proceeded to make the annexation as real as possible by building more castles. Carnarvon Castle rose huge and massive, and with it the smaller fortress of Criccieth. Conway, too, appears to have taken shape in 1283, and so also did Harlech. The castle at Aberystwyth was destroyed in 1282, but was rebuilt in 1284. Bight busy, therefore, must the Royal builder have been, and at a right heavy cost of anxiety did he take over the fierce Welsh tribes.

We say the Welsh tribes, because it is a mis- take to suppose that Edward was opposing a united nation and trying to annex it as a whole. It is the fashion of historians to talk thus, but such a view is erroneous. The people of Wales were never united in their days of independence, and, except for a short time and at irregular intervals, never owned any single leader. The struggle against Edward did bring some pro- mise of unity, and they were slowly evolving order- out of disunion, when the death of the last Llewelyn proved the croWning national disaster.

work, tapestry to cover the walls, and fires blazing in these huge fireplaces, Conway Castle might yet be the snuggest of retreats where one might, in slippered ease, laugh at the wildest hurricane that ever swept Snowdonia. And would not there be something of beauty, too? Here at the east end is the chapel, its large traceried windows still discernible, and adjoining it, to the west, the Great Hall, with its three huge fireplaces. Or -let the visitor push his way into the State apartments used by Edward and Queen Eleanor. Here is the Queen's oratory, or place of prayer, and a sanctuary, a small apse in the thickness of the wall, which, with its three tiny winclows, is a very gem of art. Here, not only Edward and his Queen, but, at a later day, Richard 11. and Earl Percy attended Mass, before setting out upon their fatal journey.

And the visitor should not fail to walk out from the Royal apartments to the platform that gives a view of the fiver. To re-people these walls and terraces with the figures that moved here six centuries ago, and to place them men- tally in relation to the enemies that surged without, is to see vividly a phase of the making of Britain, ,

div.head: WHAT MIGHT HAVE BEEN.
div.p: WHAT MIGHT HAVE BEEN.

Had Llewelyn been spared, it might easily have been that Wales would have got a Par- liament and lived alongside England in much the same way that Scotland and Ireland have done.. But when Llewelyn fell, pierced by the roadside by a casual soldier, <vho did not know his identity, and his head, in ghastly mockery, adorned the Tower of London, Wales e2;.peri- enced her undoing. There was no one to Con- tinue his policy. His death left but one great leader in Britain, and that was Edward Plan- tagenet,---the most astute soldier that ever wore the English crown. Stunned at the loss,. the Welsh people rested from the struggle in sullen anger, and nursed their hatred as best they could, under the shadow of Edward's frowning castle walls.

Having made complete such victory as can be won by the sword, Edwtrd attempted next the conquest that can only be made by affection and friendliness. He took up residence in their midst, and there was born to him, in Carnarvon Castle, the little prince, who, by a happy stroke, he agreed to call the Prince of Wales.

We offer this brief historical introduction because it will most readily explain the exist- ence and position of the Welsh Castles. As to King Edward's policy, we had better offer no opinion. It may have been a bad thing, or it may have been good that the Welsh were conquered. We only wish to make these piles of masonry -as interesting as possible, and to enable the visitor to appreciate the labour and determination which set them up in the midst of a hostile people.

div.head: CONWAY.
div.p: CONWAY.

If. only Conway remained, it would be suffi- cient to assure the fame of King Edward as a military architect. Happily the town has re- mained small, and has not outgrown the grim walls that were built to hem it in. One would have to travel far to find a better example of a walled medieval town, and the visitor who approaches it from the country will have no diffi- culty in picturing Edward's soldiers upon the ramparts of the fine old entrance gate. Standing upon a pinnacle of the castle we can grasp the scheme as a whole. The town forms a triangle, guarded on one side by, the river, and upon another by the Gyffin stream. On all sides high walls rise precipitous from the grOund, strengthened by numerous towers, and with garde-robes projecting On stone corbels, the north wall running into the river- to shut off the quay from any land Attack. The castle is a town within the town, and from the same point of vantage its chief features may be studied. Its main entrance is from the west, and a steep incline leads from the town. A deep ditch was spanned by a 'drawbridge. The tower from which the bridge was worked, com- monly called the barbican, had a portcullis, or falling door, of iron. We have but to imagine ourselves as the attacking force, and armed with nothing better than an axe, or bow and arrows, to realise .how great the task of entering such a fortress. Assuming even a successful raid through the gate and into the interior, greater difficulties wait within; for these lofty towers are excellent perches for the archer, and molten lead can fall from them with deadly effect upon unsheltered warriors in the space below.
The invention of gunpowder put a new com- plexion upon warfare, but we, only need to place these castles back into the age to which they belong to see what consumate pieces of ingenuity they were.

div.head: CASTLE AS A HOME.
div.p: THE CASTLE AS A HOME.
We have not the same opportunity of judging a castle as a place to live in. They are un- inviting enough to-day, lacking, as they do, their 'wooden floors and roofs, but, given-the wood-

div.head: BEAUMARIS.
div.p: BEAUMARIS.

At Beaumaris Castle we may study the ingenu- ities of defence to even greater advantage. Here the builders had no natural aids. The site is flat and everything had to be done in stone anti lime. The result is that we get a typical castle with every artificial aid. • The first line of defence was a huge ditch, but this has long been filled. Then the outer wall, with circular projecting towers that command every part of it. The ditch was crossed by a drawbridge, which gave access to huge gate- houses, each defended with three portcullises. To the ordinary mind this would geem quite enough. But these soldier-architects thought differently. Molten lead from the battlements, with a mixture of arrows and stones, would be sufficient discouragement for a small attacking force, but their fear was of the sudden rush of a large number. This, at any rate, we take to be the meaning of the structures placed near the gates. Let the visitor study the southern entrance. Here, opposite the gateway, is a building and passage "constructed at an inclined angle from the curtain wall and directed away from the main inner entrance. A successful inVading force would be compelled to travel in an oblique line between walls thus giving the defenders additional time to destroy them from above.

It should be noted also that a wall originally ran from the castle to the ,shore, to protect those who were landing stores. Here also is a tasteful little chapel, or oratory, as at Con- way, and the visitor may spend a delightful afternoon in studying the Great Hall and State apartments, re-peopling theca as far as may be with the sturdy men and women of the 13th centui7.•

div.head: HARLECH AND FLINT.
div.p: HARLECH AND FLINT.

Harlech, like Conway, bas the advantage of a fine position, and holds up its head \vitli pride even in the hour of dilapidation and decay. Criccjeth, too, has the advantage of an elevated site. Flint is a simple, square, with towers at the angles, the only remarkable feature being that the one at the south angle stands apart from the walls, being formerly joined to them by a drawbridge. This disjoined tower contained the chapel, and was called the donjon.

div.head: CABNARVON.
div.p: CABNARVON.

In point of size, elaborateness and workman- ship, the premier place among Welsh castles is held by the great pile at Carnarvon. We are obliged to say, however, that we have found it very uninspiring. It is so much less picturesque than Conway, and so entirely fails to rear its massive head. Even little Harlech frowns upon us more effec- tively.
Yet it is a monument of patience and power, and we must endeavour to take in its strong points. Edward chose a good site in selecting a peninsular surrounded almost entirely by water.

To the north and west lay the Menai Straits, and to the south and east the Rivers Cadnant and Seiont, advantages quite as valuable as steep and ugly cliffs. Upon a craggy hill these towers would have' been magnificent, but Ed- ward was not building with casual tourists in his mind. As at Conway, the entire town was walled in. here, too, in the massive gateways we can trace the portcullises and study the flanking towers. The King's Gate hall a statue of Edward H., and the Queen's Gate, only a little less imposing, is at the east end of the fortress. Seven towers rise above the walls, the most important being the Eagle Tower. Here, according to tradition; the first Prince of Wales was born, and a tiny chamber, twelve feet by eight, is shown as the one which witnessed this event.

Some official recognition of the tradition has beqn given by the placing of a stained-glass window containing the Prince of Wales's feathers. It is a pity that this should have been done, for this part of the Tower was not in existence when Edward 11. began his career. But he was certainly born within the castle walis, and it is a delightful story Which reveals the great Edward holding up the infant to the admiration of the Welsh, and promising that he should be the Prince of Wales. We see the best of the castle from without. Seen from within, it is spacious, but disappoint- ing. The Great Hall has gone, and there is little to show what the castle was like in its populous and Palmy days. Numerous " restor- ations " have, moreover, still further reduced the interest.
KING RICHARD H. AND THE WELSH CASTLES.

Second only in interest to the story of Ed- ward is the association of the Welsh castles with the unhappy Richard 11. Here he landed from Ireland, and here hope faded into sorrow and despair. With Richard absent, Henry of Lan- caster planned the seizure of the English throne, and it so fell that the grey castles of Edward were to witness the humiliation of the King.

Carnarvon, Conway, lihuddlan, and Flint. all played a part in the tragedy. Richard arrived at Conway from Ireland in September, 1309, to discover only 100 men to give him support. Willi the Earl of Salisbury he travelled to Beaumaris and Carnarvon. , to find the castles empty. It is said that Carnarvon had so little to offer that Bichard slept on straw within the castle walls.
Flint Castle had been granted by the King to Continued in next column

THE CASTLES OF NORTH WALES—Continued. traitors, came to Conway to invite the King thither. Only four horsemen accompanied the Earl, but he had concealed a thousand archers upon the way. In the chapel of Conway Castle the two men knelt before they began the journey. The King extracted from the Earl an oath of fidelity, and ne swore upon the sacred emblems upon the altar.

div.head: BRAVED THE QUICKSANDS.
div.p: BRAVED THE QUICKSANDS.
A Warrington Man who Crossed the Ribble Danger Spot. AN ARDUOUS FEAT.

The song sings about the quicksands of Dee, but the estuary of the Ribble, off Southport, has quite as dangerous a track of sinking sands. It is at any time foolhardy to walk upon the shivering sand, but at certain times it ends in a fatality. . In these days NN7I e n ppople will attempt anything to establish a record, and to do something which has never been done before, it is not surprising that the quicksands have been tackled.

A Southport man and Mr. Charles Herriman, of Widnes, succeeded in crossing the estuary of the Dibble from Southport to Lytham, at low, tide last wee K-end. Their feat was sup- posed to be unprecedented, and, on that sup- position, accounts of the daring performance appeared in most of the daily papers. Unfor- tunately, for the record-making of .the two ad- venturesome pedestrians, the feat. was per- formed two years ago, and that by a Warring- ton man, while sojourning on holiday at South- port. • The event was not at the. time boomed as a record in daily newspaper print, as the .record-breaker. from Warrington was too modest to proclaim his feat.

Mr. William Colter, who resides in Battersby- lane, Warrington, is -evidently the person to whom the credit for establishing the quicksand record is due, and he accomplished a still more remarkable feat than that. just announced, in that he returned by the same route as he went to Lytham by.
Journeyed Alone.

"I performed the feat now announced as having been accomplished," said Mr. Colter, "two years ago. I did the journey alone, and did not make use of sticks for testing the firm, ness of the foothold. Upon reaching Lytham, to which I had crossed from Southport, over the nibble estuary, I turned and took prac- tically the same rente back. I thus traversed ,the estuary of the Fiibble twice in one day. "I remember that.it on Friday, 7th July, 1911, and a very warm day it was I performed the hazardous feat. I left Southport about nine o'clock in the morning, and I arrived at Lytham about 12.40 p.m., thus taking, close upon four hours on the outward journey. "I left Lytham soon after, and I reached Southport at 430 p.m. I got home hungry, parched with thirst, and with my body and legs scorched through the effects of the salt water and the sun rays.

"I did not realise the danger I was courting until I was submerged over the ,knees in sand on several occasions, but I had been previously warned by an old fisherman that if I attempted to cross the estuary of tile Ribble I mint never return.
" I think there may be other holiday makers who may have completed a similar perilous journey."

div.head: DEATHS OF INFANTS.
div.p: DEATHS OF INFANTS.
DOCTOR DISCUSSES CAUSES

At the great medical conference in London, Profepsor Henry Koplik, M.D. (New York), read a paper on infant mortality in the first four weeks of life, in the course of which he said there were many conditions of both father and mother which resulted in the production of an• infant unfitted to resist the physical in- fluence of post-natal existence, with the conse- quence that many of such died. Perhaps in many instances it was fortunate this was so. Amongst the working and abso- lutely poor classes, lack of proper food, rest, and habits contributed to this premature death. The definite ills of such infants included lack of living weight, still births, acquired in- fection and constitutional disease.

As to the further life of the premature, much depended upon the mode of feeding and escape from extraneous infection. In the breast-fed infant the mortality was as low as that of the artificially •fed. The social position of the par- ents had much to do with infant mortality, amongst the well-to-do, or comfortable classes, the percentage in some cases being reduced 5 per cent. Illegitimacy was another factor in infant mortality. The illegitimate child as a rule suffered disadvantage's such as poverty, in- difference of the parents, &c.

div.head: TREACHERY AND TRAGEDY.
div.p: TREACHERY AND TRAGEDY.

:• Reminding him of the oath, the King 'crossed the river and began the journey, the Earl going kiittle way before him. When near to Aber- gele, the King saw armed bands, carrying the Earl's standards.. The trdth flaked upon him. "God of Paradise assist me," he cried, " I am betrayed." The Earl appeared with a few others and seized the King's bridle. "I have promised to conduct you to the Duke of Lancaster," was his .explanation. Richard saw that resistance was useless, and, with an imprecation, surrendered. After a call at Rhuddlan for refreshments, they came to Flint, where the King gave vent to the bitterness that filled his heart. The Duke of Lancaster marched from Holt Castle, and Richard, after a sleepless night, stood upon the castle walls of Flint to. await his approach. Eighty thousand men surrounded the castle, and the King beheld himself a cap- tive in the Midst of his own subjects. A dire fear and foreboding of his fate filled his heart,. and, standing upon the castle wall, he cried: " Good Lord(God I,commend myself into Thy' holy keeping. If they put me to death I will take it patiently, as Thou didst for us _all." He heard Mass in the chapel and dined in the donjon. Then came the meeting with his enemy in the Court.. "My lord," said Lancas- ter, "your people complain that for the space of twenty or twenty-two years you have ruled them rigorously; but, if it please God, I will help you to rule them better." Horses were ordered, and they started for Chester. Here writs were issued, in the name of the new king, Henry, for the summoning of Parliament, and the sad procession moved to London. Richard, was formally ,deposed, and died in prison, probably by starvation. Flint, Castle, standing broken and forlorn by the water side, has retained nothing to remind us of the stirring day when the throne and destinies of England changed hands within its walls. But none who know the story will with- hold a pitiful thought for the monarch who spent there that night of anguish. One day an arbitrary ruler, the next morning bowing his neck to his enemy and going forth a broken-hearted prisoner to face a jeering throng and, shameful lingering death. Such was the tragedy of Richard 11., and such the tragedy witnessed upon an autumn day in 1399 by the cold walls of the Castle of Flint. A. M.

div.head: LITERARY GLEANINGS.
div.p: LITERARY GLEANINGS.
PROFESSOR DONVDEN'S LIBRARY.
FORTHCOMING SALE IN LONDON.

The library of the late Professor Dowden, who has been a book collector for half a cen- tury and obtathed many scarce books in his special branches of English literature, is now being transferred from Dublin to Messrs. liodgson's rooms in Chancery-lane, where it will be sold, probably in two portions, during October and November. It is first and fore- most a working library •of books such as a student of literature would collect; but in other respects it shows a wide catholicity of taste.
THE LAKE POETS AND OTHERS'.
The library, is especially rich in works by NVordsworth, .Coleridge, and Shelley. In 1890 Professor Dowden edited a reprint of the first

edition of the," Lyrical Ballads" of 1798, a book which, he said, may be "considered one of the most remarkable in the whole range of English poetry." His library contains the " apparatus " for this reprint in the form of the 1798, 1800, and other: editions. There are numerous first and other early editions of Wordsworth, such, for instance, as, the very rare "Grace Darling" (with the author's signature), which consists of two leaves, printed at Carlisle, but not pub- lished; the "Evening Walk," "Descriptive Sketches," "Lines on Lamb," and so forth. There is an evecially interesting copy of the folio edition of Cowley's "Poems," which was lot 508 in the sale of Wordsworth's library at Bydal Mount in 1859, with autograph notes by both Coleridge and Wordsworth; on - the - last end paper is a pencilled' head (such as a child might draw) inscribed "Drawn by S. T. Coler- idge entirely, out of his own fancy on October 10, 1801, he being then only 29 years of age, yea, not 2 by ten days." ' In another part of the book is a long note in pencil, also by Coleridge, whilst Wordsworth has written his own name on the title-page. There are first editions of "The Ode" and "The Hebrew Ode," by Coler- idge, and of books by Charles Lamb (notably "John Woodvil," "English Dramatists," with ;N §. notes .by Barry Cornwall, and "Tales from hakespeare," with Blake's illustrations) ; three 'volumes of manuscripts by . Crabbe ; De Quin- cey's proof sheets of "The English Mail Coach," with notes -by the author; and Landor's "Literary Hours," with MS. notes by the author. There are several books—presentation copies of Scott's "lay of the Last Minstrel," and'Hogg's "The Forest Minstrel "—bound in Southey's " Cottonian " style—a style, it should be ex- plained, by which books issued in ,plain boards were covered with pieces of cloth cut out from ladies' cast-off print dresses of the day. Edi- tions of Shelley (notably "The Republican," with Shelley's "Declaration of .Rights ") and Byron figure in large numbers, as well as of Edward Fitz Gerald (the*" Omar" is of the second edition), Swinburne, William Morris, R. L. Stevenson, Matthew Arnold, Walter Pater. Charles Kingsley, and Robert Browning.
EAIILY ENGLISH BARMES.

Professor Dowden's library , contains many interesting books in early English literature. First and foremost, perhaps, is the " Poliman- tele of I.s9s,•Which contains the Second earliest printed testimony to the. fame of Shakespeare; this. particular copy is unique in • giving the author's. name at the end of the dedication, and it was from this copy, we believe, that Professor Bowden made the discovery that the book was by William Covell, of Christ's College and Queen's College, Cambridge, and not by William Clarke, to whom it had hitherto been ascribed. Both the Huth and the floe libraries contained copies, each presumably without the leaf re vealing the name of the author. Even rarer than this is the copy of Baldwin's "Beware the Cat," 1584, of which the Huth copy (No. 417)— wanting the title-page—is erroneously described as the only one known. The example of Henry Willobie's curious book, " Willobie his Avisa," is not only a very rare volume, but is interesting in having the autograph of " Kenelme Wil- loughby" on the title-page.

div.head: NIABEL BUSSELL'S JEWEL-CASE.
div.p: NIABEL BUSSELL'S JEWEL-CASE.

Mabel Hussell, who has just made such a big hit ill" Within the La', - at tue Haymarket, London, tells a good story in an article which she contributes to the August "Pearson's Magazine." . " when I knew that I was to be a real live actress and go on tour," she writes, "I. deter- mined to do we thing in style: Advice poured in from friends as to my outfit, and I started that tour with several wicker baskets, a trunk. a dressing-case, and a bag of golf clubs. "The crowning glory was the fact that I had my initials, emblazoned on every par- ticle of the luggage. • On Sunday I always drove to the station in a cab. I couldn't afford it, but I thought it was the thing to do. Once at a Midland station collected a porter, and directed him with much magnificence to 'bring along everything he could .see marked " MAL," adding 'ill's all Mine! '. •

"He Strolled away, and after a Minute Caine 'back, grinning. I say, miss,' he remarked-4'l say, miss, does this 'ere belong to you?' "1 turned, and saw him pointing to a longline of trucks containing—possibly-7-coal, cattle, and fireworks, and marked in large letters M.l-1. •
The porter certainly had the-laugh over me then, but I retorted glandiloquently : Yes, it's mine! And be very careful of the one with the tarpaulin cover—it's my jewel- case I '"
BEDOUIN TRACKERS AND THEIR WORK.

To observe and i.emember marks accurately, and to draw from them the proper inferences, is an important part of a Bedouin's education. He begins it as a baby when he goes with his mother to mind the Hock, and before he can count his fingers he knows the individual track of every animal in that Hock, to say nothing of others.

As soon as he can walk he is sent to bring in the laggards and the strayed • and as animals .the desert. are constantly disappearing he Puts his knowledge to_ a practical test from the very lirst. When he grows older he is sent farther afield, to carry iood, perhaps, or a mes- sage, to an uncle or brother, who is feeding his flock.in a distant wady. •, or it may be in search of a strayed camel, which he may have to follow for days before he even gels a glimpse of it. When he acquires a gun the tratlks of a gazelle or ibex interest him, and he learns to follow them even over granite. Above all, he learns to notice the tracks of men. From earliest childhood he is taught to recognise the foot- prints of his family, and as time goes on and experience grows his store of knowledge in- creases. It becomes second nature to him not to pass unnoticed the track of., a' man or woman; and so, when he comes upon one which he has seen before, he knows whether it belongs to a friend, or an enemy, a relative or acquaintance. In short, a knowledge of tracks is not the secret of an initiated few, but rather the 'general lore of the desert and the common heritage of all who dwell there. Without it they could neither keep their property safe nor recover it if strayed or stolen; their friendship would be without value, their enmity contemp- tible, for they tvould be able neither to Ward nor strike. To possess it is the essential con- dition of their mode of existence.

The science of °tracking, however, involves far more than the Mere recognising of known footprints. The expert will tell yciii from the examination of a track the time Of day when the impression was made. The tracks of men and camels walking in the dark are different from Those made during the day; they are less straight, lead over hard ,ground, and stumble over 'stones and bushes.—From "Sherlock Holmes in Egypt," in the -August "Strand Magazine."

div.head: UGLY WOMEN.
div.p: UGLY WOMEN.
Buitonwood Rector Says Pretty Females do not Exist.
"DOLL AND BABY FACES."

The women of Lancashire, who pride them- selves as being peaches amongst all the lasses in the country, will not •feel grateful to the Rev. A. AL Mitchell, vicar of Burtonwood Parish, near Warrington, for the sdathing remarks he has penned in his Parish Magazine upon the topic of female beauty. _
- "A day's round, in town or country," he writes, "will convince the most optimistic that beauty, womanly beauty, has gone on strike and 'downed tools.' _ _

"The very ordinary looking woman—the black- leg—has been pitchforked into her place. We do not wish to minimise the number of our beautiful women, nor to depreciate the much-boomed love- liness of our imported beauties—still, the fact stands out bold and clear in outline--beauty is not a British asset in the twentieth century. 'Tis fortunate, maybe, for our girls that : every eye• forms its own beauty'; if it were not so, the greater number of our Ells might go husband- less all their days. 'The love-blind he' endows 'the wonderful she' with a beauty and charm which he alone has been able to discover. What ho! Have we not no end of pretty girls and even prettier women? "Granted there be many pretty girls and women in varying degrees of prettiness, not doll faced, not baby faced, not expressionless—yet prettiness is not beauty—not beauty as we read of it in the history of the Ancients—not perfec- tion of feature and contour, not loveliness of expression, not grace and elegance of form. Prettiness is largely a matter of tiring the head and poising the hat. "A beautiful woman, we would think should be the natural product of the centuries 2f Chris- tianity and civilisation. Present-day Christian- ity has not given us beauty, our highly-wrought civilisation has given us the plain, irregular featured, the commercial-faced female. Nature is the Mother of beautiful daughters, she cannot bring forth the plain, the ugly: this is the work of civilisation—that withered hag, that fury, the destroyer of the beautiful and the lovely—as one, or all of the Eumenides.

div.head: WOMEN'S SAD FALL.
div.p: WOMEN'S SAD FALL.

"The woman is not to be blamed : she cannot help her sad fall from beauty; she is the heiress of preceding, decadent generations; 'tis her mis- fortune now to inherit the plain feature, the hard expression, the rough skin, the furrowed brow, the toothless gums, the thin, coarse, faded hair, the ungraceful motion, the mannish stride. Woman is entitled to a better, a nobler heritage than this.

"Conditions of life must be entirely altered to restore to her the beauty of which greed, in the name of civilisation, has robbed her. How is beauty possible to the great number, the many, many thousands employed in mills and factories and on the pit brow, condemned to a life of incessant drudgery? 'How can the chil- dren of the pale, emaciated, over-worked, un- developed mothers make any pretension to beauty, of face or form? If beauty is to be restored to the womanhood of this land, oppor- tunity must be afforded for its evolution, and the man must see that 'the woman whom Thou gayest me' is freed entirely from employments which hinder and destroy physical development on the one hand, and intellectual or soul pro- gression on the other. What have the unhappy victims of unhealthy and sweated industries, the slaves of the brickfields, dwellers in sunless streets, to do with beauty?

"It is a very plain and obvious duty not to baulk the woman, but to aid her to the utmost in her search for the piece which she has lost. The man has shamefully misused her. Yet the woman, higher in the social scale especially, is responsible for this—accentuating the absence of the beautiful in face and form by the foolish, unwomanly, if not immodest and extravagant 'stage dressing' now the fashion. The attire of the fashionably-dressed woman as she appears in the streets of London to-day, in 'the latest, loveliest thilig from Paris, you know,' certainly does attract attention, but not that attention which springs from admiration—admiration for the beautiful.

div.head: "DRESSED UP UGLINESS."
div.p: "DRESSED UP UGLINESS."

"Never more than now have women needed to temember—' beauty unadorned is adorned the most.' Marvellous costumes ala mode cannot effectually hide plain looks, nor conceal the borderland of ugliness, though they may only too successfully hide out of sight those preten- sions to prettiness which in these all-discerning days does duty for beauty—so conspicuous by its absence. Dressed-up ugliness is one of the most repulsive sights beneath God's sun: we see it every day, every hour, in the street, in the restaurant, on the grand-stand, at Royal Ascot, at Goodwood, at Society shows, in the Law Courts, in the swank, death-dealing car of Juggernaut. " Ugliness in goggles,' here is the lowest depth of ugliness, here is the grand reversion of the natural, womanly desire to have and to hold God's blessed gift of beauty. Such desire is not to be dismissed as 'vanity.' The women who tire their heads in ways past finding out, who touch up their faces,' who cultivate a pink and white complexion with the aid of a cheap enamel are, in reality, seeking to express, out- wardly and visibly, the innate desire for womanly beauty whilst doing so in the very worst, the most injurious of ways. That which is bad thereby is made worse. "Woman's search for beauty, if she sets her- self in the right way, will not be wholly in vain, seeking she shall find, find in the degree possible to her as she is—all is not lost, something ere the end may be regained if Nature's kindly, gentle lead is followed, if Nature's healing, beautifying remedies are sought for and applied. To such, entrance to the royal circle of beauty may be denied -here; to join the Helens, the Daphnes, the Elaines, the Vashtis, and the Esthers may not be possible to them—yet, setting themselves in Nature's royal road of health and beauty, they cannot fail to be uplifted above the ranks of the plain to which they find themselves condemned as the daughters of the unnatural and artificial —a brutal civilisation."

div.head: "JAUNDICED SPECTACLES." Reply to the Vicar.
div.p: "JAUNDICED SPECTACLES." Reply to the Vicar.

"Very jaundiced spectacles the Vicar of Burtonwood must have worn," said one experi- enced in the physical training of women to an " Examiner " representative, "when he went out to observe womanly beauty before he wrote his article. Perhaps he was beauty-blind, and could not see. But, because the worthy Vicar fails to observe and appreciate female beauty, we must not accept him as an absolute authority that it does not exist.

"The women, as a whole, to-day are vastly superior to what they were in the Victorian days. Physically, they are better developed, and their facial beauty is more impressive. They are, however, more self-reliant, which is in itself a phase of beauty, than the simpering, languish- ing don't feel well at all' women of the Vic- torian period. "Forty years ago it was considered most im- modest for a young woman to play hockey,- golf, or indulge in .any outdoor exercise, except a short walk. The ideal of half-a-century ago was that women should strum the harp, or do sewing work indoors, and a weak type they were. Per- haps that is the type the Vicar prefers, the class always ready to welcome him to an afternoon cup of tea, spiced with plenty of idle kossip. If such be his ideal woman, she has vanished, and a good thing, too.

div.head: INTELLECTUAL BEAUTY.
div.p: INTELLECTUAL BEAUTY.

"While there are many mill and factory girls who are plain, there are hundreds of others who are qu,ite beautiful. But the plain woman that he writes about is often intellectually superior to.the woman with a pretty face, or a fine figure. Evidently intellectual beauty does not appeal to the Vicar; he wants all the woman's charms to be displayed in face and figure, a very retrograde idea of what beauty should be. "The so-called beauty of the Helens, the Daphnes, and the Esthers is more or less a myth. Painters and sculptors in the old days used to convert their models into what their imagina- tion pictured them to be. Measurement for measurement, there are quite as fine women to- day as any ancient Helen or Daphne, and the Vicar need only come into Warrington to dis- cover—if he leaves off his jaundiced spectacles— as fine types of womanly beauty Eis ever existed in olden times.
"The teaching of drill, hygiene. and the general care given to the health of the pupils in (Continue 4 in next column.)

div.head: I- CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB. : _N,--,)."‘",,,N,,-,\.-N"...,•.,--,\,-NrevAA
div.p: I- CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB. : _N,--,)."‘",,,N,,-,\.-N"...,•.,--,\,-NrevAA
THE USEFUL TOAD.

Few creatures are more hated than the toad, and I have seen young people act very cruelly towards it. Why they should do so, Ido not know, unless it be because the toad is ugly. But even in the matter of appearances it ought not to be despised, because it has the most beautiful eye that any animal or bird can boast. Just look for this feature in a toad, and you will forget everything else about it that does Rot please you.

But do you know that it is also one of the most useful of creatures. I have been reading a little from an American scientific journal, which has interested me very much. In the United States they have plagues of insects, which destroy the crops and fruit. These pests are very serious to the farmers, who are always doing battle with them. The writer whose article I have been reading tells them that their very best friend is the toad, and that in the business of bug-destroying he is unequalled by any living animal. The amount a toad will eat is astonishing. A large specimen has been known to devour a hundred rose-beetles at a single meal. One toad needed seventy-seven myriapods—the com- mon household centipede—to satisfy his appe- tite; another, fifty-five army-worms; and yet another, sixty-five gypsy-moth caterpillars. Still another to -qs seen to eat thirty-five large, full-grown celery-worms in three hours, while another accepted eighty-six flies fed to him in less than ten minutes.

It is a common thing when the occupants of an ants' nest are swarming and the insects are emerging in large numbers to see an enterpris- ing toad sit at the entrance to the burrow and snap up every ant that domes out. The slaughter he accomplishes under such circum- stances is frightful.

The §uggestion made to farmers is that they should keep a small pond and rear their own toads, taking care to protect them from their greatest enemy, who.is— Perhaps you can guess. It is the small boy!

div.head: MIND CURE.
div.p: THE MIND CURE.

There was a boy I know of Whose clothes were made too small, His jacket always pinched him, And it did not fit at all. The sleeves were short and narrow, And the collar was too tight; And the buttons didn't suit him, And the pocket wasn't right. And so this foolish fellow,
Because his clothes were small, Was very cross aad sulky, And he would not grow at all
• For he said, "My jaaet pinches, As everybody knows, And a boy, in my opinion, Can't be bigger than his clothes." There was a little fellow
Who was sick and pale and thin; He had a tiny body, But a mighty will within. His head was always aching, And his back was always weak; And he had a voice so feeble

You could hardly hear him speak. " What ! "said this little hero, "1 will not have it so ; Because my body pinches, Shall my spirit never grow? I will not mind the backache, And I will not mind my head, If I can't be big in body, I'll be big in soul instead."

And so, with cheerful courage, • He chased hi i pains away, And all the people saw him Growing braver day by day, Till for his tiny body They did not care a fig, But everybody loved him Because his soul was big. —HARRIOTT W. SHERRATT.

div.head: ARE WE MORE SOBER?
div.p: ARE WE MORE SOBER?
NO BUSINESS TIPPLING.

Sir Thomits Barlow, the famous physician, president of the International Congress of Medicine now sitting in London, spoke on the progress of the temperance question in this country during the last generation. The pro- gress had been very remarkable indeed, in almost every rank of society, and most pleasing it was to chronicle the greater movement in our army and navy. One of the chief features of that had been the growth of an altruistic con- science amongst the officers of these services. Honour, too, ought to be given to those socie- ties like the Y.M.C.A. and the soldiers' and sailors' refuges, which had looked after the con- venience of soldiers and sailors when off duty. In the commercial class the change had been enormous, and it had been recognised that a. man in this strenuous time was not fit for com- mercial life unless he had done with all that old period of tippling, and even men who were not teetotalers themselves recognised the enor- mous value of having abstainers in their ser- vice. He might also accentuate, in this stren- uous time of the motor and the enormous acceleration of railway and steamship traffic, that it was becoming recognised by the community, and the contention that alcohol took away the sense of control had be- come accepted by the logic of fact. (Applause.)

div.head: BOOMING TRADE.
div.p: THE BOOMING TRADE.
EXPORTS STILL INCREASING.

The trade of England is going—not in the Protectionist sense—on booming. A Board of Trade return for July, issued recently, shows that the exports for the month reached a value of £47,164,208, an increase of £5,177,848 com- pared With the corresponding month last year. The imports show an increase of A;3,487,253, the total value for the month being 4;61,786,752. For the seven months ending July 31 the value of the exports totalled £304,220,016, the increase over the corresponding period last year being £36,920,611. The total value of the imports for the seven months reached the sum of 'X440,505,569, an increase of £28,353,161 over the first seven months in 1912. _ _

Raw cotton imports for July are valued at - £2,276,894, an increase of £285,915, compared with the same month of 1912, while for the seven months just completed the total is £34,811,618, a decrease of £6,397,287 compared with the same period of last year. Exports of manufactured cotton are returned at £11,615,365 for the past month, an increase of £615,064 over the figures for July, 1912; while for the first seven months of this year the total is X 75,076,894, an increase of A:5,645,166 over the figures for the same period of 1912. Only two items in the manufactures class of exports show declines for July—silk and other textile materials. The total under this head- ing is £36,971,344, an increase of £4,211,775 on the figures for July, 1912, while the total under this heading for the seven months just com- pleted is £241,868,186, an increase of £28.229,573 compared with the corresponding period of last year.

GALLANT WIDNES MAN

A daring attempt to rescue 'a boy, drowning in a deep well, was recognised at Widnes on Monday, when Major Wareing, on behalf of the Royal Humane Society, presented a certificate on vellum to the gallant, but unsuccessful rescuer, William - Itiutton, Moorfields-road, Widnes.
not see why they could not wait longer. .Mr. Grundy said it would be a waste of money to try and renovate the present hospital. Mr. Millar moved an amendment that the Matter be referred back.

Alderman Wood remarked that if the Corpora- tion were bent on a new hospital, let them secure a modern one. While they were spending money he hoped the committee would keep an eye upon something that would last. The minutes were carried, Mr. Millar with- drawing his amendment, on condition that plans for a new hospital should be considered and sub- mitted to the Council.

div.head: NEW LIBERAL VAN.
div.p: NEW LIBERAL VAN.

The Young Liberals League of Widnes have secured for their campaign a new van, which is intended to be used for touring the outlying districts of the constituency. It made its first appearance in Victoria-square, when a large and enthusiastic audience listened to speeches by Mr. J. B. Martindale and Mr'. Tom Wing, M.P., of Houghton-le-Spring Division.

div.head: JOCKEY'S WEDDING
div.p: A JOCKEY'S WEDDING

The wedding took place at Trinity Church, Runcorn, on Monday, of Thomas liulme, the steeplechase jockey, who is associated with Mr. Percy Whitaker's stable at Royston, and Miss Ada Sandbach, a local school teacher. The bride, attired in cream silk, was attended by her sister Blanche, and Vera Hulme, the sister of the bridegroom. She carried a bouquet of carnations— The best maw-was I. D. Johnson. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. C. R. Killick, vicar of Trinity.

div.head: NOT A SCOUT'S ACT.
div.p: NOT A SCOUT'S ACT.

At Runcorn Children's Court on Monday, Norman Mayers (14), William Barker (13), and William Goodier (10)/all of Halton Brook, were summoned for destroying potato. plants grow- ing in a field belonging to Mary Astbury. One boy told the magistrates that they were play- ing Boy Scouts', and that they took the potatoes to cook them -while camping out. None of the boys belonged to a Boy Scout troop, and the Bench admonished them, and advised them all to join the Scout movement. They would have to pay costs, 4s. 6d. each.

div.head: CAPTAIN AND THE GOAT.
div.p: THE CAPTAIN AND THE GOAT.

At Runcorn on Monday, Ishmael Williams, captain of the school Gaelic, was charged with bringing a goat from Rio Grande to the port of Runcorn without having the authority of the Board of Agriculture.—Supt. Ennion said that the captain, when asked if he had any 'animals on board, said he had a goat, but he had no licence.—Mr. Hough, for the defence, contended that the captain did not know he required a licence. It was a pet which he had got for his children.—A line of 20s. and 14s. 6d. costs was imposed.

div.head: SCREAMED FOR HELP
div.p: SCREAMED FOR HELP

How James Frodsham, 2, Fox-street, plunged Mrs. Bradbury; Parliament-street, Thatto Heath, in a state of alarm was told at St. Helens Court on Monday. On August Holiday Sunday night Mrs. Bradbury heard someone smash the back window and enter the house. She locked the bedroom door and screamed for help,- and her sister and a crowd came, burst in the door, and, it was said, found Frodsham in the back bedroom. Frodsham was charged with breach of the peace, and Mr. Davies said that lie would plead guilty, and undertake that he would never interfere with the woman again. Frodsham was ordered to find bail in ci:2o, and two sureties of -f'lo.

FAMOUS SKIPPER DEAD. One of the beift-known South African skippers in the person of Captain Rigby, Runcorn, was buried at /the Parish Church there on Saturday. He_ was at one time a familiar figure in the mercantile marbe. The son of a master-, builder at Runcorn, he took to the Seafaring life at an early age, and for over forty Years. was in the serrice of Messrs. Donald Currie and Co. When the South African war broke out be was cantain of the Dunottar Castle; and conveyed in his vessel to •Cape Town Lord Kitchener, Lord Roberts, and the late General Buller and Sir Hector Macdonald. On his re- tirement ,from active service Captain Rigby w'ent to live at Southport. where he died. He was seventy-three years of age.

div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.

Mr. Millar deprecated the scheme as not in keeping with the town's progress. Ten years ago, he said, it Was considered necessary to ex- tend the hospital, and a fund was raised. WOMAN WHO WON ELECTION. DEATII OF MRS. SEELY. A lady who did much for Liberalism, and in 1900 wotr an election on behalf of her husband, :Ars. Seely, wife of Colonel Seely, Minister for War, died suddenly on Saturday night, after giving birth to a daughter, who survives her mother. Mrs. Seely, who was 43 years of age, was a notable figure in political circles, and a delight- ful hostess. In 1900, when Colonel (then Captain) Seely was serving at the front in South Africa, and was at the same time the candidate for the Isle of Wight, Mrs. Seely addressed a simple, womanly letter to the electors in the following terms : My husband is away on active service in South Africa and cannot personally ask for your vote at this election. I know how very much ,he would- appreciate the honour of being elected by his friends and neighbours as member for the Isle of Wight, and you will realise how anxious I am for his success. May I hope that you will make every effort to come and vote for him? The absent husband was returned by a majority of over 1,000. •

div.head: CORPSE COMPLAINED
div.p: THE CORPSE COMPLAINED

Ai the Medical Congress in London, Dr. J. C. Al`Walter strongly advocated that the State should institute a post-mortem examination in every case of death, as it was the only possible means to ascertain what people really died of. There was recently an instance in Dublin, lie said, iii which a. doctor gave a certificate that a man died "as I am informed." On the strength of it the death was duly registered, and the insurance money drawn. At the " wake " the alleged corpse complained that he did not get his proper share of the proceeds. The whole edifice of preventive medicine and the treatment of disease in 40,000,000 of British people was based on deductions from certificates sent on to the Registrar-General, whose returns were made up of many thousands of supposed causes of death, perhaps wrong nine times out of ten.

It would be said that the current of public opinion would be against mutilation of the dead, but public opinion would rapidly come round. The ordinary medical attendant 'might he compelled to state the fact and cause of death, and he, should have power to make a post-mortem examination as 'seemed necessary— due regard being had to people's feelings.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.

"1 only ma it to 'spite you," she stammered. "I never knew it would be like this. Forgive me. Let me go ! " The old man thunderstruck by the extra- ordinary scene, had come oat and was staring at tho two girls. But he understood in a moment. "What has he done ? " roared he, bursting into angry threats against ths visitor. Alice calmed him, begged him to leave it to her, and hurried out into the dusky farmyard. There Robert was pacinig to and fro. "Alice! " he said, having no suspicion of Ma's confession. As he tried to touch her Alice shrank back. "Do you know what I have done ? " whispered he. The girl ejaculated "Yes," but was unable to utter another syllable. In bewilder- ment she saw him vanish in the darkness, and after a time she herself went in. That was the last she saw of him. . • • • • • . .

This was how Alice's first engagement ended, and for some weeks she felt that her life also must go with it. Through all that harvest to which she had looked forward she could do little but stare at the ruins of a world which bad crumbled about her. But this was only in her own soul. None suspected what she suffered. She still applied all her diligence to the affairs of home. Ada simply watched her, dazed. The shock to herself had had some extraordinary effect also. She could scarcely speak to Alice, but like some dumb animal she went about doing all sorts of things that she knew would help and please her sister. The latter saw it, but only took notice by smiling, or now and then touching Ada's neck for an instant. In the meantime old Grinnell was an altered man. The harvest had been an unusually bountiful one, and with the money Alice had supplied it was got in well and quickly, instead of lying out for weeks in the wet to be spoilt as in previous years. This atone, he said, would make a man of him again. It was the sight and the knowledge of this that first brought Alice to herself. She found all sorts of excuses for Robert, and constantly said to herself that however it had ended, if it had not been for that short engagement she would never have saved her old home. SO, as days went on, any feelings of her own were gradually lost in a sense of gratitude to that radiant figure of a lover she had once had. Ada's wonder simpl:t- grew and grew, until on Christmas Eve when they walked along the frosty hill road to listen to the pealing of the church bells she fell on her sister's neck in a flood of tears, and from that moment they found that they could talk about anything to each other. A year of hard work and brighter hopes followed. In the course of it Ada's spirits seemed to rise in a mysterious way, and one Sunday afternoon Alice met her coming home ,with Warner of the Glebe Farm. It all flashei upon Alice in as instant, and that night in the' room Ada told her all about it.

But, joyful as she appeared, this brought a deep sadness over Alice. Old memories were revived, old hopes rekindled in a way that she knew it would be mad to indulge. Even if another lover came to her she knew what her reply would be. That first figure was indeliby impressed on her heart, and to none other could she ever pretend to give allegiance. So often and often in secret Alice had to give way to her tears. As the summer came on she found it harder and harder to. resist. She would wander sometimes to that old green camp above the church where she had met Ada on her first return home two years ago. The rooks still played about it; the trains still made their way across the wide vale in front. Old ambitions could not be repressed. On the anniversary of that day in July when Ada had come to her, Alice went and sat down as she had done then. The harebells, the wild thyme, and the bedstraw were all in blossom again around her, and they all called up the old thoughts. But her father was saved, it was that which brought a proud smile of triumph to Alice's lips, although at the same moment tears started to her eyes. As they did so she leaped up frightened, for a sound of footsteps came to Her on the soft grass behind. The sun was that way, and what with that and the tears on her eyelashes the young woman could not see who it was. But there was a wild throb in her heart, for a mad fancy suddenly seized her. Although ashamed of it she had to wipe her eyes, and then she looked again. "Alice, can you ever forgive me ? " came, in that old voice that' had thrilled her from the first. As she cried out "Robert ! " and ran forward Alice was wrapped in the old silent embrace, and it was some time before they could sit down to talk. But what ,a night they all had at the Hill Varm I

div.head: COMPLER EXAMINEII STORY,
div.p: COMPLER EXAMINEII STORY,
rALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]
HER FIRST ENGAGEMENT.

that Daniel Grinnell had gone some steps furthe: downhill, at a pace made swifter by the spun of a discontented, mutinous son and a frivolous. scifish daughter. All this Ale learnt that first evening, and it gave her. soinething to think about. But she very soon decided to stay to the last minute of her fortnight.' lt continued lovely summer weather, and the visitor found time for walking in the fields. This was chiefly late in the evening as the sun was lowering to the vale and peewits and partridges could be heard very far in. the stillness. It was on coming in after one such evening ramble on her third day that Alice wrote the first letter since her return home. Next day Ada saw her go out at tea-time to catch the postman on his. bicycle at the cross-roads. This was, of course, Alice's first report to her lover. She told him of the unsatisfactory state of affairs, that she found she could be of some use, so should stay all her holiday, but that it would nOt do at all for him to come for a Sunday yet. The farmer continued to watch his daughter with astonishment. He could not longer be satisfied that it was all a device to reach some end of her own. The man was at once aware of a vast change in the house, and he felt the benefit of it. But what mostly revived his flagging energies was the discomfiture of Ada. He had not laughed so for years. The younger's resent- ment of the calm, moral authority exercised by her intrusive sister daily afforded him a sense of joy and wonder. The contest carried on between the two without as yet any open declaration of hostilities brought altogether new life to Grinnell. He frankly confessed that he had been worsted in the same engagement, but his weapons had been different. The old doctor instantly moticed the change in his patient's health, and himself, watched with the greatest interest what the development of affairs at the Hill Farm was to be.

About a week later the doctor paid another professional call. All the doors were open, but nobody was to be seen and no answer came to his loud and repeated knocks. So lie turned away, and in passing through the gate met a stranger entering. This was a young man, just dismounted from the bicycle he was wheeling, and dressed in the regular Norfolk suit, cap, stnd brown shoes. "I can't find anybody," said the doctor, and passed on. The visitor stood in the silence of the farm- yard, listened to the trot of the horse departing, and looked curiously around. Now, Ada was inside the house all the time, but was not going to trouble herself to speak to the old doctor. She did not like him, for one reason because during his late visits before her sister arrived he had ventured to speak plainly on things not strictly within the range of his pro- fession. So, at any rate, Ada had thought, and she took up an attitude accordingly. But this unknown visitor was something wholly different, so, as she had finished dressing, after a last quick look in the glass the girl ran down. The two met at the door with a pleasantly frank stare.
"Is Miss Grinnell at home " "Yes; I am Miss Grinnell." "Miss Alice, I mean. My name is Robert Win- wood."

The stare of puzzled bewilderment which Ada gave him made her look very pretty Robert thought. Of course, no confidence had been ex- changed between the two sisters. Ada did not know that Alice was engaged. But of a sudden it flashed upon her that this must be a lover. From the deepest colour her face turned quite pale. He thought it was shyness, so with a pleasant laugh put her at her ease. Then they arranged that he should wait for Alice's return. She and her father had driven over to see the lawyer, and were to get back to a late tea. So there was more than an hour, perhaps two, to get over. But for a thing of this sort Ada thought herself equal; Not supposing it possible that his companion was ignorant of his engege- ment to her sister, the visitor adopted at once a playful and familiar tone, so as they wandered about the place together their acquaintance rapidly ripened. With a shock Ada heard the gig arrive long before she had expected it. So she abruptly left her companion ,and ran, in to look at the kettle, but she had forgotten the fire, add it was nearly out. She flung on a handful of wood and plied the bellows. That was the only sound to betray what she was feeling, but to anybody familiar with bellows it was enough. When the wood flared and crackled she got up and stared from a corner of the window so as not to be seen. Outside the three were talking and laughing, even the voice of her father sounding in noisy glee. Ada scowled. "Why should Ibe left to get the tea ? " muttered she, while dropping bits of coals on to the fire. But just then Alice came running in, flushed with joy, and not noticing anything said with a tender pressure of the arm. ‘Go out to him Ada; I'll see to the tea. I meant to tell you, but you wouldn't give me a chance." Without a word Ada was gone. - -

The old farmer went in also, BO again Ada had to entertain Robert alone. In addition to getting the tea Alice had his room to get ready, and fifty other things to do. But soon they were all done, and she came. out to fetch the others to the table.

In the midst of the fun this surprise visit had a strange effect on Ada. Angry as she had been with Alice before, she now perceived for her a jealous hatred. She felt sure she could see that if this delightful young man had only seen herself first, it was she that he would have fallen in love with. Ada clung to this idea so firmly that she very quickly felt Alice had done her a great wrong in gaining the love of Robert Winwood. But this discovery also had the effect of giving her more power over herself. She hitt her feelings more deeply and put on a much pl,oasanter face. This often made her look -very bewitching, which she could easily see impressed llobert, and she was delighted. So the bright days went on. It turned out that the visitor had got his holidays too, and in face of such a reception it was not long in being arranged for him to spend them all there. After being there a week, though, everybody was con- scious of some mysterious change. There was not so much laughter and glee as there had been. Alice was troubled and talked to Robert. Site was afraid it was her doing for only the day before she had confessed to him that she had written to give up her work in the town, as it was clear that only by her staying at home could her father be saved. He had said it was like her; had said, of course, they would put off their marriage for a bit; and made light of Alice having given to her father all the money which she once told him she had saved. She asked him again if he really approved of what she had done, and once more he expressed his admiration. But she was not quite satisfied when she left him, and when she had done what she wanted to do in the house she ran out to find him again. It was a beautiful night, the last colours of the sunshine having just faded. Ada was upstairs —at least, Alice had left her there—and all the farmyard was wonderfully quiet. Alice did not like to break the quiet by calling, so she wan- dered about in all likely places, hoping to give her lover a pleasant surprise. But at the end of the rickyara, by the last stack of new hay, she suddenly stopped. She beard voices, and listened. "Why, of course, Ada, you are far more beautiful. It's an awful mistake, but I shall have to confess it. It's you I love." Alice turned away and went back to the house. She looked upstairs, but could not see Ada. She called for her, but got no answer. So the young woman went in to her father in an utterly stupe- fied conditiOn. She simply didn't understand what she was feeling. When she heard her sister leave Robert Ada had run out. Her heart was beating violently. In her anger and hatred of Alice's proper behaviour, all bad seemed so easy, but as her own victory got plainer Ada shrank back. Not until to-night, though, as she ran out, did she know that it was wicked, unspeakably wicked; but she. said "There ! " and ran with double speed. Robert was waiting, and caught her in his arms. Ile had resolved upon his confession, and he made it at once passionately. But as he looked into the dim, beautiful face against him he paused. There was twilight enough to let him see something of its expression, and he shuddered. But he felt there was no escape, and once more he gave way to his feelings. Ada did not speak. She was stunned, horrified. Suddenly she exclaimed: "It's all m) fault," and throwing him off ran to the house. Ada burst into the room when she heard het sister talking, and called her out. Alice followed her to the kitchen. - - -

-- - "Don't blame him!" cried Ada, excitedly. "It's all my fault." This behaviour helped to calm Alice. She was herself collected in a moment, and did all she could to soothe her sister. But Ada was pal 9 and tremblina.

div.head: Br ALGERNON GISSING,
div.p: Br ALGERNON GISSING,
Author of "A Secret of the North Sea," "The Keys of the House," "The Scholar of Rygate," "One of the Flock," "Joel's Defeat," &e.

It was at the Cattle Show that the thing happened, and all the world was changed fox Alice. Love was a serious matter to her, so that although she was twenty-four this was the first time she had given any encouragement to flattering attentions. But Robert was so different from anyone she had ever met. She had even confessed to herself scores of times before his confession that if only he would deign to look at her how altered all her life would become. And now it had really happened! Just because no mercenary aim had ever entered into her thoughts of love this great prize seemed to have come to her. Strong as she had felt before, she could now face the world with double vigour. The next day she returned to work with a fresh lightness of heart. So commonplace a thing as dates had not yet been mention'ed between the lovers, for in their first glow they had lost all knowledge of time. But all Robert's remarks had pointed to their home as being a thing of the close future, if not actually existing now. Alice knew no cause for delay. Their acquaint- ance was not new, and for the last year she had taken opportunities enough of making up her mind. It was now JulY.,. Perhaps by harvest! Alice was country born, and still always thought of time with reference to these natural seasons. All that day she thought of haiNest, going 1 through in her mind every detail of that time on her father's farm. As she went home in the evening, though, she found that this had made her sad. Could it possibly be four years ago! She had left home in anger, and now it seemed impossible that she had never been back to make it up. Except for a few letters to her sister, she had not even communicated with home. Even these letters had lately ceased, for she and Ada had never been great friends. But, then, it was not all her fault. Her father quarrelled with everybody, and he would not understand. How was it possible-- Oddly enough these very reflections were suddenly interrupted by an unexpected visit from her brother. She at once felt strange with him. But he bluntly told her all about the old home. She did not like the news he gave her, still less the manner in which it was told. "If everything is going wrong," said she to him, "why-do you leave father to fight it oat alone? On a farm-- "That's a fine thing for you to ask, he pointedly answered. "You took care to leave in good time. I'm going to try my luck in the town too." The interview was not successful, and did not last long. But Alice thought about it, and saw that what he said was true. She was the eldest of the family. Ought she not to have taken her dead mother's place? Her father going to be ruined! Why had she never thought of it before? With this question the thrill of her own successful love returned to her, and she could only think it was this that had changed her point of view. The fields, the farmyard, and her father, all appeared different. She at once wrote a long letter to Robert, and he wrote back the next day making an appointment to meet her. After 1 that Alice wrote once more to her, sister, and the answer she got added to her trouble. It was not that the information was more alarming—of that little or nothing was given—but the tone of Ada's letter was reckless, heartless. Then Sunday came, and she talked it all out with Robert— except about Ada's letter. Alice was ashamed of this, and was not willing to betray it to her lover. In another week would come Alice's fortnight's holiday, and they both agreed she had better spend it .at home, to see how the land lay,eneeand moret o eg ee i f wrote a anything htni n gh ecould b rsister, done.fixi So once theo day and also a spot at which they could meet to talk things over before going to the house. On the top of a steep, green bank, rising abruptly behind the village church, was an old camp, the mound in the centre of the entrench- ments being just above the level of the cock on the steeple. After walking from the station it was here Alice sat down according to her arrange- ment. Harebells, wild thyme, and bedstraw bloomed amongst the grass, and in front spread a wide vale of quiet and deserted fields. Over this the young woman was gazing. Oh, how quiet it was! A couple of rooks, coming to explore the grass, turned off abruptly on seeing the figure, and paused cautiously on the top of a tree. One croaked inquiringly. But at another sound both flew off. Ada approached singing as she came over the downs behind and carelessly threw herself to the ground. Alice looked at her, for she had hardly expected this. Neither spoke. The eyes of both then went to the vale, settling on a white trail of steam from a passing train which was burrow- ing its way amongst the trees across the land- scape. That was the sight that first took Alice from home. Again the girls looked at each other. "Well ? " said Alice. "Yes, he says you may come. This was all their greeting. But Alice could not bear it. She turned to her sister, and, dis- regarding all the coldness which even she herself felt, wrapped Ada in a real embrace. "We can't go on like this to each other," she 'muttered, as she kissed her. But she felt there was no return. • So in silence they took the way behind them by which Ada had come. Here stretched the still more quiet uplands' leading only to remote villages and isolated farms. About a mile they went in this way, and both were relieved on reaching the house. • it was a grey, gaunt place, the silence only broken by the clamour of geese and some rooks in the beech trees. The two girls entered by the back, and Ada went in to an inner room to announce their arrival. "Then send her in," was the gruff reply Alice heard, and her colour deepened. Was she wishing she had not come? She pasied her sister abruptly, and on going into the parlour shut the door. _ _

"Well, maid, you can make nothing of it, then ? " exclaimed an elderly man who lay on a couch smoking. "Yes, father, I've done well enough." "Then what have you come back for ? " said he, with an angry and suspicious stare. "Because I heard that Walter had left you, and—and I thought I should be able to help." The man made a sound which announced plainly that such tales would not do for him. This was almost worse than the reception Ada had given her. Would it be possible to stay oul her fortnight in such an atmosphere as this? Bul she recovered herself. What else should she expect? This was like him. She could hardly anticipate a tender reception, but as prolonged absence had touched her own feelings, no doubl she expected it to have done something to his. She was too young immediately to consider that life had in the meantime gone with her as she wished, whilst with her father everything had been against him. • At last, feeling perhapo vaguely something of the kind, she took a stet towards the worn - out old sofa which she remembered so well and fixed her eyes on hef father's. ,

, "Why should you not believe me ? " she said, warmly. "I am older than when I went alsay. If we parted in anger we can surely now forget all that. I ought not to have left you; but I Will only a girl then and if I hadn't gone I (should never have learnt how to help you." The old farmer only stared in bewilderment, holding his pipe a few inches from his lips. This tone and feeling alike were strange to him, and not to be met in any familiar manner. He saw, as she said, that his daughter was older, and saw also much more than this. But he didn'i understand shrinking before one he had had or his knee as an infant. That, at any rate, will not natural, so he sucked his pipe rapidly unti: it made a thick smoke, and then he said, petulantly: "Well, well,we know all about that. Any way, you can get to work now. Words 'll make bui a poor plaster." And without anything furthei Alice did go and get to work immediately. But this brief interview with her father fore- shadowed much else that was in store. She foun everything so different from what she expected. The place and its atmosphere was entire') changed from what she had fancied it. Some oi the change no doubt was in herself, but not all. The Bill- Farm was actually altered. All knem
