CRICKET RESTORES SPEECH.
DUMB BOY'S STRANGE RECOVERY.

A dumb boy has been restored to full speech by a miracle performed amidst the excitement of a cricket match. Frederick Dennison, nine- teen years of age, son of a miner, went with some inmates of the 'lnvalid Children's Society to join a Boy Scouts' camp at, Harewood, near Leeds. A cricket match was in progress between the lads. Dennison, who was one of the players, was batting, and in his excitement to " steal " a run he found himself trying to shout. Much to his astonishment he thought he heard his own voice.

He said nothing to anyone, however, but con- tinued his play. When the match was over he, stole away to the woods in order to put to the test whether he could speak or not. To his amazement he discovered that his speech had been :restored to him. .The lad was frightened, however, that it would leave him again. For a long while he ,remained among the trees, talking to himself and almost crying ,with joy at the thought of how pleased his mother would be. Then he went back to camp. and, without letting anyone know, he wrote to his mother.

The next day Dennison surprised the Scout- master by suddenly speaking to There is no impediment in the lad's speech, and the voice seems to gain strength day by day. Dennison,, became dumb after a bad attack of influenza ten years ago. A doctor, however, predicted that he would probably re- vain his speech, even after n lapse of years. The prophecy had been fulfilled in dramatic circumstances.
FIRST NEW WHEAT

First samples of new wheat, barley and oats were shown at Peterborough Corn Exchange on Saturday. in fine dry condition, in direct con- trast to those of last year. The wheat came from the Huntingdonshire fen district and was rather green, but made 335. per quarter.

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
Ladies who are Skilled as
Inventors.
A VALUABLE DISCOVERY.

Cowes week this year was a very brilliant festival, cc were more visitors than usual. The programme was exceptionally interesting. The king's double victory in his famous. old yacht, Britannia, delighted his Majesty and the Queen; and 'Prince Henry of Prussia entertained many of his friends among the aristocracy, on board his yacht the Meteor. Prince Albert, Princess Mary, Princess Patricia of Connaught, and Princess Victoria of Schleswig-Holstein, made Oequent visits from the yacht to the shore, shopping in the town. So many yachts are sailed nowadays by women and girls, or by capable men directed by them, and many prizes were won by ladies. Miss Gertrude Eadie, whose father is a well- known yachtsman, has won no fewer than fifteen races this year with her yacht, which she sails herself..

div.head: WOMAN'S INVENTION
div.p: A WOMAN'S INVENTION

Women are so often charged with laCk of inventive genius that it is A pleasure to record the suecess of Mrs. Ernest ,Hart's discovery of a method of waterproofing, which will have -A far-reaching effect on many trades and indus- tries. Tailored goods, aero fabrics, soldiers' clothing, tents, rope and ship's cables are, by Mrs. Hart's process, rendered impervious to damp or water 4 and by its means the daintiest fabrics of gossamer texture can be simultane- ously colOUred, waterproofed and rendered non-inflammable. For clothing, rubber is not used, cmisequently nci weight is add6cl during thd process , of waterproofing, and .• ladies' Mackintoshes that will stand the heaviest down- pour will not weigh more than, eight , ounces. Already big orders have been placed by the Admiralty, by railway companies and by shoe and other manufacturers with the firm who are carrying out the invention, wfaich Promises to be much more successful than any which has preceded it.
ME LACE BLOUSE

With many of the autumn tailored suits, blouses of coarse lace are being prepared; in fact, it would seem that the lace blouse will be very much in evidence again in the coming season. Light dainty laces are used also over slips, whilst the blouse trait repeats the colour- ing of the suit with which it is worn, is equally favoured. Crepe de chine, plain and embroid- ered, will be seen for the more expensive and the smartest of these garments. Silk tulle is often combined with crepe de chine to form chemisette and sleeves. Shirts are made in the richest" and heaviest fabrics. They have draped shoulders, and tile newest shapes are crossed over in front. There is no trimming, beyond buttons, the richness of the material being suited to a severity oi style. Many sumi 'mer dresses have a blouse "effect at the back,' that is, they are given the suggestion of fulness, without superfluity, and the ease characteristic of this season's fashions skirt and corsage; both fit well—the latter almost closely,- but as the material of which these frocks are made is soft, clinging and very thin, the fulness is not very noticeable.

div.head: SLEEVES AND, CORSAGES
div.p: SLEEVES AND, CORSAGES

Never was there greater diversity in sleeves than at present, for no two gowns have sleeves alike, yet there is nothing that can .be charac- terised as actually new. Designers appear to have gone to eyery period for inspiration, and often, combine two quite opposite styles in one example. :No sleeves are large, .but this part of a dress presents difficulties on account of its complexity. The. Riinons is said to have gone out,, but it is. still Very. much in evidence, although Persian. and Turkish styles have in- fluenced this seasons fashions in sleeves. It is said that Sleeveless gowns for evening wear will he revived. The shoulders of the corsage will be cut higher, and jewelled bands take the place of sleeves. Many of the low-cut corsages are triangular in shape, not square. Where the bodice is sleeveless, a kind- of mantle of some filmy fabric is fastened with a jewel to the back of the dress, and brought over the top part of the arms, for which it provides a slight coVering.

div.head: STOCKINGS.
div.p: STOCKINGS.

Novelties in the world of fashion make their appearance regularly at this tithe of year, and the stocking has come in for more than usual attention just now, probably• on account of the craze for dancing. • which has seized society this season. The ribbon used with the dancing shoe in place of the old-fashioned sandal, was not altogether satisfactory, for it slipped and fell over the ankles, tfie effect being far from neat. To obviate an untidy appearance,' a laced silk stocking has been designed that is cut open at the outer side, and laced with a con- trasting coloured silk lace., The edges of the opening are embroidered with eyelet holes, through which' tile lace passes. . Button holes, however, have been found to be an improve- ment, and to more effectually prevent the slip- ping of the ribbons which can be passed through them, and kept exactly and firmly in their place..

div.head: TANGO AND OTHER DANCES.
div.p: THE TANGO AND OTHER DANCES.

The popularity of the Argentine Tango shows no sign of abatement, and since teachers of the art have modified an re-arranged it, they claim that it is graceful and pretty, and suited to 'Londoners as well as Parisians, who have discarded the •waltz and the Boston in its faVour. There will be in the coming autumn season. exhibitions of tango dancing, tango luncheons; -teas and dances of an inforthal nature. Dancing is of more widespread inter- est. than ever, and in arranging for the measures in "'Joseph and his Brethren," which Sir Herbert Tree is producing in September, the dances have been placed under the mari- ("gement of Mr. 'Edouard Spinosa, who has made a special study of Biblical dances that played so prominent a part in the religious ritual and history of the Hebrew nation. Miriam's dance may still be witnessed in Arabia, the dancers improvising movements and steps suggested by the mood of the Moment. There are a number Of local dances of great antiquity in Britain, notably in the Midlands-and in Cornwall, and religious dances are still executed on certain saints' days' in many Boman Catholic countries.

div.head: nonAL DECORATIONS
div.p: nonAL DECORATIONS

Whilst ballrooms have not been so lavishly decorated .as in some previous seasons, floral embellishments for the table have been more profuse and costly than ever before. Houses are this year adorned with tall graceful shrubs. on the steps or in the entrance halls. Grape vines also, in tubs, are in some instances used to form an archway over the front door. Orange trees in tubs form another favourite decoration. Quite a society fad are the clipped box. tree, in all kinds of 'fantastic forms. Lawns are studied with peacocks, ducks, rab- bits, cocks and hells, .of box trees; anti some- times even tables and chairs are contrived from the same shrub. Table decorations of dyed immortelles are also deservedly popular this secason, and will be still more so next winter, when flowers will be more expensive.
DEATH OF LEEDS PROFESSOR. Professor P. H. M. Du Gilion. for some time mist Professor of French Literature 'nt the University of Leeds, died at Grange-over-Sands.
GERMAN GIRLS' 20 MILES, A DAY. German girl guides- who have been on a walk- ing tour in England, covering 20 miles each day, for three weeks, arrived at Dover on Saturday.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
A MILITARY MEETING.

Some years ago the athletic sports, held on the Parade Ground of the local Garrison, was a much anticipated fixture, which provided keen sports and an enjoyable afternoon for the Garrison.and their .friends, so the revival, which is fixed to he held on the Recreqtion Ground on Thursday afternoon next, is deserving of note. The programme—timed to start at 2.15 p.m. and finish at 6.15 p.m.—includes running, jumping, tug-of-war, bayonet fighting, 8.:,c.; altogether 17 events. No. 7 is an inter-depot relay race (one officer, one colour-sergeant or sergeant, one cor- poral, and one private, each to run 200 yards). No. 10, timed to start at 4.30 p.m., .is an amateur half-mile race, open to Warrington (NX.A.:A. permit applied for). No. 13, bayonet fighting by company teams, under a leader, six men per team. No. 14, tug-of-war, by inter-company teams of 10 a-side. No. 15 is a novel race by the bands, who also have a good musical .programme to get through; the other items are sufficiently varied to suit all classes, and the one thing most wished for is fine weather.

div.head: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS-COUNTRY RUNNING.

The legislative season for this sport will soon be round, and it behoves all interested to look up the rules, particularly those relating to the National Cross-Country Union, as these will become, automatically, the basis for regulations of the various governing bodies. The local club had three men running Inter- national for England against France, Sic., last season, and if any youth aspires to similar hon- ours, he should communicate at once with Mr. C. Berry, 9, Bedford-street, Stockton Heath. Ambitious novices are just the lads he wants to • hear from now.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 16, 1913.
130 W LING.
Rylands' Win the "Finlayson " Cup. A STIFF ENCOUNTER.
It was only by six points that the Rylands' No. 1 team captured the " Fiulayson " Cup from St. Helens Cable No. 1 team in the Works Bowling Final, on the Horse and Jockey green, on Saturday.

The rain fell heavily in the morning, but the afternoon came fine and warm. The green was in excellent condition, and had been consider- ably freshened up by the morning's rain, and was in no way "sticky."

Fifty teams have competed for the cup, and the Rylands' combination are deserving of every congratulation for winning the much-coveted trophy in such a large competition. Members of both teams played exceedingly good bowls, and some exciting ends were witnessed by the large number of spectators who had assembled.

• W. Carrington (Cable) made the most of a five-point handicap against J. Gleave (scratch), and came very near to winning. Gleave had slightly the better of matters in the early stages, and at ,the 13th end he led 14-10. It was-here that Carrington caused the hopes of the Cable men to rise, for with two singles and a double he peeled with the " wireman." Gleave, how- ever, managed to record the winning single on the next length.
W. Roughley (1), Rylands' skipper, received a trouncing at the hands of T. Tweedle (4). The Cable man took every chance, and ran to 13-4 at the 11th end, and eventually won by 15-6.

• 11. Langley (2), Rylands', had to fight hard to beat C. Follows (5), Cable. Although leading ,12-8 at the 10th end, Langley's position was in no way Secure, for the Cable man came on in -fine style, and eventually peeled with 14 at the 'l7th end. One felt rather sorry that he did not .land his next wood; but Langley. seized the opportunity and went home with a single.

In the last game, T. Humphries (1), R.yl,ap.ds', pulled up wonderfully against I. Harrison's handicap of five. Both players bovfled magnifi- cently and at the 14th end Harrison was only 10-11 in arrear. Humphries made a great effort, and with two singles and a double gained a five points' -win for his side.
A report of the whole proceedings appears in another column.
The rain of last. Saturday interfered with the annual handicap of the Warrington Liberal Association, and the games arranged for the 9th will be played, as arranged in our last issue, on August 23rd.

The return game in the Warrington and Dis- trict Association's Club Championship final will be played on the Cemetery Hotel green on Saturday next. The Conservatives have 58 points to their credit, but the Cemetery men will no doubt have little difficulty in greatly diminishing, if not totally wiping out, this majority. The Individual Merit Competition in connection with the association will be played on August 23rd. 30th and September 6th, at the Cemetery Hotel.
The annual handican in connection with the Works Association will be commenced to-day. We gave the draw for the first round last week.
" THUMB BI A S."

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT ASSOCIATION. Final Game in the Club Championship.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT ASSOCIATION. Final Game in the Club Championship.

DATE DECIDED. The return game. between the _ Senior Con- servative and the Cemetery Hotel teams, in the final for the Warrington and District Associa- ,gon Club Championship, will be played at the Winetery Hotel on August 23rd. This decision was arrived at after considerable discuSsion at Meeting Of the Association in the Pelican IWO, on Tuesday evening. The first- game between the finalists,. which was played on the Sankey-street green, resulted in the Conserva- titres winning: by 58 points.. On account -of the date clashing -with • the Individual. Merit Competition, it has been decided to avert any difficulties by ordering the first set of bowlers in the Club Championship to be in readiness for actual -Play at two o'clock, practice being allowed from 1.45.
The draw for the Individual Merit Competi- tion takes place on Wednesday next.

div.head: BAKERS AT BOWLS.
div.p: BAKERS AT BOWLS.
Interesting Prize Distribution.

The distribution of prizes in connection with the Warrington bakers' bowling mgin took place at the Blue Bell Inn, Horsemarket-street, on Saturday. In the absence of „Mr. C. E. Toft, Mr. Grealy presided, and the members spent a most enjoyable social evening. The Chairman said that on the day of the main they had a most interesting and delight- ful time. Not only did the members enjoy themselves, but the ladies' main was thoroughly appreciated by the wives of members, who showed that they were no mere' tyrOs in the art of bowling. The drive to Hoo Green was also a delightful experience, and one good thing was that the weather wat splendid for the occasion, The chief prize-winners were :—Ladies: Mrs. Cox; 2, Mrs. Woodcock. Members: 1, J. Cox, cup and medal; 2, A. Morrison; 3, B. Broadhurst; Ist consolation, W. Moores; and 25 others.

A capital programme of songs and music was contributed tO by Miss Eaton (who greatly pleased with ragtime numbers), Mrs. Cox, Miss F. Eaton, and Messrs. Cox and Barnes, with Mrs. Cox- as accompanist. The donors, .the artistes, the committee and the chairman were heartily 'thanked for Hwir services.

div.head: BOWLING FINAL. Exciting Contest and Fine Win
div.p: THE BOWLING FINAL. Exciting Contest and Fine Win
by Rylands'.
A SIX POINTS VICTORY.

It is doubtful if the final for the "Finlayson" Cup, of -the Warrington -Works. Amateur, Bowl- ing Association, ever .produced sue!): a fine game, so many exciting incidents, and such a close finish as that played on the splendid green at the Horse and Jockey, Winwick-road, Warrington, on Saturday. There was a croWd of nearly 2,000 specta- tors, anct their attention was kept on the strain from start to finish. When the last four sets took the green the game was anybody's, the respective totals then standing at uti all. Both Bylands' and St. Helens Cable players put every ounce in, but Bylands' won by six points.

It was amidst intense excitement that the last batch played, and the eagerness of the Spectators infected the players, who, in their exuberance, persistently infringed the "no running" regulation, and for that offence were frequently cautioned. When eleven couples had played, •Ilylands' only led by one point. T. Humphreys, however, brought in five more leading points, and gave victory to Bylandst. The green was _somewhat stiff On account of

the which just cleared off as the games commenced, and this rather upset the calcula- tions. of both sides, who, during the past few weeks, had javcome accustomed to dry, fiery lengths. Periraps the " stickiness " was a bit of a handicap, Mit it affected both sides equally. _llylands' won a •creditable victory, the scores being: By/ands', • 151; -Cable, 145. .The .indi- vidual totals were :

div.head: , THE GUP rKESENTED. Some Interesting Speeches.
div.p: , THE GUP rKESENTED. Some Interesting Speeches.
The victors received a most enthusiastic re- ception when their captains Mr. Mi. Houghley, stoou lorth to. receivethehanusonie cup at tue
Lands of Mrs. W. Webster. By way of_initia7

tion, Mr. .1. Willetts intimated the result, and congratulated both sides upon the tine games played and the sportsmanship each player had displayed. Mr. \V. PATRICK submitted apologies for ab- sence, the list including the name of the Mayor, and he thought that the final had passed oft excellently. Capt. G. B. CROSFIELD (president of the association), in asking Mrs. Webster to pre- sent the prizes, congratulated the teams upon the splendid match they had played. It was certainly exciting, and if they kept up such level-balanced play in the future the officials would • have to get a more drastic method of handicapping. They would have to make the players bowl blindfolded or standing on their heads. (Laughter.) Playing blindfolded might not be so difficult, as it seemed. He had heard of an army officer, who lost his sight in the Boer War, who played golf. The ball . was placed on the tee, his club was placed in front of it, and the blind man played. A caddie guided him in the direction of the hole by ring- ing a bell. If they blindfolded bowlers the)? could have a bell rung over the jack. (Laugh- ter.)
The present competition had _ been remark:
... able in that out of the 49 matches played, 16 had been won by as small a number as ten points.. . For the . annual handicap - they -had 660 entries against 600 last year.
THE CAPTMN'S SPEECH.
Mrs. Webster then presented tne cup to

- Wiiot 111 reply-, said lie was tile prollauSt IlOili lb V.04311414t01.1 that. :day, because -ins- team had -Won We cliampionsinp, and lie hoped they would also be the winners ul the Lancashire championship. (Applause.) He tnought bowling was an excellent recrea- tion lor Workers. it lurnished.: them with a 'quiet and pleasant time after their day's work, and greater interest in tne pastime Should be- assiduously encouraged. (Applause.) Captain SEYNIOUR, of the 'Cable team, in acknowledging the presentation. of watches, said he felt himself the most disappointed man in Warrington—(laughter)—as the Cable team came with every hope of winning, but they did not begrudge Hyiands' their victory. He agreed With Mr. Boughley about the excellence oi bowling as a worker's recreation, and he thought Mat if the management of firms took _ _

an interest in the men, and followed them in their recreations, the • men would reciprocate it, and they would be better at work, as well as at sport. (Applause.) Mr. J. WILLErr, in proposing thanks to -Mrs. Webster and to Captain Crosfield, remarked that Capt. Crosfield had been deeply interested in the association since its formation.

Mr. KNOTT, a member of [Viands' club, sec- onded, and said they were pleased to have won the cup, and he heartily congratulated his club ,on the fine match they played. lie hoped the runners-up would have better luck next time, provided [Viands' were not in it. (Laughter and applause.)

div.head: MB. WEBSTER REPLIES
div.p: MB. WEBSTER REPLIES

Mr. NV._ WEBSTER replied on behalf of his wife. He expressed pleasure at witnessing such a splendid game. He had seen many of the finals since- 1903, but, he had never seen a closer game than the final just decided, and he never saw better .sportsmanship displayed. Captain CROSFIELD moved a vote of thanks to the secretory and other officials .of the association. He knew and, appreciated the great amount Of work Mr. Patrick did for the. association. He gave a great amount of time the matter, and. all bowlers in the district were indebted to him. (A Voice: "About time he had a benefit," and applause.) Mrs; PATRICK said be was pleased to do- the work without any recompense, and so • long as he did his duty well' he was perfectly satis- fied. In 'competitions of that description, hOw- 'ever, the officials were always open, to critic- ism. , If that criticism was fair and-honest they did not object to it, but when it was not fair nor just, it was very heartbreaking to the offi- cials running the show. They trad a:hard task ,to successfully run the compdition, and he. aske,l not to 'be unfairly criticised. (Hear, hear.)
AFTER TEA SPEECHES,

After lett had been partaken of by the com- mittee and others, several, toasts were pro- posed, including that Of the winners and run- ners-up. Mr. Seymour (Cable) said • that although defeated; the Cable players had not been disgraced. Mr. PATRICK, replying to a toast of his health, spoke of the future of the association, and said he was' of the opinion that as long as the association was conducted on the present lines they would ,not come to the end of their tether. The working classes of the town, he said that without fear of contradiction, were rallying rOund the assocation with greater interest,- for the reason .that they knew each man had a chance of winning his own particular game. A. matter which would have to be considered was the fact that the association had grown so enormously that it ,wag an utter impossibility to get a competition through in one season, and at the same time to do full.justice.to the players. ' The work which had to •be done. was exceed- ingly heavy. It meant that the members had to sacrifice every Saturday afternoon through- out the bowling season, when they ought to be able to engage in 'recreation on • their own account. That Was a matter the public of Warrington would have to take into considera- tion, and' a meeting for the purpose would be held during the winter. This was a WOrking meres association, from the Chairman down to the humble secretary. All of them workei?trd fora living, and they sacrificed their evenings for the benefit of others, and he could assure his hearers that that was no slight task. Still when praise was bestowed' on the members of the committee, as was done from time to tune, they felt amply repaid for their labours.

div.head: CYCLIST'S NOTE – BOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLIST'S NOTE - BOOK.
Some Thoughts on Accidents, their Cause
and Means of Prevention.
USE OF THE BRAKE. (BY SILVER-STREET.")

Out of the shower of paragraphs that has tumbled on the heads of newspaper editors dur- ing the holidays, all dealing with accidents, fatal and otherwise, one cannot help feeling that the cyclist is included much too often. I was nearly saying "the cycle is responsible for much too many.," but that is not so. The aeroplane is so young and so little understood tha, we :ut- most expect to hear of one or two being killed— there is no middle. course there—eyery Week. Those who run auto cycles or cars have :Jr' enormous amount to learn yet before [nose niachines are thoroughly understood, and the _

most fertile source of acCident is the belief that it can be pulled up in "its own length." No car in the world, if it can skid at all, can be so controlled as to come to a dead-stop in twenty or thirty yards from a speed of twenty miles an hour, and that is where the mistake of a speed limit comes • in. A driver who dares to put others' lives in danger ought to be judged as cyclists, and drivers of traps, &c., have always been judged, as to whether he is "driving to the public danger," and not according to a fixed number of miles per hour, a thing most difficult to prove. • Forty miles an hour is not dangerous on the long, straight roads of East and North Yorkshire, .or of rural Warwickshire, but ten miles is far too fast in any main street of War- rington in the day time. It is the Skidding that works the mischief. .1 would like to speak of some particular cases, the accounts of which I have cut from the papers these holidays, but there "the incident is closed," with the 'inquest and the funeral.

But while motorists rely too much .on their brakes, cyclists, and especially girls, seem to forget they have any, or what. they are for. On sOme machirieS the lever is-about. four inches below the . handle-bar. Query : 'Why? And what .good is it in: an emergency? A vastlitun; her of niachines are fitted with Pedal brakes, and :unless a good hand-brake is ready, too, the first is little use in an emergency. - The natural im- pulse, when one sees danger, is not to kick one's toes, or tread water, so to speak, but to clench one's fists, and so the proper place for a brake lever is in the fingers. Some time ago I was riding with a party; one girl passed me on my left as we came down a hill, shouting "Mind !" instead of using her pedal brake. In front was

a bassinette, its contents, a lady wheeling it,and another lady, and how the cavalcade was safely avoided by this young lady charging down at ever-increasing pace, I don't know. I managed to say, "Use your brakes," and she remem- bered to kick her pedal brake into action, just as she grazed the right arm of one of the bassinette ladies, and so prevented any more scenes. priother common source of disaster is that cyclist allow their brake blocks to wear away before having them renewed. A hammer, screwdriver, and, • maybe, a knife, are all that is wanted to tit a new pair, the screwdriver to prise the old block out, the knife to pare the new one down till it ,fits, and the hammer to knock it home. And a spare pair of blocks ought always to be ready in the repair box. I Was caught napping myself by that very neglect on Whit-Monday. Running down to Preston Brook Station, I could see nothing in the way, except a motor coming over the railway bridge But when I got on the canal bridge, to my dis- may I found the motor was stretched all across the road, in the act of turning round. I crammed both brakes on, and then re-discov- ered what I had known • for several days—that the blocks would hardly act, they were so badly worn. So, as Iliad no wish to smash the car to smithereens by charging into it, I ran into the goods -yard gate. I managed to leap off before the -crash, but the rebound of the pneu- matic tyre sent the sharp edge of the right pedal into my left shin, and cut it to the bone. Next day I had new blocks puk in the brakes, and had so much LO pay for straightening the Zorks, and it Served inc right. While on that topic', May. I: say that .when in. cdnipany, a cyclist who sees something -approaching ought not to. try to turn sideways, that is, to the left, for it will endanger the per- •son-.be-is riding- with,'oi else hiMself... -His fingers, always on the little brake Lever, ought to squeeze it lightly, and, as he rings his bell, he slides to the rear without effort, and can then avoid the approaching Vehicle. If any of the party is behind him, he will hear his bell, and put his own brake on. Many nasty spills can be avoided by 'knowing that rule of club- riding. •

div.head: MARCH OF PROGRESS
div.p: THE MARCH OF PROGRESS
I came across this paragraph in the " C.T.C, Gazette ".of 1903 :

• 413ENIGHTED MAIIWICKSHIRE.—According to th 6 Herald,' the Warwickshire Chamber of Agriculture is in favour of a small tax on cycles and motor ears, and also of the compulsory displaying of a number by all vehicles driven at a greater speed than five miles an . hour! Bucolic Warwick should try again r _
One wonders if the then- editor of the
" Gazette " considers all England benighted and bucolic, now that The worst offenders are coni- .pelled to carry their own identification, and taxed—not lightly, either.

div.head: CLUB BUNS
div.p: CLUB BUNS

There were none on Saturday. Only the spout's and gutters were -running, but a good many folks were glad of a "nice sup o' rain." By-the-bye, if a Lancashire man says "this can runs" to anyone in the South of England, they laugh consumedly. • "It runs out" is what he should say, according to the Oxford man, who thinks, of course, that his way of putting it makes everything so much clearer. (Now, Mr. Editor, that isn't a "Cycling Note," but iLonly takes a line or two.) Lamp time to-night, 8.38. Next Saturday, 8.24..

div.head: SHARP RIOTING IN CANAbA
div.p: SHARP RIOTING IN CANAbA

Serious rioting took place in the .Vancouver Island mining centres, where. 3,000 men have been on strike- during the last three months. After a picketing demonstration at Nanaimo, the strikers attacked the police, • injuring several of them, one being seriously hurt„ Houses were also dama±;ed h missiles. Special police were hurried to the scene, and a force of the military may be necessary. to put down the outbreak. -

The ashes of Mr. William -Henry Brereton Evans, the Oxford cricketer and a member of the Soudan Civil Service, who perished with Colonel Cody, were buried at Tadley Church- yard, Hampshire, on .Wednesday, enclosed in a casket.

div.head: FOOTBALL COMING.
div.p: FOOTBALL COMING.
A Chat about the Warrington Team and their Future Prospects. BIG THINGS ANTICIPATED.'

(BY "SCRUM.") ... The Warrington Northern Union Rugby Foot- ball Club, who came so near to proving holders L_ the Northern Union Cup _last season, are tl..Licipating a successful season, and are rapidly tting their house in order, to be ready for a 1,,,0d set-off on September 6th.

The ground at Wilderspool is in splendid con- dition, the rain of the last few days having freshened it up considerably_ Training com- menced on Monday, there being a good turn out of players, and spectators were plentiful and much interested in, the preliminary bouts.

On Wednesday night the players indulged in punting and running, to get the stiffness out of their joints. Another practice will take place to-day at 3.30, and a small charge will be made for admittance. All last season's players are available, and the team will be considerably strengthened by the inclusion of Ruddick and Davis, late of Coventry. \

The former is, a capital half-back, and ,the latter has earned a'reputation as a' clever three- quarter. The excellent, performance the team gave in the final last season will, no doubt, have a good effect on the membership. Many appli- cations from players have been received,, and trials vill be extended to them during the next two weeks.

div.head: BRADSHAW AS CAPTAIN.
div.p: BRADSHAW AS CAPTAIN.
All the members will no doubt be glad to hear that Bert Bradshaw has been appointed captain of the first team.
Dickenson's lenefit will take place on October ith, the committee having decided to give the .dayer the rnatch against st. Helens.
, The • first match will be against Leigh, at home, on September 6tfi, and two days later Warrington Meet Huddersfield ,away.
Mr. Bradshaw, the hon. secretary, says that personally he thinks The team's prospects are exceedingly bright, and he is anxiously await- ing the opening game.

div.head: TRAINED IN A GOOD ,SCHOOL.
div.p: TRAINED IN A GOOD ,SCHOOL.

Davis, ffie new rnreequarter, is 25 years 'of age, is six feet high, and weighs 12st. 31b. He began to play Rugby football at the age of 10, on joining King Edward's Grammar Schools, Aston, .Birmingham. He then recolved an injury in the lower region of the chest, and has not played in the pack since that time.

• During three seasons with Coventry he fias played against every team at present in the Northern Union League. He is a splendid player, and hopes to play as well for Warring- ton as he did against them.
He has turned out against Warrington on four occasions, the results being a draw, a win, and two losses.

div.head: RUDDICK TO RE-APPEAR.
div.p: RUDDICK TO RE-APPEAR.
It will be remembered that Ruddick played at [all-back against Barrow at the latter end of
last season.- He created a favourable impres- sion, for he was speedy and resourceful, and not only scored twice on his own account., but frequently initiated strong attacking move- ments.
We hope to see him do big things this season.
Everything tends to Warrington having an excellent team, and it is expected that a large number will attend the practice to-day to weigh up the players'. capabilities.

With practice we should possess a team quite capable of holding its own with any in the Northern Union. The players have just. the touch -of enthusiasm and eagerness which so frequently. lead to victory.
[ALL lituHTS REsEit v ED.]

div.head: HOW TO MAKE CONVERSATION.
div.p: HOW TO MAKE CONVERSATION.

One of the chief causes of intemperance in this country is our inability to engage in.ra- tional talk. A British working man goes into a public-house to drink; a French working man goes into a café merely as an excuse for leisurely conversation, and he takes his wife and daughter with him. A young Finnish lady, who had spent six months in this coun- try once told the writer that she found us un- utterably dull and expressed the belief that the reason why we played cards so. much was because we were so badly educated that when we tried to converse with each other we ra- pidly reduced, one another to a state of corn- plete boredom. There is a good deal of truth in this. We meet a man in the train, and begin on the weather, reraark:ng "What beastly weather it .is!" and then we ge,t behind the news- paper. We indulge in such stupid re- marks as "Crossing. to-day ?", when we are in mid-channel on the way to Dover or Calais. We tell a story. backwards and refer to the hero of it as "Mr. What d'ye call him ?" - There was a time in England when brilli- ant conversat:on was the rule and not the ex- ception. Now, if a man indulges in "fine talk" we say he is an affected idiot and think he is "showing off." Many people are con- scious, even painfully conscious of their defi- ciencies in this respect, and often try to.avoid stsangers because they don't know what to talk about. At such places as bazaars, public meetings, and social gatherings of all sorts we fight shy ,of those lie do not know .inti- mately, and with old, friends we confine our illuminating reflections to the weather, our servants, and our treasured ailments.

div.head: VALUABLE ASSET
div.p: A VALUABLE ASSET

Now the art of pleasant conversation is a valuable asset both soc:ally and from a busi. ness point of view. The man or woman *ha is " interesting " is sought after at social functions, and he who can beguile his custom- ers or patrons with a pleasant flow of sensible talk will find money in the accomplishment. Silence is not golden, except when you want to go to sleep. .

"-What shill I talk about ?" is the first thought in a man's mind when he knows he his to meet those with whom he is not well acquainted. Common friends form a good basis for a be- ginning. The ' fact that both host and guest are friends of some third person .:s in itself a link, and, out of a chance remark about a third person there may result an animated discussion about his history, his habits, and the starting point for another train of thought or rminiscence and prove the ham- mer that breaks the social lice.

Common professions again are a good foun- dation on which to build, though there is here a danger of "talking top much shop."' Two lawyers or two doctors can always dis- cuss the latest developments in their profes- sion and two grocers the trend of prices or the conclaion of •business. A more fruitful source of animated inter- change of ideas is to be found in common hobbies or interests. Whether it be golf or Wagner, photography or philosophy, poultry or cricket, there is a wide field to traverse and explore ly2fore its secrets have been all unravelled and its hidden spots explored. But you may hate nothing in common. You take a lady in to dinner who knows no one whom you know, who certainly does not fol- low your occupation, and whose favourite purAuit is playing golf, while yours is feeding chickens. She is an unknown quantity. The first thing to do is to discover in what suTi- ject she is interested, to set her going, znd let her talk. If you do not interrupt, exc+pt with an occasional question, she will consider you the most delightful company, for a good talker likes a good listener. If you can get no- thing out of such a person, then find an open- ing for your own subject, and, instead of in- dulging in vague generalities that lead no- where and pretty rapidly give out, go in for detail, not too much, and keep her so inter- eeted that she asks the ouestions and you do
the exp!aininz. If she ilas noThrog to, .taiir about, she will be glad if you have.
ENOWLE.,,uE REQUIRED.

Of course all this assumes that you are intelligent enough to be interested in some- thing or other. And porhap3 we ought to have sa.d at the outsat, that no man can be a good talker ualcss he knows something well. The more things you are interesed in, the more chances you have with a stranger. Mere interest, however, is not cuough—knowledge must be forthcoming. Someone asks you anent a recent play "Have you seen so and BO ? "
"Yes, last week." "And what do you think of it ?" "It's simply r:pping ?" "And ho did you like the chief actress ?"

"Awfully." - Well, the bottom w:11 fall out of any con- versation. if you can't do any better than that. ll'Vy is the play " r:pping," and why do you like that actress "awfully ?" You can't say, because you don't think. To dis- cuss batiks, music, art, the drama, or any- thing else you must possess the critical fac- ulty, either, to explain your own opinions or to seek the bas.s of those of other people. The reading 'of sound reviews and critiques for several mouths will make you familiar with the current jargon and cause you to ap- pear wiser than you are, which is not a bad aim in conversing with those who 'have no opportunity of finding you out. Don't put on an affected voice; speak na- turally. If your voice be unpleasant in tone and your accent marred by ugly provincial- isms, get rid of them by incessant practice. After a time you can, by careful attention, hear the difference between your own tones, and those you admire in well-bred, ,well-edu- cated folks. To hear this d:fference is the first step to ovtrcom.ing it. The voice, more than anything else, is an index of education and refinement.

div.head: MATTER OF PRACTICE.
div.p: A MATTER OF PRACTICE.

Religion and politics are dangerous sub- jects, unless you know the opinions of those to whom you are speaking. Controversial topics should usually be avoAed. If thrust upon you, it is well to remember that no one is aver converted at a dinner-table or ever _convinced by argument. Therefore it is not necessary to be serious to put on your armour to tiro battle for your chef:shed, notions. They are probably quite valueless. Current topics of a non-controversial character, a test match, the boat-race, the openins, of a new church, or a recent lecture are best. Only be- ware of introducing them so suddenly and dismissincr them so quickly that they won't last out. Glide gently into the matter, discuss it in full detail, and slide out of it and into the next thing it suggests without apparent effort. All this is a matter of practice and not easy. Good conversation is an art and needs an alert brain. It's no use thinking of suit- able topics and wise remarks when you get to bed. They must be available on demand, and if you are naturally slow-witted the greater need there is of practice. You can get this practice at home. Instead of grumbling st,t the cooking, reading your letters at table, or sitting in stony silence, take every opportunity of talking fluently, lucidly, and rogically. Your family will suf- fer in the process but other families will vote toil quite a success at a little gathering, that is, when you have become proficient. Put don't practise on strangers; they don't like it.

div.head: TRA.VEL EXPERIENCES.
div.p: TRA.VEL EXPERIENCES.

Travel experiences are invaluable if you travel. If you only sit on a sandy beach and listen to the tuggers, that won't heito verm much. But the churches you have seen, the festivals at which you have been present, the, queer foods you have eaten, the little inci- dents that you have experienced, all are of use at solte tine or other. But here again it is often a question of knowledge as to whe- ther what you have to say is worth anything. To say that "Notre „Dame at Paris is a fine church," is not a very brilliant refiectlon., Why is it fine? Can you compare it with your parish church or the nearest cathedral ?1 The life and soul of all prolonged conversa-, tion is detail, not wide sweeping, meaning- less -generalites. If you talk of books, outline the story, des-. cribe the characters, tell anecdotes of the au- thor. Facts are invaluable in starting a eon.. versation and this appnes to books, friends, society or matters of public importance. When you have _failed in everything else try the topic, of :yourself or, better still, get the other person to take up.the topic. As a rule you know more of th:s subject than yom do of any other, but just because it is never so interesting to other people as it is to your- self, don't touch it if you can help it. Still, I would rather it next a man in either train. or drawing-room who told me about himself than about nothing. Even if he be a fool r can be amused with his folly, and 7r he be a wise man I can learn something for my own, use and help. Repartee; badinage, and light humour are gifts, and are not to be acquired. The man whose repartee is forced is rude, not funny, and he who would be humorous without the natural talent for it is about as graceful as a waltzing elephant. for_

div.head: DEATH OF A WARRINGTON NOTABILITY.
div.p: DEATH OF A WARRINGTON NOTABILITY.
Old Lady Who Znew the Town Seventy Years Ago.

div.head: AN HISTORICAL HOUSE.
div.p: AN HISTORICAL HOUSE.

Throug4 the passing of Mrs. Kate Davies, of 6, Lyme-street, Warrington, the borough has lost a most interesting member of its com- munity. She was one of the links between-the quiet old days of George IV. and the present time of hustle and bustle. Mrs. Davies was the widow of the late Mr. William Davies, who, for a long period, carried on the business of coppersmith at King-street . and Lyme-street: She died on Saturday in her 89th year, mourned by many friends, who held, her in the highest esteem. Until the last few weeks she was a woman of remarkable physical and mental activity, and up to some three months ago was able to get about almost as spritely as a woman half her age. Born at Woodhouses, Alvanley, she came as a bride, nearly seventy years ago, to the house in which she died. It is interesting to recall that the house in Lyme-street has been in the ,occupation of the family for over 160 years, the late Mr. NVilliam Davies having been born there in 1814. His father occupied the same abode for many years before that. Since the passing of the Reform Act in 1832, the house

was not her habit to infer that they were the °lily good days, and to mourn that they had departed. As an intelligent woman she moved with the times, and °lien has she remarked that she thought life and travel in the twentieth century was decidedly an improvement upon the "good old days" in the earlier part 'of the nineteenth century. _

In Warrington,- Mrs. Davies lived to witness immense changes in divers directions. Seventy years ago she found it a comparatively small town, almost a little country place, where the agriculturists used to foregather to sell pro- duce and discuss the gopip of the day. She lived to -see it gain rank among the largest county boroughs in England. Streets she knew in the early days vanished or were altered out of recognition, trams came, motors came, other improvements were wrought until the old lady used to ask herself if she was not living in a world different from that she first had known.

div.head: KEPT TIIE LIBERAL FLAG FLYING.
div.p: KEPT TIIE LIBERAL FLAG FLYING.

A good old Whig was Mrs. Davies, end I have heard a good story of how she kept the Liberal flag flying in Warrington in the times when Toryism swefit, the land. The incident, oft narrated by Mrs. Davies, is on a pqrallel with the Eutonsville election; described in " Pickwick Papers," and the Irish. election scenes scenes narrated in 'Handy Andy," that rollick- ing volume of -Irish humour. An election was due, and, as it was previous to the Ballot Act, the Tory party in Warrington meant to prevent the Liberals from making any show whatever. They, in fulfilment of, their purpose, commandeered every public- house, halt; in fact, every place suitable for meetings. or for use as committee rooms. As Mr. Pickwick found it at Eatonsville, every hotel was "blue." This was a smart election trick, which would have delighted the heart of a Air. Perkins or a Murtrough Murphy, and it looked as if the Liberal " buff " would find no place of resort, Mrs. Davies came to the rescue in an unostentatious but thoroughly prattical way:

Mrs. Davies, and her esteemed husband, both true Liberals, even in the days when Liberalism was at a discount, decided to help the party to which they were attached. They surrendered their house for the purpose of committee rooms. The Tories woke bp one morning to discover that the `,` Buffs" had Actually secured a strong position right in the heart of the " Blue " citadel, and great was their surprise and chagrin. •

Such an incident was a worthy subject for the descriptive pen' of Dickens, and the old house in Lyme-street Should ever be remem- bered by Liberals as the place from whence flew the flag of Liberalism when all other places were "banged. bolted and barred" against it. If we have not now the lady- who participated in that stirring episode in our midst, the house still remains as a silent memento of the event. As I have said. Mrs. Davies was a remark- able woman, and her passing- leaves a gap which can never be filled, but she has' departed ripe in years, honoured and esteemed by a large body of Lancashire and Cheshire friends, who feel the deenest sympathy with the three sons andlikree daughters left: liehind to .mourn her departure.

div.head: INTERESTING EVENTS RECALLED.
div.p: INTERESTING EVENTS RECALLED.

It seems a great pity, writes a correspondent, that someone did not -preserve a record of the reminiscences of Mrs. Kate Davies, one of 7,71 e most interesting ladies Warrington ever knew. She possessed a plethora of information about Warrington of the past, and it has to be re- gretted that this was not gleaned and stored for the behoof of generations yet to come, who, naturally, will be eager to learn about their town in times as far back as the beginning of the nineteenth century. • George .IV. was king when our. late revered .friend was-born, and she had thus lived under five sovereigns, but the reign- of kings was nothing compared with the -great reign of in- dustry, commerce and natural enterprise she had the' privilege: of witnessing. When 'she came, a bride -of-.some 'eighteen years of age, to Warrington, stage coaches were the chief mode of travelling. Several of these plied daily from

Warrington to Manchester, Liverpool and other places, and a trip to the seaport or to Cotton- opolis \vas no easy journey in those distant days.

She saw the introduction of railways and watched with intense interest the development of the ironway. Mrs. Davies was still a. young women when Stephenson first ran his "puffing Billy," between Liverpool and Manchester, but it was some time after that date before she saw a train pass through Warrington. She recalled how excited and eager Warringtonians were to see the first of Me new-fangled trains.Wliat other marvels th 6 lady lived to see—telegraphy, telephony, wireless telegraphy and other inno- vations undreamt of in Mrs. Davies's early days. .She took an enlightened interest in these, and could talk about most of them intel- ligently. The deceased lady spent lier life in wonderful times, and she lived long enough to see the descendants of those,' who, in her girl- hood days, journeyed about in lumbering car- rier's carts, fly through the air in marvellous machines.
While she loved to talk of •the old days, it
